# Finiteness of an Isogeny Class via Equidistribution

**Authors:** Jit Wu Yap

## Abstract

In a very recent, beautiful paper, Junyi Xie and Ziquan Yang [9] gave a new proof of Faltings’ isogeny theorem over number fields by reducing to Tate’s theorem over finite fields. We show that the same ideas can be adapted to prove finiteness of an isogeny class over number fields from the finiteness of an isogeny class over finite fields. Hence we obtain a new proof of the Shafarevich conjecture over number fields. The proof in this paper was obtained through the use of GPT6 Astra Ultra.

## 1. Introduction

Recently, Junyi Xie and Ziquan Yang [9] gave a beautiful new proof of Faltings’ isogeny theorem [1] (also known as Tate’s conjecture) over number fields $K$ . The main new idea is a very clever use of Yuan’s equidistribution theorem on a non-archimedean place of good reduction [9, Proposition 4.2], giving a new way to algebraize $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)$ -equivariant homomorphisms on Tate modules.

The main aim of this short note is to show that this same new idea leads to a new short proof of the finiteness of isogeny classes.

#### Theorem 1.1.

Let $K$ be a number field and $A$ an abelian variety over $K$ . Then there are only finitely many abelian varieties $A^{\prime}$ over $K$ , up to $K$ -isomorphism, that are $K$ -isogeneous to $A$ .

As in Faltings’ proof of the Mordell conjecture [1], Theorem 1.1 implies the Shafarevich conjecture over number fields. This then implies the Mordell conjecture over number fields via Parshin’s trick. Hence we obtain a new proof of the Shafarevich conjecture and the Mordell conjecture.

Other than [9, Proposition 4.2], the proof uses a result of Rémond on isomorphism classes of abelian varieties over a general field $K$ . There has been an in depth study by Gaudron and Rémond [2] on such results, as part of their work in extending Masser–Wüstholz bounds [5] to various settings. It is an interesting question to ask whether it is possible to make [9] quantitative enough to obtain a new proof of Masser–Wüstholz type bounds.

Our proof uses the finiteness of an isogeny class of abelian varieties over a finite field [6, Corollary 13.13] to deduce the corresponding statement over number fields. In [9], Tate’s theorem over finite fields is used to deduce the Faltings’ isogeny theorem. This makes one wonder if there exists a direct proof of the Mordell conjecture along this lines, where one uses the fact that the Mordell conjecture is trivially true over finite fields as $C(\mathbb{F}_{q})$ is obviously finite in size.

In [9], the non-archimedean equidistribution result [9, Proposition 4.2] was used to lift endomorphisms on the special fiber to the generic fiber. Our way (or GPT’s way) of applying [9, Proposition 4.2] is different. We instead use it to show that infinitely many torsion points cannot reduce to an abelian subvariety $B_{0}$ on the special fiber, which is not liftable. More precisely, we have the following.

#### Proposition 1.2.

Let $A_{0}$ denote the special fiber of $A$ and let $B_{0}\subseteq A_{0}$ be an abelian subvariety such that no positive dimensional abelian subvariety $C\subseteq A$ reduces to a subvariety of $B_{0}$ . Let $T$ be a $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)$ -invariant set of prime-to- $p$ torsion points that reduces to $B_{0}$ . Then $T$ is finite.

We outline the strategy of the proof of Theorem 1.1 when $A$ is simple and $\operatorname{End}(A)=\mathbb{Z}$ . Given an isogeny $\pi:A\to B$ , let $H=\ker(\pi)$ . We aim to show that $B$ embeds into $A^{n}$ for some $n\geq 1$ , which would then prove finiteness of such $B$ ’s by a result of Rémond [8, Proposition 1.4]. Note that Rémond’s result just uses abstract properties of abelian varieties over a general field $K$ .

To do so, we view the situation as trying to map $A$ to $A^{n}$ with kernel containing $H$ . Such a map is given by $(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n})$ where $e_{i}\in\operatorname{End}(A)$ . Then the kernel is given by $\bigcap_{i=1}^{n}\ker(e_{i})$ . Hence given $H$ , we will define

$$ I_{H}=\{u\in\operatorname{End}(A)\mid H\subseteq\ker(u)\}\text{ and }\tilde{H}=\bigcap_{u\in I_{H}}\ker(u). $$

Then $A/\tilde{H}$ embeds into $A^{n}$ for some $n$ and $H\subseteq\tilde{H}$ . It suffices to show that $[\tilde{H}:H]$ is uniformly bounded independent of $H$ .

Now pick a place $v$ of good reduction where $k(v)$ has characteristic $p$ , and for simplicity we shall assume that $\gcd(|H|,p)=1$ . Then over the finite field $k(v)$ , bounding $[\tilde{H}:H]$ uniformly trivially follows from the finiteness of abelian varieties of a given dimension over a finite field. If we may lift endomorphisms of $\operatorname{End}(A_{0})$ to $\operatorname{End}(A)$ , then we may bound $[\tilde{H}:H]$ as prime-to- $p$ specialize injectively. However we certainly cannot always do this. We will instead use Proposition 1.2 to show that it suffices to look at endomorphisms who do lift.

For simplicity let’s assume that $\operatorname{End}(A_{0})$ has two generators, $1$ and $\tau$ . We consider the map $G_{0}:A_{0}^{2}\to A_{0}$ , given by $(x_{1},x_{2})\mapsto x_{1}+\tau x_{2}$ . Then $\ker(\Phi)=\{x_{1}=-\tau x_{2}\}$ which does not lift by assumption. Hence by Proposition 1.2, a $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)$ -set $H$ that reduces entire to $\ker(\Phi)$ must be uniformly bounded in size. We let $m$ annlihate all such sets $H$ . Let’s say $u\in\operatorname{End}(A_{0})$ satisfies $H_{0}\subseteq\ker(u)$ with $[\ker(u):H_{0}]$ giving us our uniform bound. We write $u=a+b\tau$ . Then if $x\in H$ reduces to $x_{0}\in H_{0}$ , we have

$$ ([a]x_{0},[b]x_{0})\in\ker(\Phi)\implies m([a]x_{0},[b]x_{0})=0\implies x\in\ker(m[a]). $$

If $a$ is non-zero, it suffices to take the endomorphism $m[a]$ and so $[\tilde{H}:H]$ is still uniformly bounded on the generic fiber as desired.

After coming across [9], the author asked GPT6 Astra Ultra if it was possible to use their ideas to obtain Theorem 1.1 and an outline of a proof was given relatively quickly. The first proof used ultrafilters and is similar to the strategy in [9]. The proof in this paper was obtained after asking the model to attempt using the ideas of Gaudron–Rémond [2] in its solution. ## 2. Finiteness of Isogeny Classes

We first state a slight strengthening of [9, Proposition 4.2] that we will use. In our version, we would like to allow $H$ to be any $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)$ -invariant set of prime-to- $p$ torsion points. In [9, Proposition 4.2], an $\ell$ -divisibility condition is imposed on $H$ . We show that this is essentially unnecessary.

#### Proposition 2.1.

Let $K$ be a number field and $A/K$ an abelian variety. Let $v$ be a finite place of $K$ such that $A$ has good reduction and let $p$ be the characteristic of the residue field at $v$ . Let $H$ be a $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)$ -invariant set of prime-to- $p$ torsion points and let $V$ be the Zariski closure of $H$ . Let $Z_{0}$ be a subvariety of the special fiber $\mathcal{A}_{v}/O_{K_{v}}$ such that $H$ all reduces to $Z_{0}$ . Then the reduction of $V$ is also contained in $Z_{0}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $X$ be the Zariski closure of $H$ . Then as $X$ has a Zariski dense set of torsion points, by the Manin–Mumford conjecture [7], we have $X=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}(a_{i}+C_{i})$ , where $a_{i}$ is a point and $C_{i}$ a connected abelian subvariety. We now apply the proof of [9, Proposition 4.2] to each $a_{i}+C_{i}$ , to obtain that the reduction of $a_{i}+C_{i}$ must be contained in $Z_{0}$ and hence the reduction of $X$ must be contained in $Z_{0}$ . ∎

We remark that the proof of [9, Proposition 4.2] relies on Yuan’s equidistribution theorem [10] of small points on non-archimedean places. Yuan’s theorem relies on the arithmetic Hilbert–Samuel and the arithmetic Siu’s inequality which are rather technical. We also invoke the Manin–Mumford conjecture in the proof of our extension. However Proposition 2.1 admits a relatively elementary proof using the Arakelov–Green functions of Looper [3] which does not use Yuan’s theorem nor the Manin–Mumford conjecture. The reader may see [4, Section 8] for more details.

We now begin our proof of Theorem 1.1. The outline of our proof is already given in the introduction. Let $A$ be an abelian variety over a number field $K$ and let $\pi:A\to B$ be an isogeny over $K$ . Then $B=A/H$ where $H$ is a finite $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)$ -invariant set. We aim to show that $B$ embeds into $A^{n}$ for some $n\geq 1$ . Then the isomorphism classes of $B$ ’s is finite by [8, Proposition 1.4], where we allow $n$ to vary. This proof uses abstract properties of abelian varieties over a field $K$ and nothing special about number fields.

We may view the problem of embedding $B\xhookrightarrow{}A^{n}$ as mapping $A\to A^{n}$ , with $H$ being contained in the kernel. Such a map is given by elements $e_{1},\ldots,e_{n}\in\operatorname{End}_{K}(A)$ such that $H\subseteq\cap_{i=1}^{n}\ker(e_{i})$ . We may thus define

$$ I_{H}=\{u\in\operatorname{End}_{K}(A)\mid H\subseteq\ker(u)\} $$

and set $\tilde{H}=\bigcap_{u\in I_{H}}\ker(u)$ . Then $\tilde{H}$ is $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)$ -invariant and $H\subseteq\tilde{H}$ . The aim is to bound the index $[\tilde{H}:H]$ uniformly, depending only on $A$ and $K$ .

In Xie–Yang’s paper, they obtain Faltings’ isogeny theorem by combining their algebraization theorem [9, Proposition 4.2] with Tate’s isogeny theorem over finite fields. Similarly over here, we will use the finiteness of an isogeny class over finite fields.

We now choose a place $v$ of $K$ with good reduction for $A$ . We let $H_{p^{\prime}},H_{p}$ be the prime-to- $p$ part and $p$ -primary part of $H$ respectively. We let $H_{p^{\prime},0}$ be the reduction of $H_{p^{\prime}}$ to the special fiber, so that $|H_{p^{\prime},0}|=|H_{p^{\prime}}|$ .

#### Proposition 2.2.

There exists an $f_{0}\in\operatorname{End}_{K}(A_{0})$ such that $H_{p^{\prime},0}\subseteq\ker(f_{0})$ , and $\ker(f_{0})/H_{p^{\prime},0}$ bounded independent of $H$ .

#### Proof.

There are only finitely many abelian varieties of a given dimension over a finite field [6, Corollary 13.13]. This follows from Zarhin’s trick [6, Theorem 13.12] and the finiteness statement for principally polarized abelian varieties [6, Theorem 11.2], where the latter is straightforward over finite fields.

Now $H_{p^{\prime},0}$ gives us an isogeny $\pi:A_{0}\to B$ with kernel $H_{p^{\prime},0}$ . On the other hand, we may find an isogeny $\pi^{\prime}:B\to A_{0}$ with degree bounded independent of $H$ . Taking $f_{0}=\pi^{\prime}\circ\pi:A_{0}\to A_{0}$ gives us the desired endomorphism. ∎

We now perform the analogue of constructing the morphism $G_{0}:A\to A^{2}$ in the introduction. Replacing $A$ up to isogeny, we may assume that

$$ A=\prod_{i=1}^{r}C_{i}^{n_{i}} $$

where $C_{i}$ is $K$ -simple and $C_{i},C_{j}$ are not $K$ -isogeneous to each other for $i\not=j$ . We let $A_{0}$ and $C_{i,0}$ denote the special fiber of $A$ and $C_{i}$ at $v$ .

We let $D_{j}=\operatorname{End}_{K}(C_{j})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Q}$ , which is a division algebra, and we let $W_{j}=\operatorname{Hom}(C_{j,0},A_{0})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Q}$ . Then $W_{j}$ is a right $D_{j}$ -module by $w_{j}\cdot d_{j}:=w_{j}\circ d_{j}$ and we may choose a $D_{j}$ -basis $g_{j,1},\ldots,g_{j,r_{j}}$ of $W_{j}$ , where $r_{j}=\dim_{D_{j}}W_{j}$ . By clearing denominators, we may assume that $g_{j,i}^{\prime}s$ are all integral.

We now define $X=\prod_{i=1}^{r}C_{i}^{r_{i}}$ and let $X_{0}$ denote the special fiber of $X$ . We define the homomorphisms on special fibers $G_{0}:X_{0}\to A_{0}$ where on each $C_{j}^{r_{j}}$ , we send

$$ (x_{1},\ldots,x_{r_{j}})\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^{r_{j}}g_{j,i}(x_{i}). $$

We have the following property.

#### Proposition 2.3.

There does not exist a positive dimensional abelian subvariety $C\subseteq X$ , defined over $K$ , such that $C_{0}\subseteq\ker G_{0}$ where $C_{0}$ is the reduction of $C$ .

#### Proof.

Since $C\subseteq X$ , there must exist some $C_{j}$ with a non-zero homomorphism $f:C_{j}\to C$ and we may consider $f:C_{j}\to C\xhookrightarrow{}X$ . Then as $C_{i},C_{j}$ are not isogeneous, $f$ maps $C_{j}$ to $C_{j}^{r_{j}}$ and we may write it as $(d_{1},\ldots,d_{r_{j}})$ for $d_{i}\in D_{j}$ . Since $C\subseteq\ker(G_{0})$ , we must have

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{r_{j}}g_{j,i}\circ d_{i}=0, $$

but this contradicts the linear independence of $g_{j,i}$ as desired. ∎

Let $k$ be the residue field at $v$ . We now consider the map

$$ \Phi:\operatorname{Hom}_{K}(A,X)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Q}\to\operatorname{End}_{k}(A_{0})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Q} $$

given by $c\mapsto G_{0}\overline{c},$ where $\overline{c}$ is the reduction of $c$ . We have the following Proposition.

#### Proposition 2.4.

The map $\Phi$ is surjective.

#### Proof.

This follows from elementary linear algebra and the fact that we chose $g_{j,1},\ldots,g_{j,r_{j}}$ to be a $D_{j}$ -basis. ∎

We now apply Proposition 2.1. Let $T$ be the set of all prime-to- $p$ torsion points $x$ in $X(\overline{K})$ , such that every $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)$ -conjugate of $x$ reduces to $\ker(G_{0})$ .

#### Proposition 2.5.

$T$ is a finite subgroup of $X(\overline{K})$ . Hence there exists $m>0$ such that $mT=0$ .

#### Proof.

Observe that $T$ is $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)$ -invariant and is a subgroup of $X(\overline{K})$ . Let $C$ denote the Zariski closure of $T$ . If $T$ is infinite, then the connected component $C^{\circ}$ is an abelian subvariety. By Proposition 2.1, its reduction is hence an abelian subvariety $C^{\circ}_{0}$ that lies in $\ker(G_{0})$ , contradicting Proposition 2.4. Hence $T$ is finite as desired. ∎

Now let $f_{0}$ be the endomorphism in Proposition 2.2. By Proposition 2.4, there exists a positive integer $s$ , uniformly bounded, such that we can find $c\in\operatorname{Hom}_{K}(A,X)$ satisfying $G_{0}\overline{c}=sf_{0}$ .

#### Proposition 2.6.

We have $[m]c(H_{p^{\prime}})=0$ .

#### Proof.

Indeed as $f_{0}(H_{p^{\prime},0})=0$ , it follows that the reduction of $c(H_{p^{\prime}})$ lies in $\ker(G_{0})$ . Hence $c(H_{p^{\prime}})\subseteq T$ which gives us $mc(H_{p^{\prime}})=0$ by Proposition 2.5. ∎

We now take some embedding $X\hookrightarrow{}A^{N}$ for some $N\geq 1$ . Then $[m]c$ can be viewed as an element of $\operatorname{Hom}(A,A^{N})$ . Let $u_{1},\ldots,u_{N}\in\operatorname{End}(A)$ be the coordinate components, so that $H_{p^{\prime}}\subseteq\ker(u_{i})$ . We may find $e$ large enough so that $H_{p}\subseteq\ker([p^{e}]u_{i})$ , and so $H\subseteq\tilde{H}\subseteq\ker([p^{e}]u_{i})$ . We now bound the prime-to- $p$ part of $\tilde{H}$ , denoted by $\tilde{H}_{p^{\prime}}$ .

#### Proposition 2.7.

We have $|\tilde{H}_{p^{\prime}}|\leq C|H_{p^{\prime}}|$ , where $C>0$ is some constant independent of $H$ .

#### Proof.

By definition, we have $\cap_{i=1}^{N}\ker(u_{i})=\ker([m]c)$ . Since multiplying by powers of $p$ do not affect the prime-to- $p$ part of the kernel, we have $[m]c(\tilde{H}_{p^{\prime}})=0$ . Hence $[m]\overline{c}(\tilde{H}_{p^{\prime}})=0$ and thus $[m]G_{0}\overline{c}(\tilde{H}_{p^{\prime},0})=0$ . This gives us $[ms]f_{0}(\tilde{H}_{p^{\prime},0})=0$ . By Proposition 2.2, we have $\deg(f_{0})/H_{p^{\prime},0}$ is bounded independent of $H$ and so $|\tilde{H}_{p^{\prime},0}|/H_{p^{\prime},0}$ is bounded independent of $H$ as desired. ∎

We have now successfully controlled the prime-to- $p$ torsion part. To control the $p$ -primary part, we simply find another place $w$ where the residue characteristic is a prime $q$ different from $p$ . This bounds the $p$ -primary part too and hence $[\tilde{H}:H]$ is uniformly bounded, independent of $H$ . Hence as there are only finitely many $K$ -isomorphism classes of $A/\tilde{H}$ , it follows that there are only finitely many $K$ -isomorphism classes of $A/H$ . This finishes the proof of Theorem 1.1.

# Degree Growth of Iterates of Curves and Likely Intersections

**Authors:** Sina Saleh and Jit Wu Yap

## Abstract

We study the growth of the bidegree of an ample irreducible curve in $\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ under a product polynomial endomorphism $\varphi=(f,g)$ , where at least one of $f$ and $g$ is non-exceptional. We prove that, if the curve $C$ is not preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ for any $a,b\geq 1$ , then the bidegree of $\varphi^{n}(C)$ is asymptotic to $(\deg(g)^{n},\deg(f)^{n})$ .

As an application of this exponential growth, we prove a geometric analogue of Silverman’s theorem on the finiteness of $S$ -integral points in orbits. Namely if $C$ is not $(f^{a},g^{b})$ -preperiodic and $C^{\prime}$ is not totally invariant for $\varphi$ , then for any infinite sequence ${n_{i}}$ of positive integers, the union of the intersections

is Zariski dense in $C^{\prime}$ .

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1. Main Results

Let $X$ be a projective variety and $\varphi:X\dashrightarrow X$ a dominant rational self-map. An important birational invariant of the algebraic dynamical system $(X,\varphi)$ is the collection of dynamical degrees

$$ \{\lambda_{0}(\varphi),\lambda_{1}(\varphi),\ldots,\lambda_{\dim X}(\varphi)\}. $$

If we let $H$ be an ample divisor on $X$ , we may define the $p$ -th dynamical degree of $\varphi$ as

$$ \lambda_{p}(\varphi)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left((\varphi^{n})^{\ast}[H]^{p}\cdot[H]^{\dim(X)-p}\right)^{1/n}. $$

It is well known that this limit exists and is independent of the choice of ample divisor $H$ ; see, for example, [6, 31].

Our first result classifies the curves in $\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ whose degree under iteration by $\varphi$ grows as fast as $\lambda_{1}(\varphi)$ . As is common in complex dynamics, maps arising from algebraic groups require separate treatment. We say that a polynomial $f$ is exceptional if it is affine conjugate to either a power map or a Chebyshev polynomial. We use the notion of a weakly $\varphi$ -special curve as defined in [17, Definition 1.7]. We can now state the theorem.

#### Theorem 1.1.

Let $f,g\in\mathbb{C}[x]$ be polynomials of degrees $d,e\geq 2$ , respectively, and let $C\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be an ample irreducible curve defined over $\mathbb{C}$ . Assume that one of the following conditions holds:

- (1) $f$ is non-exceptional, and $C$ is not preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ for any $a,b\geq 1$ ; or

- (2) both $f$ and $g$ are exceptional, and $C$ is not a weakly $(f,g)$ -special curve.

If $(a_{n},b_{n})$ denotes the bidegree of $\varphi^{n}(C)$ , then there exists $M\in\mathbb{N}$ such that

$$ (a_{n},b_{n})=\frac{1}{M}(e^{n}a_{0},d^{n}b_{0}) $$

for all sufficiently large $n$ , where $(a_{0},b_{0})$ is the bidegree of $C$ .

#### Remark 1.2.

One can also study the degree growth of iterated preimages of curves. This was done by Xie [33, Proposition 8.5] for an arbitrary projective surface and $\varphi$ a dominant rational self-map of topological degree at least $2$ . Xie classifies when an infinite sequence of irreducible curves $\{C_{n}\}_{n\geq 0}$ on $X$ satisfying

$$ \varphi(C_{i+1})=C_{i} $$

for all $i\geq 0$ can have degree bounded from above. This is used as part of his proof of the dynamical Mordell–Lang conjecture for $\mathbb{A}^{2}$ .

#### Remark 1.3.

Theorem 1.1 is similar in spirit to the Kawaguchi–Silverman conjecture [15, Conjecture 6], which predicts that the exponential height growth of an algebraic point with Zariski dense orbit under a dominant self-map is given by the first dynamical degree of the map. However for Theorem 1.1, even in the case where $f,g$ both have the same degree $d\geq 2$ , it is not sufficient that the orbit of $C$ under $\varphi$ be Zariski dense, as seen by the example of $\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\{a\}$ .

The next examples show the necessity of conditions $(1)$ and $(2)$ in Theorem 1.1.

#### Example 1.4.

Let $C$ be a preperiodic curve under $\varphi$ , i.e., there exists $0\leq N<M$ such that

$$ \varphi^{N}(C)=\varphi^{M}(C). $$

Then, the set $\{\varphi^{n}(C)\}_{n\geq 0}$ contains only finitely many curves which shows that the bidegree of $\varphi^{n}(C)$ must remain bounded.

#### Example 1.5.

Let $\varphi=(z^{2},z^{2})$ and $C=\{y=\theta x\}$ for some $\theta\in\mathbb{C}^{\ast}$ . Then, $\varphi^{n}(C)=\{y=\theta^{2^{n}}x\}$ which shows that the bidegree of $\varphi^{n}(C)$ is $(1,1)$ for all $n\geq 0$ .

Another interesting class of examples arises when $\deg(f)\neq\deg(g)$ and some iterated image of $C$ is invariant under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ for some $a,b\geq 1$ . In such cases, the degree of $\varphi^{n}(C)$ still tends to infinity, but its growth rate is strictly smaller than $\lambda_{1}(\varphi)$ . The next example illustrates this phenomenon.

#### Example 1.6.

Let $\varphi=(z^{2},z^{4})$ and $C=\{y=x\}$ . Then, $\varphi^{n}(C)=\{y=x^{2^{n}}\}$ which has bidegree $(2^{n},1)$ . Thus,

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\deg(\varphi^{n}(C))^{1/n}=2 $$

whereas the dynamical degree of $\varphi$ is equal to $4$ .

We now give an application of Theorem 1.1 which is a likely intersection result in the spirit of the Zilber–Pink philosophy [36]; see also [29, 7] for likely intersection results in the context of Shimura varieties. Given two curves $C,C^{\prime}$ in a surface $X$ and an endomorphism $\varphi:X\to X$ , for dimension reasons we expect that $C\cap C^{\prime}$ should have a non-empty intersection. As $C$ is replaced by its iterates $\varphi(C),\varphi^{2}(C),\ldots$ , one expects new intersection points to appear, unless $C$ is special. We make this heuristic precise in the case of $X=\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ and $\varphi=(f,g)$ a product polynomial endomorphism. Before stating the theorem, for an endomorphism $\varphi:\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ , we say that a curve $C$ is exceptional, or totally invariant, if $\varphi^{-1}(C)=C$ .

#### Theorem 1.7.

Let $\varphi=(f,g):\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be a product polynomial endomorphism defined over $\mathbb{C}$ . Assume that $f$ and $g$ are not both exceptional. Let $C,C^{\prime}$ be irreducible curves in $\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ such that $C$ is ample and is not preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ for any $a,b\geq 1$ and $C^{\prime}$ is not exceptional. Then for any infinite subset $\{n_{i}\}_{i\geq 1}\subset{\mathbb{N}}$ , the union

$$ \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\varphi^{n_{i}}(C)\cap C^{\prime}\right) $$

is Zariski dense in $C^{\prime}$ .

Theorem 1.7 may be viewed as a geometric analogue of a theorem of Silverman on finiteness of $S$ -integral points in orbits [27], stated below.

#### Theorem 1.8 ([27]).

Let $K$ be a number field, $S$ a finite set of places and $\varphi:\mathbb{P}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be a rational map defined over $K$ . Let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(K)$ be two points such that $\alpha$ is not preperiodic and $\beta$ is non-exceptional, i.e. $|\varphi^{-n}(\beta)|\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ . Then there are only finitely many $n$ such that $\varphi^{n}(\alpha)$ is $S$ -integral relative to $\beta$ .

Given $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(K)$ , we may spread out to obtain one-dimensional closed subschemes $\tilde{\alpha},\tilde{\beta}$ of the arithmetic surface $\mathbb{P}^{1}_{O_{K}}$ . Then Theorem 1.8 is equivalent to saying that for any infinite subset $\{n_{i}\}_{i\geq 1}$ of ${\mathbb{N}}$ , the union

$$ \bigcup_{i\geq 1}\left(\varphi^{n_{i}}(\tilde{\alpha})\cap\tilde{\beta}\right) $$

is infinite, which is analogous to the conclusion of Theorem 1.7. We note that Theorem 1.7 is also closely related to a recent theorem of Baldi and Urbanik [3, Theorem 1.8]. Baldi–Urbanik’s result and Theorem 1.7 motivate the following general question.

#### Question 1.9.

Let $X$ be a variety over a field $k$ and $\varphi:X\to X$ an endomorphism. Let $V$ and $W$ be subvarieties of $X$ such that $\dim V+\dim W\geq\dim X$ and let $\{n_{i}\}_{i\geq 1}\subset{\mathbb{N}}$ be an infinite subset. Under what hypotheses can we conclude that

$$ \bigcup_{i\geq 1}\left(\varphi^{n_{i}}(V)\cap W\right) $$

is Zariski dense in $W$ ?

We may also ask a weaker version of Question 1.9 where instead of considering the union of $\varphi^{n}(V)\cap W$ over an infinite sequence, we may consider the union over all positive integers $n$ instead.

#### Question 1.10.

Suppose that we are in the setting of Question 1.9. Under what hypotheses can we conclude that

$$ \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}(\varphi^{n}(V)\cap W) $$

is Zariski dense in $W$ ?

A key ingredient in the proof of Theorem 1.7 is an upper bound for the intersection multiplicity of $\varphi^{n}(C)$ and $C^{\prime}$ at a fixed point $p$ of $\varphi$ . Our final result establishes such a bound.

#### Theorem 1.11.

Let $\varphi=(f,g)$ be a product polynomial map with $\max\{\deg f,\deg g\}\geq 1$ and $C,C^{\prime}$ curves such that $C$ is not $(f^{a},g^{b})$ preperiodic for any $a,b\geq 1$ . Let $p=(\alpha,\beta)\in(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ be a fixed point for $\varphi$ and let $d^{\prime},e^{\prime}$ be the local degree of $\alpha,\beta$ as a fixed point for $f$ and $g$ , respectively. Then there exists $c>0$ and $n_{0}\geq 1$ such that for all $n\geq n_{0}$ we have

$$ \operatorname{mult}_{p}\bigl(\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}\bigr)=\begin{cases}c\,\min\{d^{\prime},e^{\prime}\}^{n}+O(1),&\text{if }C^{\prime}\text{ is ample},\\[4.0pt]
c\,(d^{\prime})^{n},&\text{if }C^{\prime}=\{\alpha\}\times\mathbb{P}^{1},\\[4.0pt]
c\,(e^{\prime})^{n},&\text{if }C^{\prime}=\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\{\beta\}.\end{cases} $$

#### Remark 1.12.

The multiplicities

$$ \operatorname{mult}_{p}\bigl(\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}\bigr) $$

appearing in Theorem 1.11 are sometimes referred to as Milnor numbers [2]. In this language, Theorem 1.11 may be viewed as a refinement of a special case of Arnold’s conjecture [2, Problem 1994-49], which predicted that, in the general setting where $\varphi$ is a holomorphic germ fixing a point and $C,C^{\prime}$ are germs of analytic curves, these Milnor numbers grow at most exponentially. Arnold [1, Theorem 1] proved the conjecture in the case where $\varphi$ is a local biholomorphism; this corresponds to the case $d^{\prime}=e^{\prime}=1$ in Theorem 1.11. Seigal and Yakovenko [26] later gave a different proof of this result. Arnold’s conjecture is also known to hold when the derivative $D\varphi_{p}$ has exactly one zero eigenvalue; see [1, Section 5], [13, Remark 5.3], and [22]. However, Arnold’s general conjecture on the growth rate of intersection multiplicities was subsequently shown to be false by Gignac [13].

#### Remark 1.13.

Suppose that $p=(0,0)$ in the statement of Theorem 1.11. There is a formula relating the intersection multiplicity $\operatorname{mult}_{p}(\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime})$ to the multiplicities of the curves $\varphi^{n}(C)$ and $C^{\prime}$ :

$$ \operatorname{mult}_{p}(\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime})=m(\varphi^{n}(C))\,m(C^{\prime})\,\alpha\left(\nu_{\varphi^{n}(C)}\wedge\nu_{C^{\prime}}\right), $$

where $m(\varphi^{n}(C))$ and $m(C^{\prime})$ denote the corresponding curve multiplicities, and $\alpha$ is the skewness function on the valuative tree; see [8]. Using Theorem 1.1, it is straightforward to check that there exists a constant $c>0$ such that

$$ m(\varphi^{n}(C))\leq c\min\{d^{\prime},e^{\prime}\}^{n} $$

for all $n\geq 1$ . The main difficulty is therefore to show that

$$ \alpha\left(\nu_{\varphi^{n}(C)}\wedge\nu_{C^{\prime}}\right) $$

remains uniformly bounded. This boundedness, however, does not seem to follow directly from the results of [8]. We also refer the reader to the proof of [13, Theorem B], which uses the theory of the valuative tree to study the generic behavior of multiplicity growth under iteration.

### 1.2. Dynamical Degrees and Degree Growth of Curves

Many dynamical features of a dynamical system are reflected in its dynamical degrees. These include, for example, entropy, the existence of invariant fibrations, the distribution of periodic points of $\varphi$ , and the height growth of algebraic points when $\varphi$ is defined over a number field. We refer the reader to the introduction of [5] and the references therein for further discussion of the significance of dynamical degrees.

The introduction of dynamical degrees dates back to Friedland [9], building on earlier work of Gromov [14] and Yomdin [35] relating entropy to volume growth. This was later developed extensively by Russakovskii and Shiffman [23] in the case of $X=\mathbb{P}^{n}$ , and by Dinh and Sibony [6] in the general setting of dominant rational self-maps of arbitrary projective varieties. A purely algebraic definition of dynamical degrees for rational maps over algebraically closed fields was later introduced by Truong, first in characteristic zero [30] and subsequently in greater generality for correspondences over fields of arbitrary characteristic [31].

Suppose that $X$ is a complex projective surface, that $\varphi:X\to X$ is a surjective endomorphism over $\mathbb{C}$ , and that $C$ is an ample irreducible curve on $X$ . The first dynamical degree of $\varphi$ is given by

$$ \lambda_{1}(\varphi):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left([C]\cdot(\varphi^{n})^{\ast}[C]\right)^{1/n}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left([C]\cdot(\varphi^{n})_{*}[C]\right)^{1/n}. $$

Hence the first dynamical degree $\lambda_{1}(\varphi)$ can be seen as measuring the asymptotic growth of the the pushforward cycles $(\varphi^{n})_{*}[C]$ in an algebraic sense.

Observe that the cycle $(\varphi^{n})_{*}[C]$ records not only the image of $C$ , but also the generic degree with which $C$ maps onto its image, i.e. we have

$$ (\varphi^{n})_{\ast}[C]=\deg\left(\varphi^{n}|_{C}\right)\cdot[\varphi^{n}(C)]. $$

Thus, from a geometric perspective, it is natural to separate these two contributions and ask the following question.

#### Question 1.14.

Suppose $X$ is a complex projective surface and $\varphi:X\to X$ is a surjective endomorphism. For which irreducible ample curves $C\subset X$ does the limit

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\deg(\varphi^{n}(C))^{1/n} $$

exist and equal the first dynamical degree $\lambda_{1}(\varphi)$ ?

Here, the degree of a curve is measured with respect to an arbitrary fixed ample line bundle $L$ . This viewpoint retains information about the actual geometry of the orbit of $C$ , since $\deg(\varphi^{n}(C))$ depends on the curve $C$ itself, rather than only on its cohomology class $[C]$ .

Theorem 1.1 answers Question 1.14 in the case where $X=\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ , $\varphi=(f,g)$ is a product polynomial endomorphism, and $C$ is an ample irreducible curve; equivalently, $C$ has bidegree $(c_{1},c_{2})$ with $c_{1},c_{2}\geq 1$ .

### 1.3. Outline of the paper.

In Section 2, we review the basic definitions about plane curves, branches and their parametrizations, and intersection multiplicities. In Section 3, we prove a functional transcendence result for Böttcher coordinates, Theorem 3.1, which is needed in the proof of Theorem 1.1. Section 4 is devoted to the proof of Theorem 1.1, and Section 5 to the proof of Theorem 1.11. In Section 6, we prove a finiteness result regarding backward orbits and curves $C$ . In Section 7, we combine the results of Sections 4 and 5 to prove Theorem 1.7. Finally, in Section 8, we investigate the likely intersections of $\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}$ for pairs $(C,C^{\prime})$ excluded by the hypotheses of Theorem 1.7; see Theorem 8.1.
