## 2. Preliminaries on Plane Curves

In this section, we recall some background on plane curves. Our main reference is [32].

### 2.1. Plane Curves

Let $O:=(0,0)$ denote the origin in $\mathbb{C}^{2}$ . By a plane curve, we mean a set of the form

$$ \{h=0\}, $$

where $h:U\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is a holomorphic function on some open neighborhood $U$ of $O$ . Equivalently, we may take $h$ to be an element of $\mathbb{C}\{x,y\}$ , the ring of convergent power series in two variables near $O$ .

Let $C$ be a plane curve defined by $\{h=0\}$ . Suppose that $\phi,\psi:D\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ are holomorphic functions defined on an open neighborhood $D$ of $0$ , satisfying

$$ \phi(0)=\psi(0)=0 $$

and

$$ h(\phi(t),\psi(t))=0 $$

for all $t\in D$ . Then we call $(\phi,\psi)$ a parametrization of $C$ . We say that such a parametrization is a good parametrization if the map

$$ t\longmapsto(\phi(t),\psi(t)) $$

is injective for all $|t|<\epsilon$ , for some $\epsilon>0$ .

The ring $\mathbb{C}\{x,y\}$ is a unique factorization domain [32, Theorem 2.2.5]. Hence every $h\in\mathbb{C}\{x,y\}$ admits a factorization

$$ h=\prod_{i=1}^{r}h_{i}^{\alpha_{i}}, $$

where the $h_{i}$ are irreducible elements of $\mathbb{C}\{x,y\}$ and the $\alpha_{i}$ are positive integers. We refer to each curve $\{h_{i}=0\}$ as a branch of $C$ . The following fact is immediate from this factorization.

#### Fact 2.1.

A plane curve has finitely many branches.

#### Fact 2.2 ([32, Lemma 2.3.1]).

A branch of a plane curve is uniquely determined by any good parametrization of it.

The next result is the Newton–Puiseux theorem, which may be regarded as an extension of the implicit function theorem in the setting of plane curves. See [32, Sections 2.1 and 2.2].

#### Theorem 2.3 (Newton-Puiseux Theorem).

Any branch of a curve $C$ not coinciding with $\{x=0\}$ and defined by an equation $f(x,y)=0$ , where $f\in\mathbb{C}\{x,y\}$ is a convergent power series with $f(O)=0$ admits a good parametrization of the form

$$ (t^{m},\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}a_{i}t^{i}), $$

where $m\geq 1$ is an integer and $\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}a_{i}t^{i}$ is a convergent power series in a neighborhood of zero.

### 2.2. Intersection multiplicities

Let $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ be two plane curves. Suppose that $\Gamma_{1}$ is a branch given by a good parametrization $(\phi(t),\psi(t))$ , and that $\Gamma_{2}$ is defined by a convergent power series $h\in\mathbb{C}\{x,y\}$ . The intersection multiplicity of $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ at $O$ is defined by

$$ \operatorname{mult}_{O}(\Gamma_{1},\Gamma_{2}):=\operatorname{ord}_{t}\bigl(h(\phi(t),\psi(t))\bigr), $$

where $\operatorname{ord}_{t}\bigl(h(\phi(t),\psi(t))\bigr)$ denotes the order of vanishing at $0$ of the power series $h(\phi(t),\psi(t))$ . By [32, Lemma 2.3.2], this definition is independent of the choice of good parametrization of $\Gamma_{1}$ .

More generally, if $\Gamma_{1}$ is an arbitrary plane curve with branches $\Gamma_{1,1},\dots,\Gamma_{1,r}$ , we define

$$ \operatorname{mult}_{O}(\Gamma_{1},\Gamma_{2}):=\sum_{j=1}^{r}mult_{O}(\Gamma_{1,j},\Gamma_{2}). $$

Although this definition is asymmetric, intersection multiplicity is symmetric: for any two plane curves $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ , one has

$$ \operatorname{mult}_{O}(C_{1},C_{2})=\operatorname{mult}_{O}(C_{2},C_{1}). $$

See [32, Lemma 1.2.1].

## 3. Functional Transcendence of Böttcher Coordinates

The aim of this section is to establish a functional transcendence result for the Böttcher coordinate of a non-exceptional polynomial. More precisely, we study a special class of bialgebraic curves, that is, algebraic curves whose images under the Böttcher coordinate change are also algebraic. Our result may be viewed as a generalization of [25, Lemmas 5.9 and 6.11]. We refer the reader to [24] for a more general treatment of bialgebraic varieties under Böttcher coordinates, and to [21, 34] for results concerning algebraic dependence among Böttcher values. Our arguments draw heavily on ideas developed in [25] and [24]. We begin by recalling the definition of Böttcher coordinates and then prove the main result of this section, Theorem 3.1.

Let $f$ be a polynomial of degree $d\geq 2$ , and let $B_{\infty}(f)$ denote the basin of infinity of $f$ , that is, the set of points in $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ whose forward orbits under $f$ tend to infinity. Böttcher’s theorem [20, Theorem 9.1] states that there exist an open subset $U_{\infty}(f)\subset B_{\infty}(f)$ and a biholomorphism

$$ \Phi_{f}:U_{\infty}(f)\longrightarrow\mathbb{D}_{r} $$

for some $r\leq 1$ , such that

$$ \Phi_{f}(f(z))=\Phi_{f}(z)^{d} $$

for all $z\in U_{\infty}(f)$ .

Similarly, let $g$ be a polynomial, and let $\alpha$ be a superattracting point of $g$ of multiplicity $e\geq 2$ , not necessarily equal to $\infty$ . Then there exist a neighborhood $U_{\alpha}(g)$ of $\alpha$ and a Böttcher coordinate $\Phi_{g}$ , which is a biholomorphism from $U_{\alpha}(g)$ onto $\mathbb{D}_{r^{\prime}}$ for some $r^{\prime}\leq 1$ , satisfying

$$ \Phi_{g}(g(z))=\Phi_{g}(z)^{e}. $$

Let $\Psi_{f}$ and $\Psi_{g}$ denote the inverses of $\Phi_{f}$ and $\Phi_{g}$ , respectively. Then $\Psi_{f}$ and $\Psi_{g}$ satisfy the functional equations

$$ f(\Psi_{f}(z))=\Psi_{f}(z^{d}),\qquad g(\Psi_{g}(z))=\Psi_{g}(z^{e}). $$

We aim to prove the following theorem.

#### Theorem 3.1.

Assume that $f$ is not an exceptional polynomial. Let $\theta\in\mathbb{C}^{\ast}$ be a non-zero constant and $i,j\geq 1$ be integers. Assume there exists an irreducible $P\in\mathbb{C}[x,y]\setminus\{0\}$ such that

$$ P(\Psi_{f}(\theta z^{i}),\Psi_{g}(z^{j}))=0 $$

for all $z\in\mathbb{D}_{r^{\prime\prime}}$ for some $0<r^{\prime\prime}\leq\min\{r,r^{\prime}\}$ . Then $\theta$ is a root of unity, and if $C$ is the curve defined by $\{P=0\}$ , then $C$ is preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ for some integers $a,b\geq 1$ .

The main strategy of the proof of Theorem 3.1 is to reduce to the setting of $f=g$ and $\alpha=\infty$ . For example, when $f=g$ , $\alpha=\infty$ , $|\theta|=1$ , and $i=j$ , Theorem 3.1 follows readily from the results of Schmidt [25, Lemmas 5.9 and 6.11]. Also, in the case $|\theta|\neq 1$ , one shows that the Julia set of $f$ must be either disconnected or locally connected, which allows us to deduce the theorem from [24, Theorem 1.1].

From now on in this section, we shall assume we are in the situation of Theorem 3.1. Hence $f$ is a non-exceptional polynomial, and there exists an irreducible polynomial $P\in\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ along with a non-zero $\theta$ and positive integers $i,j$ such that

$$ P(\Psi_{f}(\theta z^{i}),\Psi_{g}(z^{j}))=0 $$

for all $z$ in some neighbourhood $U$ of $0$ . Our first step is to produce a relation between $\Psi_{f}(\theta^{\prime}z)$ and $\Psi_{f}(z)$ for some $\theta^{\prime}$ .

#### Lemma 3.2.

Let $\theta_{1}$ satisfy $\theta_{1}^{e}=\theta^{-1}$ and let $\theta_{2}=(\theta\theta_{1})^{d}$ . Then there exists a non-zero polynomial $P_{1}\in\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ such that

$$ P_{1}(\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}^{d-1}z),\Psi_{f}(z))=0 $$

for all $z$ in a sufficiently small neighbourhood of $0$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\varphi=(f,g)$ and let $C$ be the curve defined by $\{P=0\}$ . Then $C$ is an irreducible curve and so is the image curve $\varphi(C)$ . Thus there exists some irreducible polynomial $Q(x,y)$ such that $\varphi(C)=\{Q=0\}$ . Then for all $z\in U$ , where we possibly shrink $U$ , we have

$$ Q(f(\Psi_{f}(\theta z^{i})),g(\Psi_{g}(z^{j})))=0\implies Q(\Psi_{f}(\theta^{d}z^{id}),\Psi_{g}(z^{ej}))=0. $$

Substituting in $z^{e}$ for $z$ in $P(\Psi_{f}(\theta z^{i}),\Psi_{g}(z^{j}))=0$ , we see that $\Psi_{f}(\theta z^{ei})$ and $\Psi_{g}(z^{ej})$ are algebraically dependent. Since equation (2) tells us that $\Psi_{f}(\theta^{d}z^{id})$ and $\Psi_{g}(z^{ej})$ are algebraically dependent, we get that $\Psi_{f}(\theta^{d}z^{id})$ and $\Psi_{f}(\theta z^{ei})$ are algebraically dependent and thus so is $\Psi_{f}(\theta^{d}z^{d})$ and $\Psi_{f}(\theta z^{e})$ . Hence there exists a non-zero $R\in\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ such that

$$ R(\Psi_{f}(\theta^{d}z^{d}),\Psi_{f}(\theta z^{e}))=0. $$

Now choose $\theta_{1}$ such that $\theta_{1}^{e}=\theta^{-1}$ and substitute in $\theta_{1}z$ into $z$ . This gives us

$$ R(\Psi_{f}((\theta\theta_{1})^{d}z^{d}),\Psi_{f}(z^{e}))=0. $$

Letting $\theta_{2}=(\theta\theta_{1})^{d}$ gives

$$ R(\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}z^{d}),\Psi_{f}(z^{e}))=0. $$

Again if we let $C$ be the curve defined by $\{R=0\}$ and we let $(f,f)(C)$ be defined by $\{S=0\}$ , we get

$$ S(f(\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}z^{d}),f(\Psi_{f}(z^{e})))=0\implies S(\Psi_{f}((\theta_{2}z^{d})^{d}),\Psi_{f}(z^{ed}))=0. $$

Hence $\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}^{d}z^{d^{2}})$ and $\Psi_{f}(z^{ed})$ are algebraically dependent. Substituting in $z^{d}$ for $z$ in (3), we get that $\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}z^{d^{2}})$ and $\Psi_{f}(z^{ed})$ are algebraically dependent. Thus $\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}^{d}z^{d^{2}})$ and $\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}z^{d^{2}})$ are algebraically dependent. Replacing $z^{d^{2}}$ with $z$ gives us an algebraic relation between $\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}^{d}z)$ and $\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}z)$ and finally replacing $\theta_{2}z$ with $z$ gives us a relation between $\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}^{d-1}z)$ and $\Psi_{f}(z)$ as desired. ∎

Let $\theta^{\prime}:=\theta_{2}^{d-1}$ . Next, we show that $\theta^{\prime}$ and hence $\theta$ must be a root of unity.

#### Lemma 3.3.

$\theta$ is a root of unity.

#### Proof.

Note that since $\theta^{\prime}$ is multiplicatively dependent with respect to $\theta$ by definition, it suffices to show that $\theta^{\prime}$ is a root of unity. By Lemma 3.2 we have

$$ P_{1}(\Psi_{f}(\theta^{\prime}z),\Psi_{f}(z))=0, $$

for all $z\in D_{\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$ . We may assume by symmetry that $|\theta^{\prime}|\leq 1$ . Since the relation holds for every $z\in D_{\epsilon}$ then it must also hold for every $z\in\mathbb{D}_{r}$ . It suffices to show that $|\theta^{\prime}|=1$ and then the lemma follows from [25, Lemmas 5.9 and 6.11]. Therefore, we assume for the sake of contradiction that $|\theta^{\prime}|<1$ . It follows from the proof of [24, Claim 8.3] that $J_{f}$ must be locally connected. Therefore, by [24, Theorem 1.1] we conclude that the curve defined by $\{P_{1}=0\}$ is $f$ -special in the sense of [24]. In fact, it must be preperiodic under $(f,f)$ . This is impossible since $|\theta^{\prime}|<1$ . This contradiction shows $|\theta^{\prime}|=1$ and we conclude the proof from [25, Lemmas 5.9 and 6.11]. ∎

We recall the following theorem of Medvedev and Scanlon.

#### Theorem 3.4 (Theorem 6.24, [19]).

Let $f$ be a non-exceptional polynomial. Then if $C\subseteq\mathbb{A}^{2}$ is a curve whose Zariski closure in $\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ is ample and is invariant under $(f,f)$ , there exists $h$ and a linear polynomial $L$ such that

$$ C=\{y=L\circ h^{l}(x)\}\text{ or }\{x=L\circ h^{l}(y)\}\text{ for some }l\geq 0, $$

where $h^{r}=f$ for some $r$ and $L$ commutes with a compositional power of $f$ .

This along with Lemma 3.3 allows us to prove that the degrees $d$ and $e$ are multiplicatively dependent.

#### Lemma 3.5.

There exists $l_{1},l_{2}\geq 1$ such that $d^{l_{1}}=e^{l_{2}}$ .

#### Proof.

By (3) in the proof of Lemma 3.2, we can find an irreducible $R\in\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ such that

$$ R(\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}z^{d}),\Psi_{f}(z^{e}))=0 $$

for $\theta_{2}=(\theta\theta_{1})^{d}$ where $\theta_{1}$ satisfies $\theta_{1}^{e}=\theta^{-1}$ . By Lemma 3.3, we know that $\theta$ is a root of unity. Hence $\theta_{2}$ is a root of unity too and so we can find $m>n\geq 0$ such that $\theta_{2}^{d^{m}}=\theta_{2}^{d^{n}}$ . Let $T$ be the polynomial that defines the image of $R$ under $(f^{n},f^{n})$ . Then $T$ is irreducible and

$$ T(\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}^{d^{n}}z^{d^{n+1}}),\Psi_{f}(z^{d^{n}e}))=0 $$

for all $z$ in a small neighbourhood near $0$ . Hence

$$ T(\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}^{d^{n}}y^{d}),\Psi_{f}(y^{e}))=0 $$

for all $y$ near $0$ . Let $C_{1}$ be the curve defined by $T$ . We claim that $C_{1}$ is invariant under $(f^{m-n},f^{m-n})$ . To see this, let $C_{2}$ be the image of $C_{1}$ under $(f^{m-n},f^{m-n})$ . Then observe that for all $z$ near $0$ , we have that $(\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}^{d^{n}}z^{d}),\Psi_{f}(z^{e}))$ is a point on $C_{1}$ . Hence

$$ (f^{m-n}(\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}^{d^{n}}z^{d})),f^{m-n}(\Psi_{f}(z^{e})))=(\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}^{d^{m}}z^{d^{m-n+1}}),\Psi_{f}(z^{d^{m-n}e}))) $$

lies on $C_{2}$ for all small enough $z$ . But since $\theta_{2}^{d^{m}}=\theta_{2}^{d^{n}}$ , this is simply $(\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}^{d^{n}}z^{d^{m-n}d},\Psi_{f}(z^{d^{m-n}e}))$ which lies on $C_{1}$ since it is of the form $(\Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}^{d^{n}}y^{d}),\Psi_{f}(y^{e}))$ for $y$ small. Thus $C_{1}\cap C_{2}$ is of infinite size which implies that $C_{1}=C_{2}$ since they are both irreducible.

We now apply Theorem 3.4 to $C_{1}$ . Since it is invariant under $(f^{m-n},f^{m-n})$ , we can find a polynomial $h$ of degree $d^{\prime}$ satisfying $h^{r}=f^{m-n}$ and a linear endomorphism $L$ such that $C_{1}$ is given by $\{x=L\circ h^{l}(y)\}$ or $\{y=L\circ h^{l}(x)\}$ . Without loss of generality, let us assume that $C_{1}$ is of the former form. Then by (4), we have

$$ \Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}^{d^{n}}y^{d})=L(h^{l}(\Psi_{f}(y^{e}))) $$

for all $y$ near $0$ . Since $h^{r}=f^{m-n}$ , they share the same Julia set and Bottcher coordinates. In particular, we have $h(\Psi_{f}(y))=\Psi_{f}(y^{d^{\prime}})$ . Thus we get

$$ \Psi_{f}(\theta_{2}^{d^{n}}y^{d})=L\left(\Psi_{f}(y^{e(d^{\prime})^{l}})\right). $$

In particular by comparing the order of vanishing at $0$ , we must have $d=(d^{\prime})^{l}e$ . Since $h^{r}=f^{m-n}$ , we have $(d^{\prime})^{r}=d^{m-n}$ and in particular $d^{\prime}$ and $d$ are multiplicatively dependent. Hence so is $d$ and $e$ and so we can find $l_{1},l_{2}$ such that $d^{l_{1}}=e^{l_{2}}$ as desired. ∎

Finally using Lemmas 3.3 and 3.5, we can prove Theorem 3.1

#### Proof of Theorem 3.1.

By Lemma 3.3, we know that $\theta$ is a root of unity. By Lemma 3.5, we can find $l_{1},l_{2}>0$ such that $d^{l_{1}}=e^{l_{2}}$ . Since $\theta$ is a root of unity, there exists $m>n$ such that $\theta^{d^{ml_{1}}}=\theta^{d^{nl_{1}}}$ . Let $C$ be the curve defined by $\{P=0\}$ and let $C^{\prime}=(f^{nl_{1}},g^{nl_{2}})(C)$ . Then there is an irreducible polynomial $P_{2}\in\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ such that $C^{\prime}$ is given by $\{P_{2}=0\}$ . Then

$$ P_{2}(f^{nl_{1}}(\Psi_{f}(\theta z^{i})),g^{nl_{2}}(\Psi_{g}(z^{j})))=0\implies P_{2}(\Psi_{f}(\theta^{d^{nl_{1}}}z^{d^{nl_{1}}i}),\Psi_{g}(z^{e^{nl_{2}}j}))=0 $$

for all $z$ in a small neighbourhood near $0$ . Since $d^{l_{1}}=e^{l_{2}}$ , this is equivalent to

$$ P_{2}(\Psi_{f}(\theta^{d^{nl_{1}}}y^{i}),\Psi_{g}(y^{j}))=0 $$

for all $y$ in a small neighbourhood near $0$ . We claim that $C^{\prime}$ is invariant under $(f^{(m-n)l_{1}},g^{(m-n)l_{2}})$ . Indeed we have that

$$ \left(f^{(m-n)l_{1}}(\Psi_{f}(\theta^{d^{nl_{1}}}y^{i})),g^{(m-n)l_{2}}(\Psi_{g}(y^{j}))\right)=\left(\Psi_{f}(\theta^{d^{ml_{1}}}y^{d^{(m-n)l_{1}}i}),\Psi_{g}(y^{e^{(m-n)l_{2}}j})\right) $$

lies on $C_{2}:=(f^{(m-n)l_{1}},g^{(m-n)l_{2}})C^{\prime}$ for all $y$ near $0$ . But since $\theta^{d^{ml_{1}}}=\theta^{d^{nl_{1}}}$ and $d^{l_{1}}=e^{l_{2}}$ , replacing $y^{d^{(m-n)}l_{1}}=y^{e^{(m-n)}l_{2}}$ with $y$ , this is of the form

$$ \left(\Psi_{f}(\theta^{d^{nl_{1}}}y^{i}),\Psi_{g}(y^{j})\right) $$

and so it lies on $C^{\prime}$ too. Hence $C^{\prime}\cap C_{2}$ is infinite and so $C^{\prime}=C_{2}$ as they are both irreducible. Thus $C$ is preperiodic under $(f^{\ell_{1}},g^{\ell_{2}})$ as desired. ∎

## 4. Degree growth for $\varphi^{n}(C)$

Given a curve $C\subseteq(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ , let $(a,b)$ be its bidegree and let $(a_{n},b_{n})$ be the bidegree of $\varphi^{n}(C)$ . Our aim in this section is to use the results of Section 3 to prove Theorem 1.1 which asserts that, for any ample curve $C$ , the integers $a_{n}$ and $b_{n}$ grow on the order of $e^{n}$ and $d^{n}$ , respectively, unless $C$ is preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ or an algebraic coset in the case where $f$ and $g$ are both exceptional.

Let us quickly recall the definition of bidegree of a curve. On $(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ , the Picard group can be identified with $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ via $\pi_{1}^{*}O(a)\otimes\pi_{2}^{*}O(b)\mapsto(a,b)$ , where $\pi_{i}$ are the projection maps $\pi_{i}:(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}$ . Let $f,g:\mathbb{A}^{1}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}$ be two polynomials of degree $d$ and $e$ respectively with $d,e\geq 2$ . The bidegree of a curve is defined to be the image of its linear equivalence class under this identification. Then the map $\varphi=(f,g):(\mathbb{A}^{1})^{2}\to(\mathbb{A}^{1})^{2}$ naturally extends to the compactification $\varphi:(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}\to(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ .

The first step in the proof of Theorem 1.1 is to observe that the bidegree of $\varphi^{n}(C)$ grows at the maximum possible rate provided that the degrees of the restrictions $\varphi^{n}|_{C}$ remain bounded. To see this, we need the following lemma from intersection theory.

#### Lemma 4.1.

Let $f,g$ be two polynomials of degree $d,e$ respectively and let $\varphi:(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}\to(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ be the endomorphism $(f,g)$ . Let $C$ be an irreducible curve with bidegree $(a,b)$ and $\varphi^{n}(C)$ have bidegree $(a_{n},b_{n})$ . Let $d_{n}$ be the degree of the map $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ . Then

$$ (e^{n}a,d^{n}b)=(d_{n}a_{n},d_{n}b_{n}). $$

#### Proof.

Since $\varphi^{n}:(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}\to(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ is a flat and proper morphism, the projection formula [28, Tag 0B0C] applies and we have an equality of intersection numbers

$$ \varphi^{n}_{*}(C)\cdot L=C\cdot(\varphi^{n})^{*}L $$

where $\varphi^{n}_{*}(C)$ is the proper pushforward of $C$ via $\varphi^{n}_{*}$ . If we pick $L$ to have bidegree $(1,0)$ , then $(\varphi^{n})^{*}L$ has bidegree $(d^{n},0)$ and $C\cdot(\varphi^{n})^{*}L=d^{n}b$ .

On the other hand, by the definition of the proper pushforward, we have

$$ \varphi^{n}_{*}(C)=[K(C):K(\varphi^{n}(C))]\cdot[\varphi^{n}(C)] $$

where $K(C),K(\varphi^{n}(C))$ denotes the function field of $C$ and $\varphi^{n}(C)$ respectively. Then $[K(C):K(\varphi^{n}(C))]$ is exactly the degree of the map $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ . Thus we get $d_{n}b_{n}=d^{n}b$ as desired. Similarly one gets $e^{n}a=d_{n}a_{n}$ . ∎

From Lemma 4.1, we see that if $d_{n}$ remains bounded, then $a_{n},b_{n}$ will necessarily grow on the order of $e^{n},d^{n}$ , respectively. Hence we shall now assume that the degree of $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ is unbounded as $n$ goes to $\infty$ and show that this forces $C$ to be of a special form.

We sketch our strategy to show this. We first analyze the case where $(f,g)=(z^{d},z^{e})$ . In this case, it is not hard to directly characterize when $\deg(\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C))$ is unbounded. It turns out that this occurs only when $C$ is a translate of an algebraic subgroup.

For general polynomials $f,g$ , we use the Bottcher coordinates to transform the situation back to $(z^{d},z^{e})$ . Under the Bottcher coordinates $\Phi$ , the curve $C$ is transformed to an analytic curve $\Phi(C)$ satisfying the unbounded degree hypothesis for $(z^{d},z^{e})$ . It turns out that even though $\Phi(C)$ is analytic, it still must be a translate of an algebraic subgroup if the degree of $\varphi^{n}$ remains unbounded. We then use the transcendence results of Section 3 to show that this forces a forward image of $C$ to be $(f^{a},g^{b})$ -invariant.

As a warm up, we handle the case of an algebraic curve for $(z^{d},z^{e})$ .

#### Proposition 4.2.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}$ be an algebraic curve and let $\varphi=(z^{d},z^{e})$ . If the degree of $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ is unbounded as $n\to\infty$ , then $C$ is a translate of an algebraic subgroup.

#### Proof.

Let $d_{n}$ be the degree of $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ and let $G=\operatorname{Stab}_{\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}}C$ be the stabilizer of $C$ . Our aim is to show that if $d_{n}$ is unbounded, then $G$ must be positive dimensional.

For a generic choice of $(\alpha,\beta)\in C$ , we have $d_{n}$ distinct pairs $(\alpha_{i},\beta_{i})\in C$ such that

$$ (\alpha_{i}^{d^{n}},\beta_{i}^{e^{n}})=(\alpha^{d^{n}},\beta^{e^{n}}). $$

Thus $\alpha_{i}=\omega_{i}\alpha,\beta_{i}=\omega_{i}^{\prime}\beta$ for some $d^{n}$ th root of unity $\omega_{i}$ and $e^{n}$ th root of unity $\omega_{i}^{\prime}$ . Since there are infinitely many $(x,y)\in C$ , by pigeonhole we can find a pair $(\omega,\omega^{\prime})\in\mu_{d^{n}}\times\mu_{e^{n}}$ such that $(\omega x,\omega^{\prime}y)\in C$ for infinitely many $x,y$ . This implies that $(\omega,\omega^{\prime})$ is in our stabilizer $G$ .

If $G$ is a finite set, since $d_{n}$ is unbounded we may choose $n$ large enough such that $d_{n}>|G|$ . Then for most $(x,y)\in C$ , we can find a pair $(\omega,\omega^{\prime})\in\mu_{d^{n}}\times\mu_{e^{n}}$ such that $(\omega,\omega^{\prime})\not\in G$ and $(\omega x,\omega^{\prime}y)\in C$ . Again by pigeonhole, we can find a pair $(\omega,\omega^{\prime})\not\in G$ such that $(\omega x,\omega^{\prime}y)\in C$ for infinitely many pairs $(x,y)$ . This contradicts $(\omega,\omega^{\prime})\not\in G$ and thus $G$ must be infinite.

In particular, $G$ must be positive dimensional. Since $C$ is an irreducible curve and is stabilized by $G$ , it must be a translate of $G$ as desired. ∎

We now move onto the case where $C\subseteq\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}$ is possibly analytic and we have to possibly restrict to an open ball. Here, we will add in an additional assumption that the closure of $C$ passes through $(0,0)$ inside $\mathbb{A}^{2}$ . The proof of Proposition 4.2 no longer applies since there are many analytic subgroups of $\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}$ that are not algebraic. For example, the curve parametrized by $f(t)=(e^{t},e^{t\alpha})$ with $\alpha$ irrational will be an analytic subgroup that is not algebraic. We instead directly analyze the Puiseux series of $C$ .

#### Lemma 4.3.

Let $\mathbb{D}_{r}\subset\mathbb{C}$ be an open disc of radius $r$ with $r<1$ and let $C\subset(\mathbb{D}_{r})^{2}$ be a non-horizontal/vertical complex analytic curve passing through $(0,0)$ . Let $\varphi:(\mathbb{D}_{r})^{2}\to(\mathbb{D}_{r})^{2}$ be given by $(z^{d},z^{e})$ where $d,e\geq 2$ . Assume that the degree of $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ is unbounded as $n\to\infty$ . Then $C$ must contain the analytic curve given by $(z^{i},cz^{j})$ for $z$ near $0$ , some $i,j\in\mathbb{N}$ and $c\in\mathbb{C^{\ast}}$ .

#### Proof.

We may assume that $C$ is given by the zero locus of a power series $F(x,y)=0$ near $(0,0)$ . By Puiseux’s theorem, we may parametrize its branches by $(z^{j},a(z))$ for some $j>0$ and where $a(z)$ is a power series in $z$ that converges near $0$ . Let $C_{1},\ldots,C_{r}$ be the branches of $C$ at $(0,0)$ . Then for some $i$ , the degree of $\varphi^{n}:C_{i}\to\varphi^{n}(C_{i})$ is unbounded as $n\to\infty$ . Thus we may assume that $C$ is given by $C_{i}$ and so that $C$ is parametrized by some $(z^{j},a(z))$ .

As in the proof of Proposition 4.2, we know that the stabilizer of $C$ contains infinitely many pairs of roots of unity $(\omega_{i},\omega_{i}^{\prime})$ . In particular, for any $z$ near $0$ we must have

$$ (\omega_{i}z^{j},\omega_{i}^{\prime}a(z))=((z^{\prime})^{j},a(z^{\prime})) $$

for some other $z^{\prime}$ near $0$ . Then $z^{\prime}=\omega z$ where $\omega^{j}=\omega_{i}$ and $a(\omega z)=\omega_{i}^{\prime}a(z)$ . Since there are only finitely many possible $\omega$ ’s, there exists a $\omega$ satisfying $\omega^{j}=\omega_{i}$ such that $a(\omega z)=\omega_{i}^{\prime}a(z)$ for infinitely many $z$ and so $a(\omega z)=\omega_{i}^{\prime}a(z)$ as power series.

Now assume that $a(z)$ is not a monomial. If $j_{1}$ and $j_{2}$ are the two smallest degrees with non-zero coefficients of $a(z)$ , by comparing the coefficients we must have

$$ \omega^{j_{1}}=\omega^{j_{2}}=\omega_{i}^{\prime}. $$

Hence $\omega^{j_{2}-j_{1}}=1$ and so the order of $\omega$ is bounded. This implies that the order of both $\omega_{i}$ and $\omega_{i}^{\prime}$ are bounded, which is a contradiction as the stabilizer contains infinitely many distinct pairs. Hence $a(z)$ must be a monomial and so $C$ is of the form $\{x^{i}=cy^{j}\}$ . ∎

We now move onto the general case where $f,g$ are both polynomials of degree $d,e\geq 2$ . We will be assuming that $f$ is not exceptional. As mentioned at the beginning of the section, we will use the Bottcher coordinates to conjugate to the situation of $(z^{d},z^{e})$ and then apply Lemma 4.3. However Lemma 4.3 requires our curve $C$ to pass through $(0,0)$ and so we will need to show that $C$ passes through a pair of superattracting periodic points.

#### Lemma 4.4.

Let $f,g$ be polynomials of degree $d,e\geq 2$ and let $C\subseteq(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ be a curve. Let $\varphi$ be the endomorphism $(f,g)$ and assume that the degree of $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ is unbounded as $n\to\infty$ . Then there exists $\alpha$ such that $(\infty,\alpha)\in C$ and the forward orbit of $\alpha$ under $g$ contains a superattracting periodic point for $g$ . Furthermore, the local degree of $\varphi^{n}$ when restricted to $C$ at $(\infty,\alpha)$ is unbounded as $n$ goes to infinity.

#### Proof.

If $(\infty,\infty)\in C$ , then we are done. Otherwise, we let $\{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{r}\}$ be the points of $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ such that $(\infty,\alpha_{i})\in C$ . For convenience, we will let $p_{i}=(\infty,\alpha_{i})$ . Let $d_{n}$ be the degree of $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ . Then for any open set $U\subseteq C$ , we have that

$$ \varphi^{n}:(\varphi^{n})^{-1}(\varphi^{n}(U))\to\varphi^{n}(U) $$

is a $d_{n}$ to $1$ map. For each $n$ , we let $U_{n}$ be a small open neighbourhood around $p_{1}$ . If we take $U_{n}$ sufficiently small depending on $n$ , the preimage $(\varphi^{-n})(\varphi^{n}(U_{n}))$ splits into disjoint open sets, each containing a point of $\varphi^{-n}(\varphi^{n}(p_{1}))$ that lies on $C$ . But since $\infty$ is totally invariant by $f$ , we know that

$$ \varphi^{-n}(\varphi^{n}(p_{1}))\cap C\subseteq\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{r}\} $$

which is a finite set independent of $n$ . Thus for each $n$ , we can find some $1\leq i\leq r$ and a neighbourhood $V$ about $p_{i}$ in $C$ such that $\varphi^{n}:V_{i}\to\varphi^{n}(V_{i})$ has degree $\geq\frac{d_{n}}{r}$ . We can then find a fixed $p_{i}$ such that as $n$ goes to infinity, we can find an open neighbourhood $V_{n}$ such that the degree of $\varphi^{n}:V_{n}\to\varphi^{n}(V_{n})$ goes to infinity.

If we let $\pi_{i}:(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}$ denote the projection maps for $i=1,2$ . We have the following commutative diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V_{n}\cap C} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi^{n}(V_{n})\cap\varphi^{n}(C)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{2}(V_{n}\cap C)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g^{n}(\pi_{2}(V_{n}\cap C)).} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi^{n}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{2}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{2}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g^{n}} $$

Since the degree of $\varphi^{n}|_{V_{n}\cap C}$ goes to infinity, it follows that the degree of $g^{n}:\pi_{2}(V_{n})\to\pi_{2}(\varphi^{n}(V_{n}))$ goes to infinity as well. Since $\alpha_{i}\in\pi_{2}(V_{n}\cap C)$ for all $n$ , it follows that the multiplicity of $\alpha_{i}$ as a root of $g^{n}(z)=g^{n}(\alpha_{i})$ goes to infinity as $n\to\infty$ . By [27, Lemma 4.3], this implies that the forward orbit of $\alpha_{i}$ contains a superattracting periodic point as desired. ∎

With Lemma 4.4, we can apply Lemma 4.3 along with the results of Section 3 to deduce that the bidegree of $\varphi^{n}(C)$ must grow on the order of $(e^{n},d^{n})$ unless some forward image of $C$ is invariant under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ .

#### Theorem 4.5.

Let $f,g\in\mathbb{C}[x]$ be polynomials of degrees $d,e\geq 2$ , respectively, and let $C\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be an ample irreducible curve defined over $\mathbb{C}$ . Assume that one of the following conditions holds:

- (1) $f$ is non-exceptional, and $C$ is not preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ for any $a,b\geq 1$ ; or

- (2) both $f$ and $g$ are exceptional, and $C$ is not a weakly $(f,g)$ -special curve.

If $(a_{n},b_{n})$ denotes the bidegree of $\varphi^{n}(C)$ , then there exists $M\in\mathbb{N}$ such that

$$ (a_{n},b_{n})=\frac{1}{M}(e^{n}a_{0},d^{n}b_{0}) $$

for all sufficiently large $n$ , where $(a_{0},b_{0})$ is the bidegree of $C$ .

#### Proof.

First, suppose that both $f$ and $g$ are exceptional. Using the standard semiconjugacy from an exceptional polynomial to a power map given by the identity in the monomial case and by $z\mapsto z+z^{-1}$ in the Chebyshev case, we reduce to the case of $(f,g)=(z^{d},z^{e})$ . The result then follows from Lemma 4.1 and Proposition 4.2.

Now, assume that $f$ is non-exceptional. By Lemma 4.1, we know that

$$ (a_{n},b_{n})=\frac{1}{d_{n}}(e^{n}a_{0},d^{n}b_{0}) $$

where $d_{n}$ is the degree of $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ . Hence it suffices to prove that $d_{n}$ is eventually constant. Since $d_{n}$ is a non-decreasing sequence of positive integers, it suffices to prove that if $d_{n}$ is unbounded, then there is a forward image of $C$ under $\varphi$ which is $(f^{a},g^{b})$ -invariant.

Now assume that $d_{n}$ is unbounded as $n\to\infty$ . By Lemma 4.4, there exists $\alpha$ such that $(\infty,\alpha)\in C$ and the forward orbit of $\alpha$ under $g$ contains a superattracting periodic point of $g$ . By replacing $C$ with a forward image under $\varphi$ , we may assume that $\alpha$ is a superattracting periodic point. Also by replacing $\varphi$ with an iterate $\varphi^{k}$ , we may assume that $\alpha$ is a superattracting fixed point, with multiplicity $e^{\prime}\geq 2$ .

Let $\Phi_{f}:B_{\infty}\simeq\mathbb{D}_{r}$ be the Bottcher coordinates for $f$ at $\infty$ and let $\Phi_{g}:B_{\alpha}\simeq\mathbb{D}_{r^{\prime}}$ be the Bottcher coordinates for $g$ at $\alpha$ , where $B_{\infty},B_{\alpha}$ are neighbourhoods of $\infty$ and $\alpha$ respectively. By possibly shrinking them, we may assume that $r=r^{\prime}$ and also that $U=C\cap(B_{\infty}\times B_{\alpha})$ is an irreducible analytic curve. Then if $\Phi=(\Phi_{f},\Phi_{g})$ , we have that $\Phi(U)$ is an analytic curve in $(\mathbb{D}_{r})^{2}$ .

By Lemma 4.4, we know that the local degree of $\varphi^{n}$ when restricted to $C$ at $(\infty,\alpha)$ is unbounded. Since $(\infty,\alpha)$ is superattracting, we know that $\varphi^{n}(U)\subseteq U$ . In particular, if we let $\phi=(z^{d},z^{e^{\prime}})$ , this means that the degree of $\phi^{n}:\Phi(U)\to\phi^{n}(\Phi(U))$ is unbounded as $n\to\infty$ . By Lemma 4.3, this means that $\Phi(U)$ contains an analytic curve given by $(cz^{i},z^{j})$ for $z$ near $0$ , some $i,j\in\mathbb{N}$ and $c\in\mathbb{C}$ .

If we let $\Psi_{f},\Psi_{g}$ be the inverse of the Bottcher coordinates of $f$ at $\infty$ and $g$ at $\alpha$ , then $(\Psi_{f},\Psi_{g})$ is the inverse to $\Phi$ . Thus if $P$ is the irreducible polynomial defining $C$ , this implies that

$$ P(\Psi_{f}(cz^{i}),\Psi_{g}(z^{j}))=0 $$

for all $z$ near $0$ . As $C$ is not horizontal nor vertical, we know that $c\not=0$ . Since $f$ is non-exceptional, we can then apply Theorem 3.1 to conclude that some forward image of $C$ under $(f,g)$ is invariant under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ as desired. ∎

## 5. Intersection multiplicity growth at fixed points

The goal of this section is to prove Theorem 5.5, from which Theorem 1.11 follows. Recall that in Theorem 1.11, we are interested in bounding from above the intersection multiplicity of $\varphi^{n}(C)$ and $C^{\prime}$ at $p$ as $n$ goes to infinity where $p$ is assumed to be a fixed point under the product map $(f,g)$ .

Let $C_{1},\ldots,C_{r}$ be the branches of $C$ at $p$ . Then the branches of $\varphi^{n}(C)$ at $p$ are given by $\varphi^{n}(C_{1}),\ldots,\varphi^{n}(C_{r})$ . Given a branch $C_{i}$ , we may parametrize it by $(a(z),b(z))$ , where $a(z),b(z)$ are power series, so that $\varphi^{n}(C_{i})$ is parametrized by $(f^{n}(a(z)),g^{n}(b(z)))$ . If $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ is injective, then $(f^{n}(a(z)),g^{n}(b(z)))$ will be a good parametrization of $\varphi^{n}(C_{i})$ if $(a(z),b(z))$ is a good parametrization for $C_{i}$ . Thus to understand the intersection multiplicity $i_{p}(\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime})$ , it suffices to understand

$$ \operatorname{ord}_{z}(P(f^{n}(a(z)),g^{n}(b(z)))) $$

where $\operatorname{ord}_{z}$ is the order of vanishing at $z=0$ and $P$ is the defining equation of $C^{\prime}$ . Our approach to analyzing the growth rate of the order of vanishing follows the strategy of [1, Theorem 1] and uses the Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem to show that the multiplicities exhibit the expected growth.

We start with the following proposition, which is key to our analysis of the case when $(f,g)$ is fixed at $p=(p_{1},p_{2})$ and $f$ and $g$ have local degree at least $2$ at $p_{1}$ and $p_{2}$ , respectively.

#### Proposition 5.1.

Let $P_{1},\ldots,P_{r}\in\mathbb{C}[[z]]$ be non-zero power series such that $P_{i}(0)\not=0$ for all $i=1,2,\ldots,r$ . Let $c_{1},\ldots,c_{r}$ be non-zero complex numbers. Then

$$ \operatorname{ord}_{z}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{r}c_{i}P_{i}(z)^{n}\right) $$

is bounded unless $P_{i}(z)/P_{j}(z)$ is a root of unity for some $i\not=j$ .

To prove Proposition 5.1, we need two auxiliary lemmas. The first is about the coefficient of $z^{m}$ in $P_{i}(z)^{n}$ .

#### Lemma 5.2.

Let $P(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}a_{i}z^{i}$ with $a_{0}\not=0$ . Then the coefficient of $z^{m}$ in $P(z)^{n}$ is given by $Q_{m}(n)a_{0}^{n}$ , where $Q_{m}(x)$ is a polynomial of degree at most $m$ that depends only on the coefficients $a_{0},\dots,a_{m}$ .

#### Proof.

The proof is by induction on $m$ . The base case $m=0$ is clear since the constant coefficient in $P(z)^{n}$ is equal to $a_{0}^{n}$ . This shows that

$$ Q_{0}(n)=1, $$

for all $n\geq 0$ .

Now suppose that the coefficient of $z^{k}$ in $P(z)^{n}$ is given by $Q_{k}(n)a_{0}^{n}$ for all $0\leq k\leq m-1$ where $Q_{k}$ is a polynomial of degree $k$ depending only on the coefficients $a_{0},\dots,a_{k}$ . Let $a_{m,n}$ be the coefficient of $z^{m}$ in $P(z)^{n}$ . We can write

$$ \displaystyle P(z)^{n+1} \displaystyle=P(z)^{n}P(z) \displaystyle=\left(a_{0}^{n}Q_{0}(n)+\cdots a_{0}^{n}Q_{m-1}(n)z^{m-1}+a_{m,n}z^{m}+\cdots\right)(a_{0}+\cdots+a_{m}z^{m}+\cdots). $$

This shows that

$$ a_{m,n+1}=a_{0}a_{m,n}+a_{0}^{n}Q_{m-1}(n)a_{1}+\cdots+a_{0}^{n}Q_{0}(n)a_{m}. $$

Define $a^{\prime}_{m,n}=\frac{a_{m,n}}{a_{0}^{n}}$ for all $n\geq 0$ . Then, by the above equation we get

$$ a^{\prime}_{m,n+1}=a^{\prime}_{m,n}+\frac{\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}Q_{i}(n)a_{m-i}}{a_{0}}. $$

By the inductive hypothesis

$$ \frac{\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}Q_{i}(n)a_{m-i}}{a_{0}} $$

is a polynomial of degree at most $m-1$ depending only on $a_{0},\dots,a_{m}$ . Therefore, the above recurrence from (7) shows that $a^{\prime}_{m,n}$ must be a polynomial of degree at most $m$ depending only on the coefficients $a_{0},\dots,a_{m}$ . The desired conclusion follows since $a_{m,n}=a^{\prime}_{m,n}a_{0}^{n}$ . ∎

The second lemma is about the case when $\sum_{i=1}^{r}c_{i}P_{i}(z)^{n}$ is identically zero.

#### Lemma 5.3.

Let $P_{1},\ldots,P_{r}\in\mathbb{C}[[z]]$ be non-zero power series and let $Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{r}$ be non-zero power series too. If

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{r}Q_{i}(z)P_{i}(z)^{n}=0 $$

for all $n\equiv k\pmod{l}$ , where $k,l$ are positive integers, then $P_{i}(z)/P_{j}(z)$ is a root of unity for some $i\not=j$ .

#### Proof.

First, by replacing $Q_{i}(z)$ with $Q_{i}(z)P_{i}(z)^{k}$ and $P_{i}(z)$ with $P_{i}(z)^{l}$ , it suffices to prove that $\sum_{i=1}^{r}Q_{i}(z)P_{i}(z)^{n}=0$ for all $n\geq 1$ , then $P_{i}(z)=P_{j}(z)$ for some $i\not=j$ .

We now consider the expression

$$ P_{1}(z)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{r}Q_{i}(z)P_{i}(z)^{n}\right)-\sum_{i=1}^{r}Q_{i}(z)P_{i}(z)^{n+1}=\sum_{i=2}^{r}\big(P_{1}(z)Q_{i}(z)-P_{i}(z)Q_{i}(z)\big)P_{i}(z)^{n}=0. $$

If any of $P_{1}(z)Q_{i}(z)-P_{i}(z)Q_{i}(z)=0$ , we obtain $P_{1}(z)=P_{i}(z)$ as desired. Else, we obtain the case of $r-1$ power series. If $r=2$ , then since $P_{2}(z)\not=0$ , we must have $P_{1}(z)=P_{2}(z)$ . If $r>2$ , we can apply induction and we are done. ∎

We can now prove Proposition 5.1.

#### Proof of Proposition 5.1.

Suppose there is an increasing sequence of positive integers $\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}$ such that $\operatorname{ord}_{z}(\sum_{i=1}^{r}c_{i}P_{i}(z)^{a_{n}})$ goes to $\infty$ as $n$ goes to $\infty$ . For each $i$ , we write $P_{i}(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{ij}z^{j}$ . Then by Lemma 5.2, the coefficient of $z^{m}$ in $P_{i}(z)^{n}$ is given by $Q_{i,m}(n)a_{i0}^{n}$ where $Q_{i,m}$ is a polynomial of degree $m$ that depends only on the coefficients of $P_{i}$ , since $a_{i0}\not=0$ .

Hence by our assumption that $\operatorname{ord}_{z}(\sum_{i=1}^{r}c_{i}P_{i}(z)^{a_{n}})$ going to $\infty$ as $n$ goes to $\infty$ , we have that

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{r}c_{i}Q_{i,m}(a_{n})a_{i0}^{a_{n}}=0 $$

for all sufficiently large $n$ , depending on $m$ . We now apply Proposition 3.2 of [12], or more precisely the discussion before Proposition 3.2. Letting

$$ b_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}c_{i}Q_{i,m}(n)a_{i0}^{n}, $$

we may split it into a finite disjoint union of nondegenerate linear recurrences, each of the form $c_{n}=b_{nk+l}$ for some $k$ and $l$ , that depend only on the coefficients $a_{i0}$ and not on $m$ . Then by [12, Proposition 3.2], as one of these nondegenerate linear recurrence must attain $0$ infinitely many times, it must be identically $0$ . In particular we can find $k$ and $l$ such that

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{r}c_{i}Q_{i,m}(n)a_{i0}^{n}=0 $$

for all $n\equiv k\pmod{l}$ .

Observe that $k,l$ depend only on $a_{i0}$ and not on $m$ . In particular, we obtain

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{r}c_{i}P_{i}(z)^{n}=0 $$

for all $n\equiv k\pmod{l}$ . By Lemma 5.3, this implies that $P_{i}(z)/P_{j}(z)$ is a root of unity for some $i\not=j$ as desired. ∎

The following lemma allows us to change to a more convenient coordinate system in our proof of Theorem 5.5.

#### Lemma 5.4.

Let $F(x,y)\in\mathbb{C}[[x,y]]$ and suppose $\sigma_{1}(x),\sigma_{2}(x)\in\mathbb{C}[[x]]$ are such that $\sigma_{1}(0)=\sigma_{2}(0)=0$ . Let $\ell_{1},\ell_{2}$ be positive integers and let $S$ be the set of $(i,j)$ for which $x^{i}y^{j}$ has a non-zero coefficient for $F$ and let $T$ be the corresponding set for $F(\sigma_{1}(x),\sigma_{2}(y))$ . Then,

$$ \min_{(i,j)\in S}\{\ell_{1}i+\ell_{2}j\}\leq\min_{(i,j)\in T}\{\ell_{1}i+\ell_{2}j\}. $$

Moreover, equality happens if both $\sigma_{1}$ and $\sigma_{2}$ have an inverse under composition in $\mathbb{C}[[x]]$ .

#### Proof.

We have

$$ F(\sigma_{1}(x),\sigma_{2}(y))=\sum_{i,j\in S}a_{i,j}\sigma_{1}(x)^{i}\sigma_{2}(y)^{j} $$

For each term $a_{i,j}\sigma_{1}(x)^{i}\sigma_{2}(y)^{j}$ , since $\sigma_{1}(0)=\sigma_{2}(0)=0$ , the monomials appearing in

$$ a_{i,j}\sigma_{1}(x)^{i}\sigma_{2}(y)^{j} $$

are all divisible by $x^{i}y^{j}$ . Thus certainly we must have

$$ \min_{(i,j)\in T}\{l_{1}i+l_{2}j\}\geq\min_{(i,j)\in S}\{l_{1}i+l_{2}j\}. $$

Note that if $\sigma_{1}$ and $\sigma_{2}$ have inverses $\sigma_{1}^{-1}$ and $\sigma_{2}^{-1}$ , then applying the lemma to $(F,\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2})$ and then to $(F(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}),\sigma_{1}^{-1},\sigma_{2}^{-1})$ we get

$$ \min_{(i,j)\in S}\{\ell_{1}i+\ell_{2}j\}\leq\min_{(i,j)\in T}\{\ell_{1}i+\ell_{2}j\}\leq\min_{(i,j)\in S}\{\ell_{1}i+\ell_{2}j\} $$

which gives us the second conclusion of the lemma. ∎

We can now prove our main theorem that computes the intersection multiplicity $\operatorname{mult}_{p}(\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime})$ at a fixed point $p$ for $\varphi$ . To simplify the situation, we will replace $C$ with an analytic branch at $p$ , so that $C$ is given by a good parametrization $(a(z),b(z))$ . We will also assume that $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ is injective, which Section 4 shows we can usually assume. By translating, we may assume that $p=(0,0)$ is the origin of $\mathbb{A}^{2}$ .

#### Theorem 5.5.

Let $f,g$ be convergent power series in $\mathbb{C}\{z\}$ such that $(0,0)\in(\mathbb{A}^{1})^{2}$ is a fixed point for $\varphi=(f,g)$ . Let $C$ be an analytic branch passing through $(0,0)$ with good parametrization $(a(z),b(z))$ and let $C^{\prime}$ be an analytic curve given by

$$ F(x,y)=\sum_{(i,j)\in S}c_{i,j}x^{i}y^{j} $$

where $S$ is a subset of $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{2}$ and $c_{i,j}$ are non-zero complex numbers. Suppose that the branch $C$ is not preperiodic under $\varphi$ and the restriction $\varphi^{n}:C\longrightarrow\varphi^{n}(C)$ is locally injective for every $n\geq 1$ . Then, we have

$$ i_{(0,0)}(\varphi^{n}(C),C^{\prime})=\min_{(i,j)\in S}\{d^{n}k_{1}i+e^{n}k_{2}j\}+O(1) $$

where

$$ \operatorname{ord}_{z}(f(z))=d,\,\operatorname{ord}_{z}(g(z))=e,\,\operatorname{ord}_{z}(a(z))=k_{1}\text{ and }\operatorname{ord}_{z}(b(z))=k_{2}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ is injective,

$$ (f^{\circ n}(a(z)),g^{\circ n}(b(z))) $$

is a good parametrization for $\varphi^{n}(C)$ . Thus we have

$$ i_{(0,0)}(\varphi^{n}(C),C^{\prime})=\operatorname{ord}_{z}\left(\sum_{(i,j)\in S}c_{i,j}f^{\circ n}(a(z))^{i}g^{\circ n}(b(z))^{j}\right). $$

Suppose we have proven the theorem for an iterate $\varphi^{M}$ instead of $\varphi$ . Observe that replacing $C$ with $\varphi^{j}(C)$ , changes $(k_{1},k_{2})$ to $(d^{j}k_{1},e^{j}k_{2})$ . So, for any $0\leq j\leq M-1$ we must have

$$ \displaystyle i_{(0,0)}(\varphi^{Mn+j}(C),C^{\prime})=i_{(0,0)}(\varphi^{Mn}(\varphi^{j}(C)),C^{\prime}) \displaystyle=\min_{(i,j)\in S}\{d^{Mn}d^{j}k_{1}i+e^{Mn}e^{j}k_{2}j\}+O(1) \displaystyle=\min_{(i,j)\in S}\{d^{Mn+j}k_{1}i+e^{Mn+j}k_{2}j\}+O(1). $$

Therefore, it suffices to prove Theorem 5.5 for an iterate $\varphi^{M}$ instead of $\varphi$ .

Case 1: $d\not=e$ . Let us assume $d>e$ . The order of vanishing of each term is given by $d^{n}k_{1}i+e^{n}k_{2}j$ . Then since $d>e$ , for suitably large values of $n$ there is a unique minimal value among $d^{n}ik_{1}+e^{n}jk_{2}$ with $(i,j)\in S$ . Indeed, it is given by $(i^{\prime},j^{\prime})$ where $i^{\prime}$ minimizes all values of $i$ that appear in $S$ , and $j^{\prime}$ minimizes all values of $j$ that the pair $(i^{\prime},j)$ appears in $S$ . Thus for large enough $n$ , we have

$$ \operatorname{ord}_{z}\left(\sum_{i,j\in S}c_{i,j}f^{n}(a(z))^{i}g^{n}(b(z))^{j}\right)=d^{n}i^{\prime}k_{1}+e^{n}k_{2}j^{\prime}=\min_{(i,j)\in S}\{d^{n}k_{1}i+e^{n}k_{2}j\} $$

as desired.

Case 2: $d=e=1$ . This case follows from [1, Theorem 1].

Case 3: $d=e\geq 2$ . Since $0$ is a fixed point for both $f$ and $g$ of multiplicity at least 2, we can conjugate them to the form $z^{d}$ . If $\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}$ are the conjugacies for $f$ and $g$ respectively, we may formally conjugate $(f,g),(a(z),b(z))$ and $F(x,y)$ by $(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2})$ and thus assume that $f(z)=g(z)=z^{d}$ . We may assume so since, by Lemma 5.4, this does not change the minimum of $\{d^{n}k_{1}i+e^{n}k_{2}j\}$ . Thus we would like to compute

$$ \operatorname{ord}_{z}\left(\sum_{(i,j)\in S}c_{i,j}a(z)^{d^{n}i}b(z)^{d^{n}j}\right)=\operatorname{ord}_{z}\left(\sum_{(i,j)\in S}c_{i,j}\left(a(z)^{i}b(z)^{j}\right)^{d^{n}}\right). $$

Let $L=\min_{(i,j)\in S}\{k_{1}i+k_{2}j\}$ . Then $z^{L}\mid a(z)^{i}b(z)^{j}$ for any $(i,j)\in S$ . Factoring it out, we wish to show that

$$ \operatorname{ord}_{z}\left(\sum_{(i,j)\in S}\left(\frac{a(z)^{i}b(z)^{j}}{z^{L}}\right)^{d^{n}}\right) $$

is uniformly bounded over all $n\geq 1$ . Let $S^{\prime}$ be the subset of pairs $(i,j)$ for which $k_{1}i+k_{2}j=L$ . Then it suffices to show that

$$ \operatorname{ord}_{z}\left(\sum_{(i,j)\in S^{\prime}}\left(\frac{a(z)^{i}b(z)^{j}}{z^{L}}\right)^{d^{n}}\right) $$

is uniformly bounded over all $n\geq 1$ as the other terms will vanish to an order that goes to $\infty$ as $n$ goes to $\infty$ . Let $A_{i,j}(z)=\frac{a(z)^{i}b(z)^{j}}{z^{L}}$ . Then for $(i,j)\in S^{\prime}$ , we have $A_{i,j}(0)\not=0$ . Thus we are in the position to apply Proposition 5.1 and deduce that the order of vanishing is bounded, unless

$$ \frac{a(z)^{i}b(z)^{j}}{z^{L}}=\zeta^{\prime}\frac{a(z)^{i^{\prime}}b(z)^{j^{\prime}}}{z^{L}} $$

for some root of unity $\zeta^{\prime}$ and distinct pairs $(i,j),(i^{\prime},j^{\prime})$ . This implies that $\frac{a(z)^{i}}{b(z)^{j}}$ is a root of unity $\zeta$ for some integers $i,j$ that are both non-zero.

If this is the case, then we can find an infinite sequence of positive integers $\{n_{i}\}$ such that $\zeta^{d^{n_{i}}}$ are all equal, say to $\tilde{\zeta}$ . Then $(a(z)^{d^{n_{i}}},b(z)^{d^{n_{i}}})$ give rise to a solution to $x^{i}=\tilde{\zeta}y^{j}$ and hence form an analytic branch of it, since in the case of $d=e\geq 2$ , the conjugacy actually converges in a neighbourhood. Since there are only finitely many analytic branches, there must exist $i,j$ such that $(a(z)^{d^{n_{i}}},b(z)^{d^{n_{i}}})$ and $(a(z)^{d^{n_{j}}},b(z)^{d^{n_{j}}})$ define the same branch. Conjugating back, this implies that $\varphi^{n_{i}}(C)=\varphi^{n_{j}}(C)$ and so $C$ is preperiodic, which is a contradiction. Thus

$$ \operatorname{ord}_{z}\left(\sum_{(i,j)\in S^{\prime}}\left(\frac{a(z)^{i}b(z)^{j}}{z^{L}}\right)^{d^{n}}\right) $$

is bounded independently of $n$ as desired. ∎

We end this section by noting that Theorem 1.11 follows immediately from Theorem 5.5.

## 6. Finiteness of Backward Orbit on Curves

The aim of this section is to prove the following result which will be needed in the proof of Theorem 1.7.

#### Theorem 6.1.

Let $C\subset\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be an ample irreducible curve over $\mathbb{C}$ and $\varphi=(f,g):(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}\to(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ a product endomorphism of rational maps over $\mathbb{C}$ with degrees $d_{1},d_{2}\geq 2$ . Let $p\in(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}(\mathbb{C})$ be a non-periodic point for $\varphi$ such that $p\in\varphi^{n}(C)$ for infinitely many positive integers $n$ . Then $C$ is preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ for some $a,b\geq 1$ .

Clearly we may reduce to the case where $(f,g,C)$ are all defined over a field $K$ which is finitely generated over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . If $K=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , then Theorem 6.1 follows easily from the dynamical Bogomolov conjecture for $(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{n}$ proven by Ghioca–Nguyen–Ye [11, 10].

In general, we would like to apply the strategy used by Mavraki and the second named author in [18, Section 5] by reducing to the case of function fields over a curve. We thus need a geometric dynamical Bogomolov conjecture for $(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ . Such a result was proven by Mavraki–Schmidt [17], but only when $f,g$ are of the same degree. Luckily for us, it is straightforward to modify their argument to the case of different degrees, which we will do so now.

Let $K=k(B)$ be the function field of a smooth projective curve over an algebraically closed characteristic zero field $k$ and let $\varphi=(f,g)$ be our product endomorphism on $(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ that is defined over $K$ . For $p=(x,y)\in(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}(\overline{K})$ , we set $\widehat{h}_{\varphi}(p):=\widehat{h}_{f}(x)+\widehat{h}_{g}(y)$ .

#### Proposition 6.2.

Assume that both $f$ and $g$ are not isotrivial. Let $C\subseteq(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ be an ample irreducible curve that contains a generic sequence of points $\{p_{n}\}$ with $\widehat{h}_{\varphi}(p_{n})\to 0$ . Then $C$ is $(f^{a},g^{b})$ -preperiodic for some $a,b\geq 1$ .

#### Proof.

We apply [16, Theorem 1.1] to obtain that outside of finitely many exceptions for $p=(x,y)\in C(\overline{K})$ , we have

$$ \widehat{h}_{f}(x)=0\implies\widehat{h}_{\varphi}(p)=0. $$

It follows that $C$ contains infinitely many preperiodic points $p=(x,y)$ by choosing $x$ to be preperiodic, as $f,g$ are both not isotrivial and hence $\widehat{h}_{g}(y)=0$ implies that $y$ is preperiodic. We now apply [10, Theorem 1.1], which gives us $a,b\geq 1$ such that $C$ is preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ as desired. ∎

We now handle the case where at least one of $f$ or $g$ is isotrivial. Here, we say $f$ is isotrivial to mean there exists a mobius transformation $M$ such that $M\circ f\circ M^{-1}$ is defined over $\overline{k}$ .

#### Proposition 6.3.

Assume that $f$ is isotrivial. Let $C\subseteq(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ be an ample irreducible curve that contains a sequence of points $\{p_{n}\}$ with $\widehat{h}_{\varphi}(p_{n})\to 0$ . Then $g$ is also isotrivial. Furthermore if $M_{1},M_{2}$ are möbius transformations such that $M_{1}\circ f\circ M_{1}^{-1}$ and $M_{2}\circ g\circ M_{2}^{-1}$ are both defined over $k$ , then $(M_{1},M_{2})(C)$ is also defined over $k$ .

#### Proof.

Again by [16, Theorem 1.1], outside of finitely many exceptions for $p=(x,y)\in C(\overline{K})$ , we have

$$ \widehat{h}_{f}(x)=0\implies\widehat{h}_{\varphi}(p)=0. $$

Now assume without loss of generality that $k=\overline{k}$ . Since $f$ is isotrivial, all preperiodic points of $f$ are defined over a finite extension $K^{\prime}$ of $K$ . Each such preperiodic point $x$ corresponds to a $\varphi$ -preperiodic point $p$ on $C$ and hence a $g$ -preperiodic point $y$ . Furthermore as $(x,y)$ lie on a curve $C$ , it follows that $y$ is defined over a finite extension $L$ of $K^{\prime}$ with $[L:K^{\prime}]$ bounded solely in terms of $\deg C$ . Applying [17, Corollary 4.9], it follows that $g$ is also isotrivial.

Now assuming that $g$ is isotrivial, it follows that $(M_{1},M_{2})(C)$ contains infinitely many $(M_{1}\circ f\circ M_{1}^{-1},M_{2}\circ g\circ M_{2}^{-1})$ -preperiodic points and hence infinitely many points of $(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}(k)$ . Then $(M_{1},M_{2})(C)$ must be defined over $k$ as desired. ∎

We are now ready to begin the proof of Theorem 6.1.

#### Proof of Theorem 6.1.

We may assume that $f,g$ and $C$ are all defined over $K$ which is finitely generated over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . We will induct on the transcendence degree of $K$ .

We first handle the case where $\operatorname{trdeg}(K)=0$ , i.e. $K\subseteq\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Then there exist infinitely many $p_{n}$ such that $\varphi^{n}(p_{n})=p$ and $p_{n}\in C$ . Since $p$ is non-periodic, each $p_{n}$ is distinct and if $p_{n}=(x_{n},y_{n})$ and $\deg f,\deg g\geq 2$ , we have

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\widehat{h}_{f}(x_{n})=\widehat{h}_{g}(y_{n})=0. $$

Thus by [10, Theorem 1.1], it must be that $C$ is preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ as desired.

We now handle the case where $\operatorname{trdeg}(K)=m+1$ , assuming the case of $\operatorname{trdeg}(K)=m$ . Taking the compositum with $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , we may assume that $K=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(V)$ for some normal projective irreducible variety $V$ by [4, 1.4.10]. Pick $m$ algebraically independent elements $t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}$ and let $k$ be the algebraic closure of $t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}$ inside $K$ . Then $K$ is finitely generated and of transcendence degree one over $k$ . Since $k$ is algebraically closed in $K$ , it follows that $K=k(B)$ for a smooth projective curve $B$ over $k$ . We may replace $k$ with $\overline{k}$ and hence assume that $k$ is algebraically closed.

Now as in the case of $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , we have a sequence of distinct points $\{p_{n}\}$ with $\widehat{h}_{\varphi}(p_{n})\to 0$ that lie on $C$ . If $f,g$ are both not isotrivial, it follows that $C$ is $(f^{a},g^{b})$ -preperiodic by Proposition 6.2. If $f,g$ are isotrivial, then if $M_{1}\circ f\circ M_{1}^{-1},M_{2}\circ g\circ M_{2}^{-1}$ are both defined over $k$ where $M_{1},M_{2}$ are mobius transformations, by Proposition 6.3 it follows that $(M_{1},M_{2})(C)$ is also defined over $k$ . Conjugating by $M_{1},M_{2}$ , we are reduced to the case where $\operatorname{trdeg}(K)=m$ , which we may now conclude by induction as desired. ∎

## 7. Proof of Theorem 1.7

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.7. Recall that the theorem asserts that, if the pair $(C,C^{\prime})$ satisfies its hypotheses, then

$$ \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\varphi^{n_{i}}(C)\cap C^{\prime}\right) $$

is Zariski dense in $C^{\prime}$ , where $\varphi$ is a product polynomial endomorphism of $(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ .

Our proof follows the general strategy employed by Silverman in his proof of Theorem 1.8. We first use Theorem 1.1 to show that the degree of $\varphi^{n}(C)$ grows on the order of $\lambda_{1}(\varphi)^{n}$ . This plays the role of the exponential growth of the canonical height $\widehat{h}_{\varphi}$ under iteration in Silverman’s argument. Next, Theorem 6.1 implies that the only points of $X$ that can occur infinitely often in the intersections $\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}$ are periodic points of $\varphi$ . A crucial step is therefore to use Theorem 5.5 to bound the intersection multiplicities of $\varphi^{n}(C)$ and $C^{\prime}$ at such points. The following lemma establishes the required bound when $p$ is a non-exceptional fixed point of $\varphi$ .

#### Lemma 7.1.

Assume that $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ is injective for all $n\geq 1$ , $p$ is a fixed point of $\varphi$ , and $C^{\prime}$ is an ample irreducible curve. If either $d\not=e$ or $p$ is non-exceptional for $\varphi$ , we have

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{mult}_{p}(\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime})}{d^{n}}=0. $$

#### Proof.

Let $p=(\alpha,\beta)$ . By Theorem 5.5, if $d_{i},e_{i}$ are the multiplicity of $\alpha,\beta$ as a fixed point of $f$ and $g$ respectively, then we have

$$ \operatorname{mult}_{p}(\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime})\leq O(\min\{d_{i},e_{i}\}^{n}). $$

Thus for the limit to not go to zero, we must have $d_{i}=e_{i}=d$ , which implies that $d=e$ and that $p$ is exceptional for $\varphi$ . ∎

We now analyze the multiplicity growth of exceptional points. We first handle the case where both $f$ and $g$ are not exceptional. Then the only exceptional point is $(\infty,\infty)$ .

#### Lemma 7.2.

Let $\varphi=(f,g)$ , $f$ and $g$ be two non-exceptional polynomials of degree $d\geq 2$ , and $C$ be an ample irreducible curve in $\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ . Assume that $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ is injective for all $n\geq 1$ . Then for all $n$ and all irreducible curves $C^{\prime}\subset\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ with proper intersection with the iterates of $C$ , we have

$$ \varphi^{n}(C)\cdot C^{\prime}-i_{(\infty,\infty)}(\varphi^{n}(C),C^{\prime})\geq d^{n}+O(1). $$

#### Proof.

We may assume without loss of generality that both $C$ and $C^{\prime}$ pass through $(\infty,\infty)$ because otherwise

$$ i_{(\infty,\infty)}(\varphi^{n}(C),C^{\prime})=0 $$

for all $n\geq 0$ and the desired inequality is immediate.

Let $C^{\prime}$ be given by the polynomial $F=\sum_{(i,j)\in S}c_{i,j}x^{i}y^{j}$ and let it have bidegree $(v,u)$ . Changing charts by setting $X=\frac{1}{x}$ and $Y=\frac{1}{y}$ , we get the curve $\tilde{C^{\prime}}=\sum_{(i,j)\in S}c_{i,j}X^{v-i}Y^{u-j}$ and we are interested in the intersection multiplicity at $(0,0)$ . Let $\tilde{C_{n}}$ be our curve $\varphi^{n}(C)$ in this new chart and let the branches of $\tilde{C_{0}}$ at $(0,0)$ be given by $(t^{k_{w}}x_{w}(t),t^{s_{w}}y_{w}(t))$ where $x_{w}(0)y_{w}(0)\neq 0$ for $1\leq w\leq l$ . Then Theorem 5.5 tells us that

$$ i_{(\infty,\infty)}(\varphi^{n}(C),C^{\prime})=i_{(0,0)}(\tilde{C}_{n},\tilde{C^{\prime}})\leq\sum_{w=1}^{l}d^{n}\min_{(i,j)\in S}\{(v-i)k_{w}+(u-j)s_{w}\}+O(1). $$

Let $\tilde{C}_{n}$ have bidegree $(a_{n},b_{n})$ . Observe that

$$ \sum_{w=1}^{l}k_{w}=i_{(\infty,\infty)}(C\cap(\{\infty\}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}))\leq C\cdot(\{\infty\}\times\mathbb{P}^{1})=b_{0} $$

and similarly

$$ \sum_{w=1}^{l}s_{w}=i_{(\infty,\infty)}(C\cap(\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\{\infty\}))\leq C\cdot(\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\{\infty\})=a_{0}. $$

Hence if $(i_{1},j_{1})\in S$ such that $x^{i_{1}}y^{j_{1}}$ has non-zero coefficient, we get

$$ \sum_{w=1}^{l}\min_{(i,j)\in S}\{(v-i)k_{w}+(u-j)s_{w}\}\leq\sum_{w=1}^{l}((v-i_{1})k_{w}+(u-j_{1})s_{w}) $$

$$ \leq v\sum_{w=1}^{l}k_{w}+u\sum_{w=1}^{l}s_{w}\leq vb_{0}+ua_{0}=C\cdot C^{\prime}. $$

Equality only holds if $i_{1}=j_{1}=0$ and so if equality holds for all pairs $(i,j)\in S$ , this means that $S=\{(0,0)\}$ which is not possible. Thus

$$ \sum_{w=1}^{l}\min_{(i,j)\in S}\{(v-i)k_{w}+(u-j)s_{w}\}\leq vb_{0}+ua_{0}-1. $$

Since $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ is injective and $d=e$ , using the proof of Theorem 1.1, the bidegree of $\varphi^{n}(C)$ must be equal to $(d^{n}a_{0},d^{n}b_{0})$ . Hence,

$$ \varphi^{n}(C)\cdot C^{\prime}=d^{n}vb_{0}+d^{n}ua_{0}. $$

Using (9) and (10) we conclude that

$$ d^{n}\left(\sum_{w=1}^{l}\min_{(i,j)\in S}\{(v-i)k_{w}+(u-j)s_{w}+1\}\right)\leq\varphi^{n}(C)\cdot C^{\prime}-d^{n}. $$

Our desired inequality now follows from (8). ∎

If $g$ is exceptional. Then it is possible that $(\infty,0)$ is an exceptional point for $\varphi$ . We strengthen Lemma 7.2 to handle this too.

#### Lemma 7.3.

Let $\varphi=(f,g)$ , where $f$ is a non-exceptional polynomial of degree $d\geq 2$ and $g$ is assumed to be an exceptional polynomial of degree $d$ with $\{0,\infty\}$ as its exceptional points. Let $C$ be an ample irreducible curve in $\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ . Assume that $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ is injective for all $n\geq 1$ . If $C^{\prime}$ is non-exceptional for $\varphi$ and intersects the iterates of $C$ properly, for all $n\geq 1$ we have

$$ \varphi^{n}(C)\cdot C^{\prime}-i_{(\infty,0)}(\varphi^{n}(C),C^{\prime})-i_{(\infty,\infty)}(\varphi^{n}(C),C^{\prime})\geq d^{n}+O(1). $$

#### Proof.

If either $C$ or $C^{\prime}$ only contains one of $(\infty,\infty)$ and $(\infty,0)$ , then we may change charts and apply the same argument as Lemma 7.2. Hence we assume that $C$ contains both $(\infty,\infty)$ and $(\infty,0)$ . We again let the branches at $(\infty,\infty)$ of $C$ , after changing charts to $(0,0)$ , be given by $(t^{k_{w,1}}x_{w,1}(t),t^{s_{w,1}}y_{w,1}(t))$ for $1\leq w\leq l_{1}$ and the branches at $(\infty,0)$ be given by $(t^{k_{w,2}}x_{w,2}(t),t^{s_{w,2}}y_{w,2}(t))$ for $1\leq w\leq l_{2}$ .

Then we have

$$ i_{(\infty,\infty)}(\varphi^{n}(C),C^{\prime})\leq\sum_{w=1}^{l_{1}}d^{n}\min_{(i,j)\in S}\{(v-i)k_{w,1}+(u-j)s_{w,1}\}+O(1), $$

$$ i_{(\infty,0)}(\varphi^{n}(C),C^{\prime})\leq\sum_{w=1}^{l_{2}}d^{n}\min_{(i,j)\in S}\{(v-i)k_{w,2}+js_{w,2}\}+O(1). $$

We now observe that

$$ \sum_{w=1}^{l_{1}}k_{w,1}+\sum_{w=1}^{l_{2}}k_{w,2}=i_{(\infty,\infty)}(C,\{\infty\}\times\mathbb{P}^{1})+i_{(\infty,0)}(C,\{\infty\}\times\mathbb{P}^{1})\leq C\cdot(\{\infty\}\times\mathbb{P}^{1})=b_{0} $$

and similarly one obtains

$$ \sum_{w=1}^{l_{1}}s_{w,1}\leq a_{0},\quad\sum_{w=1}^{l_{2}}s_{w,2}\leq a_{0}. $$

Thus if $(i_{1},j_{1})\in S$ , we have

$$ \sum_{w=1}^{l_{1}}\min_{(i,j)\in S}\{(v-i)k_{w,1}+(u-j)s_{w,1}\}+\sum_{w=1}^{l_{2}}\min_{(i,j)\in S}\{(v-i)k_{w,2}+js_{w,2}\} $$

$$ \leq\sum_{w=1}^{l_{1}}\left((v-i_{1})k_{w,1}+(u-j_{1})s_{w,1}\right)+\sum_{w=1}^{l_{2}}\left((v-i_{1})k_{w,2}+j_{1}s_{w,2}\right) $$

$$ \leq(v-i_{1})b_{0}+ua_{0}\leq C\cdot C^{\prime}. $$

Now note that if we can find a pair $(i_{1},j_{1})\in S$ with $i_{1}\neq 0$ , the above inequality becomes a strict inequality and the conclusion of the lemma follows in a similar manner to Lemma 7.2. So, assume no such pair exists for the sake of a contradiction. This implies that the polynomial defining $C^{\prime}$ has no dependence on $x$ which means that $C^{\prime}$ must be a horizontal curve. This contradicts the assumption that $C^{\prime}$ passes through both $(\infty,\infty)$ and $(\infty,0)$ and finishes the proof. ∎

We are now ready to complete the proof of Theorem 1.7. We recall the statement here for convenience.

#### Theorem 7.4.

Let $\varphi=(f,g):\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be a product polynomial endomorphism defined over $\mathbb{C}$ . Assume that $f$ and $g$ are not both exceptional. Let $C,C^{\prime}$ be irreducible curves in $\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ such that $C$ is ample and is not preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ for any $a,b\geq 1$ and $C^{\prime}$ is not exceptional. Then for any infinite subset $\{n_{i}\}_{i\geq 1}\subset{\mathbb{N}}$ , the union

$$ \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\varphi^{n_{i}}(C)\cap C^{\prime}\right) $$

is Zariski dense in $C^{\prime}$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose for the sake of contradiction that there is an infinite sequence $\{n_{i}\}$ and a finite set $X\subset\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ such that

$$ \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\varphi^{n_{i}}(C)\cap C^{\prime}\right)\subset X. $$

Since $C$ is not preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ for any $a,b\geq 1$ , Theorem 4.5 implies that after replacing $C$ by an iterate, we may assume that $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ is injective for all $n\geq 1$ .

First suppose that $d>e$ . If $C^{\prime}$ is not of the form $\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\{\alpha\}$ , then $\varphi^{n}(C)\cdot C^{\prime}$ must grow with the exponential rate $d$ by Theorem 1.1. On the other hand, using Lemma 7.1 and Theorem 6.1 we have

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{mult}_{p}(\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime})}{d^{n}}=0 $$

for any given point $p$ . This clearly shows that the union of the sets $\varphi^{n_{i}}(C)\cap C^{\prime}$ cannot be contained in any given finite set.

Now suppose $C^{\prime}=\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\{\alpha\}$ . In this case, $\varphi^{n}(C)\cdot C^{\prime}$ grows at the exponential rate $e$ by Theorem 1.1. If $\alpha$ is not periodic under $g$ , we can use Theorem 6.1 to conclude the proof. If $\alpha$ is periodic, we may replace $\varphi$ with an iterate to assume that $\alpha$ is fixed. Since $C^{\prime}$ is non-exceptional, the multiplicity of $g$ at the fixed point $\alpha$ is strictly less than $e$ . Hence, for any fixed point of $\varphi$ in $\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\{\alpha\}$ we must have

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{mult}_{p}(\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime})}{e^{n}}=0. $$

which concludes the proof.

For the rest of the proof we assume that $d=e$ . Let $p\in X$ be non-periodic. Since $C$ is not preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ for any $a,b\geq 1$ , it follows from Theorem 6.1 that

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{mult}_{p}(\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime})}{d^{n}}=0. $$

For periodic points in $X$ , since $X$ is a finite set, we may replace $C$ with an iterate $\varphi^{k}(C)$ and $\varphi$ with $\varphi^{\ell}$ for some $k,\ell\geq 1$ and assume all periodic points in $X$ are fixed points. If $C^{\prime}$ is a non-exceptional horizontal or vertical curve, the proof proceeds in a manner similar to the case $d>e$ . We may therefore assume that $C^{\prime}$ is ample. For non-exceptional points in $X$ , Lemma 7.1 again implies that

$$ \operatorname{mult}_{p}\bigl(\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}\bigr)=o(d^{n}). $$

For exceptional points, Lemmas 7.2 and 7.3 show that the sum of their intersection multiplicities is at most

$$ \varphi^{n}(C)\cdot C^{\prime}-d^{n}+O(1). $$

Hence

$$ \displaystyle\varphi^{n}(C)\cdot C^{\prime}-\sum_{p\in X}\operatorname{mult}_{p}\bigl(\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}\bigr) \displaystyle=\varphi^{n}(C)\cdot C^{\prime}-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\in X\\
p\text{ exceptional}\end{subarray}}\operatorname{mult}_{p}\bigl(\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}\bigr) \displaystyle\quad-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\in X\\
p\text{ non-exceptional}\end{subarray}}\operatorname{mult}_{p}\bigl(\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}\bigr) \displaystyle\geq d^{n}+O(1)-o(d^{n}). $$

In particular, for all sufficiently large $n$ , the intersection $\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}$ cannot be contained in $X$ , contradicting our assumption on $X$ . This completes the proof of Theorem 7.4. ∎

## 8. Degenerate cases of Theorem 1.7

It is natural to ask what can be said about the intersections

$$ \varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime} $$

when the pair $(C,C^{\prime})$ is excluded by the hypotheses of Theorem 1.7. The aim of this section is to classify precisely those excluded pairs $(C,C^{\prime})$ for which the intersections

$$ \varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime} $$

are contained in a prescribed finite set for infinitely many values of $n$ .

#### Theorem 8.1.

Suppose that we are in the setting of Theorem 1.7 and the tuple $(C,C^{\prime})$ belongs to one of the following classes:

- (a) $C$ is arbitrary and $C^{\prime}$ is exceptional; or

- (b) $C$ is horizontal or vertical and $C^{\prime}$ is non-exceptional; or

- (c) $C$ is ample and preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ for some $a,b\geq 1$ and $C^{\prime}$ is non-exceptional.

Then there exists a finite set $X\subset C^{\prime}$ such that

$$ \varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}\subseteq X $$

for infinitely many $n$ if and only if we are in one of the following situations

- (a’) The pair $(C,C^{\prime})$ is of type $(a)$ and

$$ C\cap C^{\prime}\subset\operatorname{Prep}(\varphi); $$

- (b’) The pair $(C,C^{\prime})$ is of type $(b)$ and either (1) $C$ is preperiodic under $\varphi$ and the iterates $\varphi^{n}(C)$ do not stabilize to $C^{\prime}$ ; or (2) $C$ is not preperiodic and $C$ and $C^{\prime}$ are both horizontal or both vertical;

- (c’) The pair $(C,C^{\prime})$ is of type $(c)$ , $\deg(f)=\deg(g)$ , and the iterates $\varphi^{n}(C)$ do not stabilize to $C^{\prime}$ .

- (c”) The pair $(C,C^{\prime})$ is of type (c), $\deg(f)>\deg(g)$ , and $C^{\prime}$ is of the form $\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\{\gamma\}$ for some $\gamma\in\operatorname{Prep}(g)$ .

We first need the following proposition to show that, in the case $\varphi=(f,\operatorname{id})$ , the bidegree of the curves $\varphi^{n}(C)$ grows proportionally to $(1,\deg(f)^{n})$ , provided that $C$ is ample.

#### Proposition 8.2.

Let $\varphi=(f,\operatorname{id})$ for some polynomial $f$ and assume that $C$ is an ample irreducible curve. Then the degree of $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ is uniformly bounded over all $n$ .

#### Proof.

Given $p=(x,y)\in C$ , the preimages of $\varphi^{n}(p)$ for the map $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ are given by $(x^{\prime},y)$ where $f^{n}(x^{\prime})=f^{n}(x)$ . Since $C$ is not horizontal or vertical, there can only be a bounded number of possible such points $(x^{\prime},y)$ on our curve $C$ . Hence the degree of $\varphi^{n}:C\to\varphi^{n}(C)$ is uniformly bounded over all $n$ . ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 8.1.

We begin by showing that for each of the conditions $(a^{\prime})$ - $(c^{\prime\prime})$ , we can find a finite set $X$ such that

$$ \varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}\subset X $$

for infinitely many $n\geq 0$ .

Condition $(a^{\prime})$ . We note that in this case we have

$$ \varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}=\varphi^{n}(C\cap C^{\prime}). $$

Therefore, $C\cap C^{\prime}\subset\operatorname{Prep}(\varphi)$ implies that

$$ X:=\bigcup_{n\geq 0}\varphi^{n}(C\cap C^{\prime}), $$

is a finite set and finishes the proof for this case.

Condition $(b^{\prime})$ . In the case $(b^{\prime}):(2)$ we can take $X=\emptyset$ . So, assume we are in case (1). Suppose that $\varphi^{N}(C)=\varphi^{N+k}(C)$ for some $k\geq 1$ . For any $0\leq r\leq k-1$ we let

$$ X_{r}:=\bigcup_{n\geq 0}\varphi^{N+r+nk}(C)\cap C^{\prime}=\varphi^{N+r}(C)\cap C^{\prime}. $$

If $X_{r}$ is a finite set, we can conclude that $\varphi^{N+r+nk}(C)\cap C^{\prime}$ is always contained in $X_{r}$ . The only way this does not happen is if

$$ \varphi^{N+r}(C)=C^{\prime} $$

for all $0\leq r\leq k-1$ . This means that $C$ must eventually stabilize to $C^{\prime}$ and finishes the proof for $(b^{\prime}):(1)$ .

Condition $(c^{\prime})$ . The proof of this case is identical to $(b^{\prime}):(1)$ .

Condition $(c^{\prime\prime})$ . We must have $\deg(f)^{a}=\deg(g)^{b}$ which shows that $a<b$ . Since $C$ is preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ , there exists $\alpha,\beta\geq 0$ such that

$$ \left(f^{\alpha+na},g^{\beta+nb}\right)C=\left(f^{\alpha},g^{\beta}\right)(C), $$

for all $n\geq 0$ . At the expense of replacing $(\alpha,\beta)$ with $(\alpha+n^{\prime}a,\beta+n^{\prime}b)$ for some $n^{\prime}\geq 0$ we may assume without loss of generality that $\alpha<\beta$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\left(f^{\beta+nb},g^{\beta+nb}\right)C \displaystyle=\left(f^{n(b-a)},\operatorname{id}\right)\left(f^{\beta-\alpha},\operatorname{id}\right)\left(f^{\alpha+na},g^{\beta+nb}\right)C \displaystyle=\left(f^{n(b-a)},\operatorname{id}\right)\left(f^{\beta-\alpha},\operatorname{id}\right)\left(f^{\alpha},g^{\beta}\right)C \displaystyle=\left(f^{n(b-a)},\operatorname{id}\right)\left(f^{\beta},g^{\beta}\right)C, $$

for every $n\geq 0$ . Similarly for every $\beta^{\prime}\geq\beta$ we must have

$$ \displaystyle\left(f^{\beta^{\prime}+nb},g^{\beta^{\prime}+nb}\right)C \displaystyle=\left(f^{n(b-a)},\operatorname{id}\right)\left(f^{\beta^{\prime}},g^{\beta^{\prime}}\right)C $$

for every $n\geq 0$ . Equation (12) yields

$$ \varphi^{\beta^{\prime}+nb}(C)\cap C^{\prime}=\left(f^{n(b-a)},\operatorname{id}\right)\left(f^{\beta^{\prime}},g^{\beta^{\prime}}\right)C\cap C^{\prime}=\left(f^{n(b-a)},\operatorname{id}\right)\left(\left(f^{\beta^{\prime}},g^{\beta^{\prime}}\right)C\cap C^{\prime}\right), $$

where in the last equality we use the assumption that $C^{\prime}$ is of the form $\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\{\gamma\}$ . But note that

$$ \left(\left(f^{\beta^{\prime}},g^{\beta^{\prime}}\right)C\cap C^{\prime}\right)\subset\operatorname{Prep}(\varphi) $$

for every $\beta^{\prime}\geq\beta$ . To see this, note that $C$ is not horizontal or vertical and that $\left(f^{\beta^{\prime}},g^{\beta^{\prime}}\right)C$ is preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ . The desired conclusion follows.

We now prove the opposite direction of the theorem. Suppose that there exists a finite set $X$ such that

$$ \varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}\subset X $$

for infinitely many $n$ . Now assume $(C,C^{\prime})$ is of type $(a)$ . Then, since $C^{\prime}$ is exceptional, we must have

$$ \varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}=\varphi^{n}(C\cap C^{\prime}). $$

Therefore, $\varphi^{n}(C\cap C^{\prime})\subset X$ for infinitely many values of $n$ which shows that all the points in $C\cap C^{\prime}$ must be preperiodic. Thus, condition $(a^{\prime})$ holds as desired.

Now suppose that $(C,C^{\prime})$ is of type $(b)$ . Then, if $C$ is not preperiodic, the curves $\varphi^{n}(C)$ must all be disjoint. The hypothesis that $\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}$ is contained in a finite set for infinitely many $n$ implies that, for some $n_{0}$ , we must have

$$ \varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}=\emptyset $$

for all $n\geq n_{0}$ . Thus $C^{\prime}$ is parallel to $\varphi^{n_{0}}(C)$ , and consequently to $\varphi^{n}(C)$ for all $n\geq n_{0}$ . Hence we are in situation $(b^{\prime}):(2)$ .

If $C$ is preperiodic, then it is straightforward to see that the only obstruction to $\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}$ being contained in a finite set infinitely often occurs when $\varphi^{n}(C)$ eventually stabilizes to $C^{\prime}$ . This shows that we must be in situation $(b^{\prime}):(1)$ .

Finally suppose that $(C,C^{\prime})$ is of type $(c)$ . So, $C$ is preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ for some $a,b\geq 1$ . If $\deg(f)=\deg(g)$ , then we must have that $a=b$ which means that $C$ is preperiodic under $\varphi$ . So, the only obstruction to $\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}$ being contained in a finite set infinitely often occurs when $\varphi^{n}(C)$ eventually stabilizes to $C^{\prime}$ . Thus, we must be in situation $(c^{\prime})$ .

Now suppose that $\deg(f)>\deg(g)$ . We must have $\deg(f)^{a}=\deg(g)^{b}$ which shows that $a<b$ . Since $C$ is preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ , there exists $\alpha,\beta\geq 0$ such that

$$ \left(f^{\alpha+na},g^{\beta+nb}\right)C=\left(f^{\alpha},g^{\beta}\right)(C), $$

for all $n\geq 0$ . Recall that by equation (12), for every $\beta^{\prime}\geq\beta$ we must have

$$ \displaystyle\left(f^{\beta^{\prime}+nb},g^{\beta^{\prime}+nb}\right)C \displaystyle=\left(f^{n(b-a)},\operatorname{id}\right)\left(f^{\beta^{\prime}},g^{\beta^{\prime}}\right)C, $$

for every $n\geq 0$ . This means that after replacing $\varphi$ with $\varphi^{\beta^{\prime}}$ and $C$ with an iterate $\varphi^{\beta^{\prime}}(C)$ for some $\beta^{\prime}\geq\beta$ , we may assume without loss of generality that $\varphi=(f,\operatorname{id})$ .

Using Proposition 8.2, the degree of $\varphi^{n}$ restricted to $C$ remains bounded. Hence, after replacing $C$ with an iterate if necessary, we assume that $\varphi^{n}:C\longrightarrow\varphi^{n}(C)$ is generically one to one for all $n\geq 1$ . If we let $(c_{1},c_{2})$ be the bidegree of $C$ , it follows from Lemma 4.1 that the bidegree of $\varphi^{n}(C)$ is equal to $(c_{1},d^{n}c_{2})$ .

Now suppose that $p=(p_{1},p_{2})$ is a point such that

$$ p\in\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime} $$

for infinitely many values of $n$ . Then there exist points $p_{1}^{i}$ and an infinite sequence $\{n_{i}\}_{i\geq 0}\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that

$$ f^{n_{i}}(p_{1}^{i})=p_{1} $$

for all $i\geq 1$ , and

$$ (p_{1}^{i},p_{2})\in C $$

for all $i\geq 1$ . If $p_{1}$ is not periodic under $f$ , then the points $p_{1}^{i}$ must take infinitely many distinct values. It follows that $C$ contains infinitely many points on the horizontal curve $\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\{p_{2}\}$ , and hence

$$ C=\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\{p_{2}\}, $$

contradicting our assumption that $C$ is ample. Therefore, $p_{1}$ is periodic under $f$ , and consequently $p$ is periodic under $\varphi$ .

Thus, after replacing $X$ by a subset, we may assume without loss of generality that

$$ X\subset\operatorname{Per}(\varphi). $$

Moreover, after replacing $\varphi$ by an iterate, we may assume that

$$ X\subset\operatorname{Fix}(\varphi). $$

Suppose now that $C^{\prime}$ is not of the form $\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\{\gamma\}$ . Then $C^{\prime}$ has bidegree $(c_{1}^{\prime},c_{2}^{\prime})$ with $c_{1}^{\prime}\neq 0$ . Hence

$$ \varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime} $$

has at least $d^{n}c_{1}^{\prime}c_{2}$ intersection points, counted with multiplicity. On the other hand, by Theorem 5.5, for every $p\in X$ , the multiplicity of $p$ in the intersection $\varphi^{n}(C)\cap C^{\prime}$ remains bounded independently of $n$ . Since $X$ is finite, this contradicts the fact that the total intersection multiplicity grows at least like $d^{n}c_{1}^{\prime}c_{2}$ . We conclude that

$$ C^{\prime}=\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\{\gamma\} $$

for some $\gamma\in\mathbb{P}^{1}$ .

It remains to show that $\gamma\in\operatorname{Prep}(g)$ . Assume without loss of generality that

$$ C\cap C^{\prime}\subset X $$

after replacing $C$ with an iterate $\varphi^{n_{0}}(C)$ . Let $(\rho,\gamma)$ be a point in $C\cap C^{\prime}$ . Since $C\cap C^{\prime}\subset X$ , we have

$$ (\rho,\gamma)\in\operatorname{Per}(\varphi). $$

In particular,

$$ \rho\in\operatorname{Per}(f). $$

Recall also that $C$ is preperiodic under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ . If $\gamma\notin\operatorname{Prep}(g)$ , then the orbit of $(\rho,\gamma)$ under $(f^{a},g^{b})$ would intersect $\{\rho\}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ in a dense subset. This is impossible, since $C$ is neither horizontal nor vertical. Therefore,

$$ \gamma\in\operatorname{Prep}(g). $$

This shows that we are in situation $(c^{\prime\prime})$ and finishes the proof.

∎
