We now say that a GVF $K$ is existentially closed if for any such finite type scheme $X$ , the analytification map $X(K)\to X_{\operatorname{GVF}}$ has dense image. By [51, Theorem 2.5.3], following [68] and [4], the globally valued fields $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[1]$ and $\overline{k(t)}[1]$ are existentially closed, where we use the standard global Weil heights on $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ and $\overline{k(t)}$ for our height functions.

## 5. Non-Archimedean Canonical Measures for Valued Fields

Our goal in this section is to show that the strategy of [45] and [73] to prove the Bogomolov conjecture in the case where we have a place of bad reduction carries over from the discretely valued setting to the general (height one) valued setting. Ideally, we would like to apply these arguments to the limiting abelian variety $A_{\omega}/K^{\prime}_{\omega}$ (after completing at a place $v$ of bad reduction) in order to conclude. However, $(K^{\prime}_{\omega},v)$ will no longer be a discretely valued field.

Let $A$ be an abelian variety over an algebraically closed nonarchimedean (non-trivally) valued field $K$ with valuation $v.$ As in [73], we let $b(A)$ be the dimension of the abelian part of the reduction of $A$ at $v.$ Given a subvariety $X\subset A,$ we can make sense of the abelian part of $X$ as follows. For a Mumford model $\mathcal{A}$ of $A$ over $K,$ we can write it as a quotient $p:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}$ of a semiabelian formal scheme, which itself has another quotient $q:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}$ to an abelian formal scheme. Let $\mathcal{X}$ be the Zariski closure of $X$ in $\mathcal{A},$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ a quasicompact open subscheme of $\mathcal{E}$ such that $p(\mathcal{Y})=\mathcal{X}.$ Then, we let $b(X)$ be the dimension of $q(\mathcal{Y});$ this is well-defined by [73, Lemma 4.2].

The statement that Yamaki proves that we wish to generalize is the following.

#### Theorem 5.1 (Theorems 5.3, 5.4 from [73]).

Let $S$ be an irreducible normal projective variety over an algebraically closed field, and let $F$ be its field of fractions. Let $A$ be an abelian variety over $\overline{F},$ and endow $\overline{F}$ with the function field height as in [73, §0.5]. Let $X$ be a subvariety of $A,$ and $G_{X}\subset A$ the stabilizer of $X.$ Suppose that for some place $v$ of $\overline{F}$ arising from a codimension one point of the normalization in some finite extension of $F$ , either:

- (i) $\dim(X/G_{X})>b((X/G_{X})_{v}),$ or

- (ii) $\dim(X/G_{X})\geq b((A/G_{X})_{v})$ and $X$ is not a special subvariety (see [73, Definition 2.5]).

Then, $X$ does not have a Zariski dense set of small points.

#### Remark 5.2.

In the case that $b(A_{v})=0$ for some place $v$ (i.e. $A$ has totally degenerate bad reduction at $v$ ), this result is due to [45].

#### Remark 5.3.

Note that if $X$ is an ample divisor in $A$ , then its stabilizer $G_{X}$ is finite, so $\dim(X/G_{X})=\dim X.$ Furthermore, $\dim X\geq b(A_{v})$ if $v$ is a place of bad reduction, since $b(A_{v})\leq\dim A-1=\dim X.$

The main thing we need to check is that one can remove the assumption that $(K,v)$ is a discretely valued field through the proofs of [73, Theorems 5.3, 5.4]. We can do this because of the recent work of Gubler and Stadlöder, [44], which proves a lot of the results about the Chambert-Loir measures discussed in [48] but without the discrete valuation assumption.

One of the key structural results used by Yamaki for Theorem 5.1(i) is [48, Theorem 1.1], which states that one can express the tropicalization of a closed subvariety $X$ of $A$ as a union of certain canonical simplices, and furthermore the Monge-Ampère measure associated with an ample line bundle $L$ can be expressed as sums of the Lebesgue measure supported on these simplices. The result cited only applies to discretely valued fields; however, we may replace this result with [44, Corollary 1.4] and the discussion in the proof of [44, Proposition 6.3] to get the analogous result for our more general (non-discretely valued) situation, which for completeness we state below.

#### Theorem 5.4.

Let $(K,v)$ be a complete nonarchimedean valued field which is algebraically closed. Let $A$ be an abelian variety over $K,$ $X$ a closed subvariety of $A,$ and let $L$ be an ample line bundle. Then, the tropicalization of the Monge-Ampère measure of $L,$ which we denote $\mu^{\text{trop}}_{X_{v},L},$ can be expressed as

$$ \sum r_{j}\mu_{\Delta_{j}}, $$

where the $\Delta_{j}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are polysimplices and $\mu_{\Delta_{j}}$ is the Lebesgue measure supported on the polysimplex $\Delta_{j}.$

Yamaki’s proof of Theorem 5.1(i) also requires that the following bound on the dimension of polysimplices holds, which we state in our more general setting.

#### Proposition 5.5.

In the setting of the previous theorem, the union of these polysimplices is the tropicalization of $X,$ and we can take them to be precisely the non-degenerate strata (as in [48, §6.3]) of a strictly polystable alteration of $X.$ In particular, the dimension of these polysimplices all lie between $\dim X-b(X_{v})$ and $\dim X.$

#### Remark 5.6.

In the case where $K$ is the algebraic closure of a discretely valued field, this is given by [48, Theorem 1.1] and [73, (4.6.14)].

Note that these strictly polystable alterations exist by the polystable alteration theorem [2, Theorem 5.2.19], for instance, which proves the existence of an alteration $\mathscr{X}^{\prime}\to\mathscr{X}$ with $\mathscr{X}^{\prime}$ strictly polystable and with smooth generic fiber (that is, strongly nondegenerate; see [6, §4.4]).

#### Proof of Proposition 5.5.

The fact that these polysimplices correspond to the non-degenerate strata follows from the proof of [44, Proposition 6.3], which proves that the Monge-Ampère measure is a sum of the Lebesgue measures supported precisely on the polysimplices that are non-degenerate in the skeleton of a polystable alteration $\mathcal{X}^{\prime}$ . Furthermore, these remain polysimplices when we pass to the tropicalization, since by [44, Theorem 7.8] the tropicalization restricted to each of these polysimplices is a linear isomorphism.

Then, the fact that the union of the simplices is equal to the entire tropicalization of $X$ follows by the arguments outlined in [44, Remark 7.2]. For the dimension bound, we use the definition of non-degeneracy, where the dimension of the strata is preserved when passing to the abelian part, and the dimension of the corresponding polysimplex is preserved under tropicalization; see [44, Equation (6.2.1)]. Combining this with the fact that for a strata $S$ in the special fiber of the skeleton $\mathcal{X}^{\prime}$ with corresponding canonical face $\Delta_{S},$ $\dim\Delta_{S}=\dim X-\dim S,$ yields the desired result (see the discussion in [44, §5.4], for instance). ∎

The remainder of Yamaki’s proof of Theorem 5.1(i) modulo the equidistribution result carries over, replacing “simplex” with “polysimplex.” Indeed, [73, Proposition 4.5] holds in our more general setting as well, since the facts they use only rely on results in [46, §3], which do not require the discrete valuation assumption.

We now turn to Theorem 5.1(ii). For this case, Yamaki makes use of Gubler’s result [73, Corollary A.2], which states that the lower bound given in Proposition 5.5 is attained. In the proof of this corollary (which in turn is a corollary of [73, Theorem A.1]), we can use [43, Corollary 1.4] to replace [48, Theorem 6.7] (since we are only concerned with studying $c_{1}(\overline{L}|_{X})^{\wedge d}$ ) as well as the same replacements we used in the proof of Proposition 5.5. This leaves us with proving Theorem A.5 in the same appendix. Thus, in order to show that [73, Theorem 5.4] applies in the more general valued field setting (assuming equidistribution), it suffices to check that [73, Theorem A.5] holds in this more general setting. That is, we need to show the following.

#### Theorem 5.7.

Let $\mathcal{A}_{0}$ be a Mumford model of $A$ over $K^{\circ},$ the valuation ring of our complete and algebraically closed nonarchimedean valued field $K.$ Let $\mathcal{X}_{0}$ be the Zariski closure of $X$ in $\mathcal{A}_{0},$ and let $\varphi:\mathcal{X}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}_{0}$ be a strongly non-degenerate strictly polystable alteration. Then, there is a $b(X)$ -dimensional stratum of the special fiber of $\mathcal{X}^{\prime}$ whose corresponding polysimplex is non-degenerate.

Note that the use of semistable in [73, Theorem A.5] suffices for their purposes because the appendix starts with $X\subset A$ defined over a field with a discrete valuation, to which de Jong’s semistable alteration theorem applies. However, in the case that $X$ is defined over a field with an arbitrary height one valuation rather than a discrete valuation, we only have the polystable alteration theorem of [2, Theorem 5.2.19], so we must show the theorem in the setting of strongly non-degenerate strictly polystable alterations.

#### Proof.

The proof of [73, Theorem A.5] occurs after passage to the completion of the algebraic closure, and so the only potential places where the proof uses the discretely valued field hypothesis is in assuming the alteration is semistable. These arise in citations of §4-5 of [48] throughout the proof. But the results §4 of [48] work in the more general setting, so it is just the results of §5 of ibid. that we need to generalize from strictly semistable to the case of strongly non-degenerate strictly polystable schemes. However, all of the results in [48, §5] carry over to strongly non-degenerate strictly polystable schemes by [48, Remark 5.19]. Hence, one can follow the proof word-for-word in [73, Theorem A.5] to prove the above theorem. ∎

To obtain our generalization of Theorem 5.1 ([73, Theorem 5.4]), we also need to generalize [73, Lemma 2.12], which for us takes the following form.

#### Lemma 5.8.

Let $A$ be an abelian variety over an algebraically closed nonarchimedean GVF $K.$ Then, for any irreducible closed subvariety $X\subset A$ such that $\dim X/G_{X}=0,$ $X$ can only have a dense set of small points if it is special.

#### Remark 5.9.

The notion of a special subvariety from [73, Definition 2.5] extends to this setting, where we let $k$ be the height zero subfield of $K$ and we allow the point $x$ to have canonical height zero in general.

#### Proof.

The only part of the proof of this lemma which doesn’t immediately generalize is the claim, which is part of [73, Proposition 2.11], that $X/G_{X}$ being special holds if and only if $X$ is. Furthermore, to prove that claim along the lines of Yamaki’s proof, it suffices to check the following if $\phi:A\rightarrow B$ is a homomorphism of abelian varieties, then the map sends points of canonical height zero on $A$ to points of canonical height zero on $B,$ and furthermore that this restricted map is surjective. For the first fact, this follows since for any ample symmetric line bundles $L,M$ on $A,B,$ respectively, there is some integer $n>0$ such that $L^{\otimes n}\otimes\phi^{*}M^{-1}$ is ample, meaning that $n\hat{h}_{L}(x)\geq\hat{h}_{M}(\phi(x))\geq 0$ for all $x\in A;$ in particular, if $x$ is canonical height zero, $\phi(x)$ is too.

For the surjectivity statement, recall that there exists an abelian variety $C/K$ such that $B\times C$ is isogeneous to $A,$ where the homomorphism $A\rightarrow B\times C$ composed with the projection to $B$ is just $\phi.$ Now, composing with its dual, we get a map $[n]:B\times C\rightarrow B\times C.$ Finally, let $y\in B(K)$ be a height zero point. Then, observe that the canonical height of any pre-image $y^{\prime}$ of $y$ is zero, since $\hat{h}(y)=n^{2}\hat{h}(y^{\prime})=0.$ So then taking the image of $(y^{\prime},z)$ under $B\times C\rightarrow A$ where $z$ is any height zero point of $C,$ we find that its image in $A$ is a height zero point whose image under $\phi$ is $y,$ as desired. ∎

As a consequence of the above, by applying Theorem 4.9 in place of the equidistribution argument and following Yamaki’s proof of Theorem 5.1 ([73, Theorem 5.4]), we obtain the following.

#### Theorem 5.10.

Let $K$ be a nonarchimedean countable GVF with height zero subfield $k,$ and let $A$ be an abelian variety over $K$ . Assume that $\Tr_{\overline{K}/\overline{k}}(A)=0$ . Let $X$ be a subvariety of $A$ and $G_{X}$ the stabilizer of $X$ . Assume that $X$ is not of the form $x+B$ , where $x$ is a point of canonical height zero and $B$ is an abelian subvariety. Let

$$ \Omega^{\prime}=\{v\in\Omega\mid A\text{ has bad reduction at }v\} $$

and assume for a positive measure of places of $\Omega^{\prime}$ , we have $\dim(X/G_{X})\geq b((A/G_{X})_{v}).$ Then $X$ does not have a dense set of small points.

## 6. Bogomolov Conjecture for Divisors over GVFs

Let $K$ be a nonarchimedean GVF, which we may assume to be algebraically closed and let $k$ be its height zero subfield. Let $A$ be an abelian variety over $K$ . Assume that $A$ is traceless, i.e. $\Tr_{K/k}(A)=0$ . We aim to prove the Bogomolov conjecture for divisors $D$ in this setting.

#### Theorem 6.1.

Let $K$ be an algebraically closed non-archimedean GVF and $k$ its height zero subfield. Let $A/K$ be a $K/k$ -traceless abelian variety and let $D$ be a geometrically integral divisor in $A$ . Let $L$ be a symmetric ample line bundle on $A$ . Then

$$ \widehat{h}_{A,L}(D)=0\implies D=x+B $$

where $B\subseteq A$ is an abelian subvariety.

Let $k_{0}=\mathbb{Q}$ if $K$ is of characteristic $0$ and $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ if $K$ is of characteristic $p$ . Fix some $n\geq 3$ not divisible by the characteristic of $K$ . Then after choosing level $n$ -structure, $A$ defines a point on $\mathcal{A}_{g,n}.$ Now the Hodge bundle $\omega$ on $\mathcal{A}_{g,n}$ extends to an ample line bundle on the minimal compactification of $\mathcal{A}_{g,n}$ . This gives us an adelic line bundle $\overline{\omega}\in\widehat{\Pic}(\mathcal{A}_{g,n}/k_{0})$ . We define the Faltings height $h_{\omega}$ for non-archimedean GVFs to be the height induced by this ample adelic line bundle $\overline{\omega}$ . Since $\omega$ is ample, we have

$$ h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)=0\implies A\text{ is defined over }k $$

where $k$ is the height zero subfield of $K.$

We first begin the proof in the case where $A$ has bad reduction. In this case, we can apply the equidistribution arguments of Ullmo [71] and Zhang [82], which have been adapted to function fields by Gubler [45] and Yamaki [73]. We will construct a height function $h_{\partial\mathcal{A}_{g,n}}$ on $\mathcal{A}_{g,n}.$ that measures bad reduction of $A$ . To do this, fix a toroidal compactification $\overline{\mathcal{A}_{g,n}}$ of $\mathcal{A}_{g,n}$ over $\Spec\mathbb{Z}[1/n,\zeta_{n}],$ and let $\partial\mathcal{A}_{g,n}$ be $\overline{\mathcal{A}_{g,n}}-\mathcal{A}_{g,n}.$ Note that this is a relative effective Cartier divisor (see [32, Theorem 6.7]), so we may then consider the line bundle $\mathcal{O}(\partial\mathcal{A}_{g,n})$ on $\overline{\mathcal{A}_{g,n}}.$ We can then restrict this data to lie over $k_{0}$ . We hence obtain a model adelic line bundle $\overline{\mathcal{O}(\partial\mathcal{A}_{g,n})}\in\widehat{\Pic}(\mathcal{A}_{g,n}/k_{0})$ . We may therefore define the height $h_{\partial\mathcal{A}_{g,n}}$ by taking the height functional induced by $\overline{\partial\mathcal{A}_{g,n}}$ . For convenience, we abbreviate this as $h_{\partial\mathcal{A}_{g}}$ .

#### Proposition 6.2.

View $K=(K,(\Omega,\mathcal{A},\nu),\phi)$ as an adelic curve and assume that $K$ is a non-archimedean GVF. The set $\{\omega\in\Omega\mid A\text{ has bad reduction at }\omega\}$ is a measurable subset of $\Omega.$ It has positive measure if and only if $h_{\partial\mathcal{A}_{g}}(A)>0$ .

#### Proof.

Since $K$ is a non-archimedean GVF, the set of places $\omega\in\Omega$ with residue characteristic different from the characteristic of $K$ has measure zero. We may thus remove those places and assume the residue characteristic of all $\omega\in\Omega$ is equal the characteristic of $K$ .

Fix the data of $h_{\partial\mathcal{A}_{g,n}}$ as above, and consider the section $s$ of $\mathcal{O}(\partial\mathcal{A}_{g,n})$ on $\overline{\mathcal{A}_{g,n}}$ which cuts out $\partial\mathcal{A}_{g,n}.$ Note that for an absolute value $\omega$ for our adelic curve $K,$ $A$ has good reduction at $\omega$ if and only if, if $R$ is the valuation ring corresponding to the absolute value $\omega,$ the morphism $\Spec K\rightarrow\mathcal{A}_{g,n}$ extends to $\Spec R.$ In particular, as $n$ is not divisible by the characteristic, this occurs if and only if the pullback of $s$ to $\Spec K$ has norm at least $1$ with respect to $\phi(\omega)$ when we take the analytification of the adelic line bundle (see [78, §3.3.1]).

Therefore, if we pullback the adelic line bundle $\overline{\partial\mathcal{A}_{g,n}}$ to $K$ and consider this section $s,$ we see that the set of places $\omega\in\Omega$ such that $A$ has bad reduction at $\omega$ where the residue characteristic of $\omega$ doesn’t divide $n$ is precisely the set

$$ \{\omega\in\Omega|\,\,\|s\|_{\overline{\partial\mathcal{A}_{g,n}},\omega}<1\}, $$

which is measurable since Yuan–Zhang adelic line bundles induce Chen–Moriwaki adelic line bundles.

Since

$$ h_{\partial\mathcal{A}_{g,n}}=\int_{\Omega}\log||s||^{-1}_{\omega}d\nu(\omega), $$

and $\log||s||^{-1}_{\omega}\geq 0$ as $s$ is an effective section of $\overline{\mathcal{A}_{g,n}}$ , it follows that $h_{\partial\mathcal{A}_{g,n}}(A)>0$ if and only if there is a set of positive measure in $\Omega$ for which $A$ has bad reduction. ∎

#### Proposition 6.3.

In the setting of Theorem 6.1, assume that $h_{\partial\mathcal{A}_{g}}(A)>0$ . Then Theorem 6.1 is true.

Before we turn to the proof of Proposition 6.3, we have the following useful lemma.

#### Lemma 6.4.

Suppose that $\phi:A\rightarrow B$ is a homomorphism of abelian varieties. Then, the image of a subvariety with canonical height zero (with respect to any ample symmetric line bundle) has canonical height zero.

#### Proof.

For the case of dimension zero subvarieties, this follows from the argument in Lemma 5.8. In general, say that $V$ is a positive-dimensional subvariety of $A.$ As $\widehat{h}_{A,L}(V)=0$ , by [51, Proposition 2.6.8], after passing to a countable GVF extension, we obtain a Zariski dense set of height zero points for $V$ . Then $\phi(V)$ also contains a Zariski dense set of height zero points, and hence the canonical height of $q(V)$ must be zero by [51, Proposition 2.6.10]. ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 6.3.

First, we may assume that $\Stab(D)$ is finite. Otherwise, if $B$ is the stabilizer, we may work with the image of $D$ in $A/B$ instead, where we now have finite stabilizer. Now as $\widehat{h}_{L}(D)=0$ and $L$ is ample, by Proposition 4.8, we may pass to a countable extension $K^{\prime}/K$ such that $D(K^{\prime})$ contains a generic sequence $(x_{n})$ of small points. Then, base changing to the GVF $K^{\prime},$ $h_{\partial\mathcal{A}_{g}}(A)$ is still positive, and hence we still have a positive measure set of bad reduction places.

We now apply Theorem 5.10. As $\Stab(D)$ is finite and $A_{v}$ has bad reduction, we certainly always have $\dim(D/\Stab(D))=g-1\geq b(A_{v})$ . Hence $D$ cannot have a dense set of small points unless it is a special subvariety. Since $A$ is traceless, this means that $D$ is a torsion translate of an abelian subvariety, as desired. ∎

We are now left with the case where $h_{\partial\mathcal{A}_{g}}(A)=0$ , i.e. the case of almost everywhere good reduction. It is useful to analyze the case of global function fields first, say $K=\mathbb{C}(B)$ where $B$ is a curve over $\mathbb{C}.$ In this case, we have good reduction literally everywhere. Furthermore, let’s assume $D$ is symmetric, ample, and endow $L=O(D)$ with the canonical metric after fixing a rigidification $0^{*}L\simeq K$ , where $0:K\to A$ is the zero section. Let $s\in H^{0}(A,L)$ be the global section corresponding to $D$ . We have the formula

$$ \widehat{h}_{A,L}(D)=\sum_{v\in M_{K}}\int\log|s(x)|_{v}d\mu_{A,v}. $$

Since $A$ has good reduction at $v$ for all places $v,$ $\mu_{A,v}$ is supported exactly at the Shilov point and hence $\log|s(x)|_{v}=\log\sup\limits_{x\in A^{\an}_{v}}|s(x)|_{v}$ . Since $\widehat{h}_{A,L}(D)=0$ , we have

$$ \sum_{v\in M_{K}}\log\sup\limits_{x\in A^{\an}_{v}}|s(x)|_{v}=0. $$

This consequence has already been observed by Yamaki [75] in his proof of Bogomolov conjecture for divisors in the everywhere good reduction case.

On the other hand, the key formula of Moret-Bailly [61], in the reformulation of Bost [8] (see [37, Equation A.4] for the function field case), gives us

$$ \widehat{\mu}(\pi_{*}\overline{L})=-\frac{1}{2}h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A). $$

Here, $\widehat{\mu}$ is the average slope of the adelic vector bundle $\pi_{*}\overline{L}$ , where an element $x\in\pi_{*}\overline{L}$ corresponding to a global section $s$ is given the metric $|x|_{v}:=\sup|s|_{v}$ . If $\dim H^{0}(A,L)=1$ , say if $D$ is the theta divisor of a principally polarized abelian variety, then we automatically get that

$$ -\frac{1}{2}h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)=0 $$

which implies that $A$ is isotrivial. For a general symmetric divisor $D$ , if $K$ is of characteristic zero then we can get a contradiction by using semistability of the metrized vector bundle $\pi_{*}\overline{L}$ [9] which tells us that $\hat{\mu}(\pi_{*}\overline{L})$ bounds above the slope of any line (in particular, the line generated by $s,$ whose slope is zero). If $K$ is of positive characteristic, then the situation is more complicated but one can still arrive at a contradiction by constructing many small sections of $\overline{L}^{2}$ .

For a general countable GVF $K$ , viewing $K$ as an adelic curve instead, we may view $\pi_{*}\overline{L}$ as an adelic vector bundle in the sense of Chen–Moriwaki [16, Theorem 6.1.13]. However, the formula (6.1) is not known to hold in the setting of a general adelic curve and indeed, it seems that would require understanding various compactifications of symmetric line bundles $\mathcal{L}$ on an abelian scheme $\mathcal{A}/S$ when $S$ is only quasi-projective (see [10] for the case of the principal theta divisor).

However, luckily for us, we only have to handle the case where $A/K$ has almost everywhere good reduction. For an abelian scheme $\mathcal{A}/S$ , Tang [70] has proven that given a symmetric rigidified relatively ample line bundle $L$ on $\mathcal{A}$ , we have a canonical isomorphism

$$ \det(\pi_{*}L)^{\otimes 24}\simeq(e^{*}\omega_{A}^{\vee})^{\otimes 12d} $$

where $d$ is the rank of the locally free sheaf $\pi_{*}L$ and $e:S\to A$ is the zero section. Using this, we prove the following.

#### Proposition 6.5.

Let $(K,(\Omega,\mathcal{A},\nu),\phi)$ be an adelic curve and let $A/K$ be an abelian variety. Let $L$ be a rigidified symmetric ample line bundle on $A$ and endow $L$ with the canonical metric. Then there is an isomorphism

$$ \det(\pi_{*}L)^{\otimes 24}\simeq(e^{*}\omega_{A}^{\vee})^{\otimes 12d} $$

such that for every non-archimedean place $v\in\Omega$ of good reduction, the isomorphism extends to an isometry

$$ \det(\pi_{*}\overline{L}_{v})^{\otimes 24}\simeq(e^{*}\overline{\omega}_{A,v}^{\vee})^{\otimes 12d}. $$

#### Proof.

This follows immediately from [70, Theorem 1.3] and the universal nature of the construction given in [70, §3]. Indeed choosing his canonical isomorphism over $K$ , if $v$ is a place of good reduction for $A$ , we let $\mathcal{A}_{v},\mathcal{L}_{v},\mathcal{\omega}_{\mathcal{A}_{v}}$ be the canonical models for $(A,L,\omega_{A})$ . Then, the canonical isomorphism given by [70, Theorem 1.3] between $\det(\pi_{*}\mathcal{L}_{v})^{\otimes 24}$ and $(e^{*}\mathcal{\omega}_{\mathcal{A}_{v}}^{\vee})^{\otimes 12d}$ must induce our canonical isomorphism over $K,$ giving us the isometry we desired. ∎

As a consequence, we obtain the following.

#### Proposition 6.6.

Let $(K,(\Omega,\mathcal{A},\nu),\phi)$ be a non-archimedean adelic curve and let $A/K$ be an abelian variety. Assume that $A$ has almost everywhere good reduction and let $L$ be a symmetric ample line bundle and endow $L$ with its canonical adelic metric $\overline{L}$ . Then if $H^{0}(A,L)$ has a basis $\{s_{1},\ldots,s_{N}\}$ with

$$ \int_{\Omega}\log\sup|s_{i}|_{v}d\nu(v)\leq 0 $$

for all $i$ , we must have $h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)=0$ .

#### Proof.

By Proposition 6.5, viewing $\det(\pi_{*}\overline{L})$ as a Chen-Moriwaki adelic line bundle [16, §4.1.1.7], we have

$$ 24\widehat{\deg}\det(\pi_{*}L)=(-12d)\widehat{\deg}(e^{*}\overline{\omega_{A}}), $$

since we have an isometry of adelic line bundles over almost every place. As $\widehat{\deg}(e^{*}\overline{\omega_{A}})=h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)$ (see for example [78, Section 5.5]), we have

$$ \widehat{\deg}\det(\pi_{*}L)=-\frac{d}{2}h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A). $$

Now using our basis of sections $s_{1},\ldots,s_{N}$ , we obtain a section $s_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge s_{N}$ of $\det(\pi_{*}L)$ which satisfies

$$ |s_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge s_{N}|_{v}\leq\prod_{i=1}^{N}\sup|s_{i}|_{v} $$

for all places $v$ . Hence

$$ \int_{\Omega}\log|s_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge s_{N}|_{v}^{-1}d\nu(v)\geq-\int_{\Omega}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log\sup|s_{i}|_{v}\right)d\nu(v)\geq 0. $$

We therefore conclude that

$$ -\frac{d}{2}h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)\geq 0\implies h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A)=0 $$

as desired (since the Faltings height is nonnegative). ∎

We are now ready to begin the proof of the Bogomolov conjecture over GVF for divisors in the (almost) everywhere good reduction case. We will say a section $s$ has small average if it satisfies (6.2).

#### Theorem 6.7.

Assume that $A/K$ has almost everywhere good reduction. Then Theorem 6.1 is true.

#### Proof.

We may assume that $K$ is algebraically closed. As in the proof of Theorem 6.3, we may assume that $\Stab(D)$ is finite. Then $D$ is an ample divisor. Now by replacing $D$ with $D+[-1]^{*}D$ , we may assume that $D$ is symmetric, at the cost of losing the integrality of $D$ . Let $L=O(D)$ and endow $L$ with the canonical metric by fixing a rigidification $e^{*}L\simeq K$ where $e:K\to A$ is the zero section. Let $s$ be the canonical (up to scaling) section of $L$ with $\divv(s)=D$ . View $K=(K,(\Omega,\mathcal{A},\nu),\phi)$ as an adelic curve. Therefore, we have

$$ \widehat{h}_{A,L}(D)=\widehat{h}_{A,L}(A)+\int_{\Omega}\left(\int_{A^{\an}_{v}}\log|s(x)|_{v}d\mu_{A,v}\right)d\nu(v)=\int_{\Omega}\log\sup_{x\in A^{\an}_{v}}|s(x)|_{v}d\nu(v), $$

where the second equality follows because $A$ has good reduction at every place outside a set of measure zero. Now by assumption, $\widehat{h}_{A,L}(D)=0$ and since $\widehat{h}_{A,L}(A)=0$ , we obtain

$$ \int_{\Omega}\log\sup|s(x)|_{v}d\nu(v)=0 $$

and hence $s$ has small average. We now aim to construct many small sections of the adelic line bundle $\overline{L}^{2}$ . This step appears in Yamaki’s proof ([75]). To do this, fix a prime $\ell$ which is different from the characteristic $p$ of $K.$ Then, for $q\in A[\ell^{\infty}],$ let $t_{q}:A_{K}\rightarrow A_{K}$ be the translation by $q$ isomorphism, and let $D_{q}=t_{q}^{*}D+t_{-q}^{*}D.$ These are all divisors which are symmetric and linearly equivalent to $L^{\otimes 2},$ whose section is given by $s(x+q)s(x-q);$ we abbreviate this as $s_{q}.$ Then as $\sup|s(x+q)|,\sup|s(x-q)|=\sup|s(x)|$ , the sections $s(x+q),s(x-q)$ certainly have small average and so does $s_{q}$ .

#### Proposition 6.8.

There exists $q_{0},\ldots,q_{g}\in A[\ell^{\infty}]$ such that $D_{q_{0}}\cap\cdots\cap D_{q_{g}}=\emptyset$ .

#### Proof.

Observe that given $x\in A(K)$ , the set of $q\in A(K)$ such that $x\in D_{q}$ forms a proper subvariety. We now construct inductively $q_{0},\ldots,q_{g}$ such that for $0\leq j\leq g,$ the irreducible components $\cap_{i=0}^{j}D_{q_{i}}$ all have codimension $j.$ Given $D_{q_{0}},\ldots,D_{q_{j}}$ , we choose points $x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}$ from each of the irreducible components of $\cap_{i=0}^{j}D_{q_{i}}$ . Since $A[\ell^{\infty}]$ is Zariski dense in $A$ , we may find $q_{j+1}\in A[\ell^{\infty}]$ such that $D_{q_{j+1}}$ does not contain any of the $x_{i}$ ’s. Then $D_{q_{g+1}}$ intersects any irreducible component of $\cap_{i=0}^{j}D_{q_{i}}$ properly, and hence the irreducible components of $\cap_{i=0}^{j+1}D_{q_{i}}$ has codimension $j+1$ as desired, finishing the induction. ∎

Proposition 6.8 gives us sections $s_{0},\ldots,s_{g}$ of $\overline{L}^{2}$ which all have small average, such that they form a basepoint free set, and thus we obtain a morphism $f:A\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{g}_{K}$ given by the sections $s_{0},s_{1},\ldots,s_{g}.$ We now want to produce enough sections to obtain a closed embedding, not just basepoint freeness.

#### Proposition 6.9.

There exists finitely many torsion points $x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}\in A[\ell^{\infty}](K)$ such that $\prod_{i=1}^{m}f_{x_{i}}:A\to(\mathbb{P}^{g}_{K})^{m}$ factors into $A\to B\xhookrightarrow{}(\mathbb{P}^{g}_{K})^{m}$ , where $B$ is an abelian variety over $K$ , $\pi:A\to B$ is an isogeny and $f_{x}$ is given by $f\circ t_{x}:A\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{g}.$

#### Proof.

We have to be careful in this proposition as $K$ may be of positive characteristic and hence an injection on the level of points need not imply a closed embedding due to inseparability.

For each $x\in A(K),$ let $\Gamma_{x}=(f_{x},f_{x})^{-1}(\Delta)\subseteq A\times A,$ where $\Delta$ is the diagonal of $\mathbb{P}^{g}\times\mathbb{P}^{g}$ . Then $\Gamma_{x}$ is a closed subscheme of $A^{2}$ . We will consider the intersection $\bigcap_{x\in A[\ell^{\infty}](K)}\Gamma_{x}$ which is a closed subscheme. We define

$$ H=\{a\in A\mid f\circ T_{a}=f\}. $$

This is a closed subscheme of $A$ , where given an affine scheme $S$ we have

$$ H(T)=\{a\in A(S)\mid f_{S}\circ T_{a}=f_{S}\}. $$

Note that $H$ must factor through $T_{x}^{-1}(f^{-1}(f(x)))$ for all $x\in A(K),$ and hence is a finite group scheme, since the fiber of $f$ over some point is finite (for instance by using the construction in Proposition 6.9). We define $B=A/H$ so that we have an isogeny $\pi:A\to B$ .

#### Lemma 6.10.

View $A\times_{B}A$ as a closed subscheme of $A\times A$ . We have $R=A\times_{B}A$ .

#### Proof.

Let $S$ be an affine $K$ -scheme. Recall that $R=\cap_{x\in A[\ell^{\infty}](K)}\Gamma_{x}$ , where

$$ \Gamma_{x}(S)=\{(a,b)\in A(S)^{2}\mid f_{S}(a+x_{S})=f_{S}(b+x_{S})\}. $$

By definition it is clear that $(A\times_{B}A)(S)\subseteq\Gamma_{x}(S)$ for any $x$ and so we have $A\times_{B}A\subseteq R$ .

For the reverse inclusion, let $(a,b)\in R(S)$ . Set $h=b-a\in A(S)$ . Then by definition, we have

$$ (f_{S}\circ T_{h})(x_{S}+a)=f_{S}(x_{S}+a)\text{ for all }x\in A[\ell^{\infty}](K) $$

where $x_{S}$ denotes the base change to $S$ . We claim that $\{x_{S}+a\}$ as $x$ ranges over $A[\ell^{\infty}](K)$ forms a scheme-theoretic dense set. If this were true, then $f_{S}\circ h=f_{S}$ and hence we get the reverse inclusion $R\subseteq A\times_{B}A$ , giving us equality $R=A\times_{B}A$ as desired.

It now suffices to prove that $\{x_{T}\}$ is scheme-theoretically dense in $A_{T}$ . But $A[\ell^{\infty}](K)$ is Zariski dense in $A(K)$ and hence is scheme-theoretically dense in $A$ as $A$ is reduced. Then scheme-theoretic density in $A_{T}$ follows from [27, Lemma IX.4.4]. ∎

Using Lemma 6.10, by Noetherianness we may find finitely many $x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}\in A[\ell^{\infty}](K)$ such that $A\times_{B}A=\cap_{i=1}^{m}\Gamma_{x_{i}}$ . If we let $f_{i}$ denote the morphism $f_{x_{i}}$ , then $\prod_{i=1}^{m}f_{i}:A\to(\mathbb{P}^{g})^{m}$ factors through $A\to B\to(\mathbb{P}^{g})^{m}$ . We claim that $B\to(\mathbb{P}^{g})^{m}$ has to be a closed immersion. By [67, Tag 04XV], as $B$ is projective, it suffices to show that it is a monomorphism. This can be checked by using test schemes $T$ , in which case it is straightforward using the fact that $A\times_{B}A=\cap_{i=1}^{m}\Gamma_{x_{i}}$ , finishing the proof of our Proposition. ∎

Using the Segre embedding, we may embed $(\mathbb{P}^{g})^{m}$ into $\mathbb{P}^{(g+1)^{m}-1}$ . Let $M$ be the pullback of $O(1)$ to $B$ , so that $\pi^{*}M=\otimes_{i=1}^{m}t_{x}^{*}L^{2}$ . Let $M^{\prime}=M\otimes[-1]^{*}M$ , so that $M^{\prime}$ is symmetric. Then

$$ \pi^{*}M^{\prime}\simeq\bigotimes_{i=1}^{m}\left(t_{x}^{*}L^{2}\otimes t_{-x}^{*}L^{2}\right)\simeq\bigotimes_{i=1}^{m}L^{4}\simeq L^{4m}, $$

where the second isomorphism is by the theorem of the square. Endowing $M^{\prime}$ with a canonical adelic metric $\overline{M}$ , we obtain that $\pi^{*}\overline{M}^{\prime}=\overline{L}^{4m}$ .

Now using the embedding $B\xhookrightarrow{}(\mathbb{P}^{(g+1)^{m}-1})$ , we obtain a set of sections $\{s_{1},\ldots,s_{N}\}$ for $M$ , such that under pullback to $A$ by $\prod_{i=1}^{m}f_{i}$ , they have small average for the adelic line bundle $\otimes_{i=1}^{m}t_{x}^{*}\overline{L}^{2}$ . Applying $[-1]^{*}$ gives us a corresponding set of sections $\{s^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,s^{\prime}_{N}\}$ for ${-1}^{*}M$ whose pullback to $A$ have small average for $\otimes_{i=1}^{m}t^{*}_{-x}\overline{L}^{2}$ .

Now observe that products of small average sections still have small average. Hence $\{s_{i}\otimes s^{\prime}_{j}\}$ give us a set of small average sections for $\overline{M}^{\prime}$ . Furthermore, they induce a closed immersion of $B$ to projective space, say $\mathbb{P}^{N}$ . Then by ampleness, we know that for some large enough $n$ , we have a surjection $H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{N},O(n))\to H^{0}(B,(M^{\prime})^{n})$ . On the other hand, taking products of $\{s_{i}\otimes s^{\prime}_{j}\}$ gives us a basis of $H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{N},O(n))$ with small average, and hence $(\overline{M}^{\prime})^{n}$ is a symmetric adelic line bundle on $B$ with a basis of small average sections. Applying Proposition 6.6 gives us that $h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(B)=0$ . This implies that $B$ is defined over the height zero subfield, contradicting the fact that $A$ is traceless as desired. ∎

## 7. Height Equidistribution and Inequalities

The aim of this section is to extend two known Arakelov theoretic results from the case of number/function fields to the setting of general countable GVFs. The first is the following height equidistribution property over GVFs. Let $K$ be a non-archimedean GVF and let $X$ be a projective variety over $K$ . Let $\overline{L},\overline{M}$ be two adelic line bundles on $X$ so that $L$ and $M$ are both big. Assume there exists some $a>0$ so that $a\overline{L}-\overline{M}$ is nef. Let $D$ be a geometrically integral divisor on $X,$ and assume that $h_{\overline{L}}(X)=0$ . Then we wish to prove that

$$ h_{\overline{L}}(D)=h_{\overline{M}}(D). $$

We view this as a more refined version of equidistribution which gives us information even if the related Chambert-Loir measures for $\overline{L}$ and $\overline{M}$ are trivial. When $K$ is a global field, this would follow by using [14, Lemma 6.1] and the fact that there is a generic sequence of points $(x_{n})$ that is simultaneously small for both $\overline{L}$ and $\overline{M}$ . Sédillot [65, Proposition 5.5] gives an extension to this for adelic curves but he requires the assumption that $L$ is ample and $D$ is a Cartier divisor. The ampleness condition is fine for our application but we would like to remove the Cartier assumption. The usual approach by Chambert-Loir and Thuillier uses the arithmetic Siu inequality by Yuan [79] which seems to be not known in the general adelic curve case yet.

The second result that we need is an arithmetic Brunn–Minkowski type inequality. Given nef semipositive line bundles $\overline{L},\overline{M}$ on $X$ such that $L,M$ are both big, we have

$$ \overline{L}^{d}\cdot\overline{M}=0\implies\overline{M}^{d+1}=0. $$

Over number fields, this is implied by a result of Chen [20, Theorem 1.1] which is a refinement of the arithmetic isoperimetric inequality and the arithmetic Brunn–Minkowski inequality. The arithmetic Brunn–Minkowski inequality was established previously by Yuan [80] and as noted, can be viewed as a higher dimensional generalization of the arithmetic Hodge index theorem.

As we were unable to find a reference for a function field version of Chen’s result, although the same proof most likely works, we instead rederive both (7.1) and (7.2) from the arithmetic Hodge index theorem for GVFs. Note that we only need the inequality part of the arithmetic Hodge index, which is much easier than determining the equality cases.

The arithmetic Hodge index theorem states that if $\overline{L}_{1},\ldots,\overline{L}_{n-1}$ are nef adelic line bundles with each $L_{i}$ big and $\overline{M}$ an integrable adelic line bundle, then

$$ M\cdot L_{1}\cdots L_{n-1}=0\implies\overline{M}^{2}\cdot\overline{L}_{1}\cdots\overline{L}_{n-1}\leq 0. $$

For number fields this is by Yuan [77] and for function fields, this is by Carney [13]. For GVFs, we prove this using a continuity argument on the GVF analytification. Recall that $k_{0}$ is $\mathbb{Q}$ if $K$ is characteristic zero and $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ otherwise. First, we may find a quasi-projective variety $U$ over $k_{0}$ , a flat family $\mathcal{X}\to U$ and adelic line bundles $\overline{\mathcal{L}},\overline{\mathcal{M}}\in\widehat{\Pic}_{\operatorname{int}}(\mathcal{X}/k_{0})$ such that $\Spec K$ maps to the generic point of $U,$ and we recover back $(X,L,M)$ after base changing to $\Spec K$ . Note that if $\overline{L}$ is nef, then we can find such a model with $\overline{\mathcal{L}}$ being nef and hence $\iota^{*}\overline{\mathcal{L}}$ is nef for any map $\iota:\Spec L\to U$ .

#### Proposition 7.1.

Assume that $\overline{L}_{1},\ldots,\overline{L}_{n-1}$ are nef and geometrically big line bundles. Then for any integrable $\overline{M}$ , we have

$$ M\cdot L_{1}\cdots L_{n-1}=0\implies\overline{M}^{2}\cdot\overline{L}_{1}\cdots\overline{L}_{n-1}\leq 0. $$

#### Proof.

Let $\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{U}$ be our flat family. Since big line bundles are exactly those which can be written as $A\otimes E$ , where $A$ is ample and $H^{0}(X,E)>0$ [55, Corollary 2.2.7], by further shrinking $U$ , we may assume that for every $s\in\mathcal{U}$ , the line bundle $\mathcal{L}_{i,s}$ is big on the fiber $\mathcal{X}_{s}$ . By flatness, we may also assume that $\mathcal{M}_{s}\cdot\mathcal{L}_{1,s}\cdots\mathcal{L}_{n-1,s}=0.$ We form the Deligne pairing

$$ \overline{\mathcal{N}}=\langle\mathcal{M},\mathcal{M},\mathcal{L}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{L}_{n-1}\rangle\in\widehat{\Pic}(\mathcal{U}/k_{0}). $$

We now pick some $t\in\Frac(U)\setminus k_{0}$ for which $h(t)>0$ , which we may assume exists as otherwise the GVF structure is trivial and every intersection product is zero. Further shrinking $\mathcal{U}$ , we may assume that $t$ is regular so that we obtain a map $\pi:\mathcal{U}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}$ induced by $t$ . We let $\mathcal{U}_{0}$ denote its generic fiber so that it is a variety over $k(t)$ .

We now consider the GVF analytification $\mathcal{U}^{\operatorname{GVF}}_{0}$ over the base GVF $k(t).$ Taking the height of the adelic line bundle $\overline{N}$ defines a continuous function for us

$$ h_{\overline{N}}:\mathcal{U}^{\operatorname{GVF}}_{0}\to\mathbb{R}. $$

Furthermore, we know from the function field arithmetic Hodge index that $h_{\overline{N}}(x)\leq 0$ when evaluated at any $\overline{k(t)}$ -point $x$ . By existential closedness ([4, Theorem 2.1]), such points are dense and so $h_{\overline{N}}\leq 0$ by continuity, proving our arithmetic Hodge index for the GVF point $\Spec K$ inside $\mathcal{U}_{0}^{\operatorname{GVF}}$ . ∎

Using Proposition 7.1, we can prove the following mixed-intersections inequality which will be useful for us later.

#### Proposition 7.2.

Let $X$ be a projective variety over $K$ and let $\overline{L}$ and $\overline{M}$ be nef semipositive adelic line bundles which are geometrically big. Then if $d=\dim X$ , we have

$$ \overline{L}^{d}\cdot\overline{M}=\overline{L}^{d+1}=0\implies\overline{M}^{d+1}=0. $$

#### Proof.

By replacing $\overline{M}$ with $\overline{M}_{\varepsilon}=\overline{M}+\varepsilon\overline{L}$ , we may assume that the geometric degrees $d_{i}=L^{n-i}\cdot M^{i}$ are all positive. We define $I_{j}=\overline{L}^{n+1-j}\cdot\overline{M}^{j}$ , so that $I_{0}=I_{1}=0$ and we wish to prove that $I_{n+1}=0$ . In fact we will prove that $I_{j}=0$ for all $0\leq j\leq n+1$ .

To do so, we set

$$ c_{j}=\frac{d_{j+1}}{d_{j}},\quad N_{j}=M-c_{j}L,\quad\overline{N}_{j}=\overline{M}-c_{j}\overline{L}. $$

Then

$$ N_{j}\cdot L^{n-1-j}\cdot M^{j}=0 $$

so that we can apply Proposition 7.1 to $\overline{N}_{j}$ with $(n-1-j)$ copies of $\overline{L}$ and $j$ copies of $\overline{M}$ . We obtain

$$ (\overline{M}-c_{j}\overline{L})^{2}\overline{L}^{n-1-j}\overline{M}^{j}\leq 0. $$

Expanding out, we obtain $I_{j+2}-2c_{j}I_{j+1}+c_{j}^{2}I_{j}\leq 0$ . Now by induction, starting with $I_{1}=I_{0}=0$ , we have

$$ I_{j},I_{j+1}=0\implies I_{j+2}\leq 0\implies I_{j+2}=0 $$

as by nefness, we must have $I_{j+2}\geq 0$ . Hence $I_{n+1}=0$ , finishing our proof. ∎

We now prove our height equidistribution property for divisors. If $X$ is a projective variety, then for any effective divisor $D$ we prove the following.

#### Proposition 7.3.

Let $X$ be a projective variety over $K$ and $\overline{L},\overline{M}$ two nef line bundles such that $L$ and $M$ are both geometrically semiample and big. Assume there exists some $a>0$ such that $a\overline{L}-\overline{M}$ is nef. Then $h_{\overline{L}}(X)=0$ implies that for any geometrically integral effective divisor $D$ of $X$ , we have

$$ \frac{h_{\overline{L}}(D)}{\deg_{L}(X)}=\frac{h_{\overline{M}}(D)}{\deg_{M}(X)}. $$

where $h_{\overline{L}},h_{\overline{M}}$ are the un-normalized heights (that is, $h_{\overline{L}}(D)=\widehat{\deg}(\overline{L}^{d}|_{D})$ ).

#### Proof.

Let $d=\dim X$ . We first check that all mixed intersections between $\overline{L}$ and $\overline{M}$ vanish on $X.$ Indeed since $a\overline{L}-\overline{M}$ is nef, it follows from $\overline{L}^{d+1}=0$ that $(\overline{L}+\overline{M})^{d+1}=0$ too. Expanding out, as each term is non-negative by nefness, it follows that each mixed intersection must be zero.

We now prove that for any integrable adelic line bundle $\overline{N}$ , we have

$$ \frac{\overline{L}^{d}\cdot\overline{N}}{\deg_{L}(X)}=\frac{\overline{M}^{d}\cdot\overline{N}}{\deg_{M}(X)}. $$

Let $\overline{L}_{t}=(1-t)\overline{L}+t\overline{M}$ and let

$$ F(t)=\frac{\overline{L}_{t}^{d}\cdot\overline{N}}{L_{t}^{d}}. $$

Let $\overline{\Delta}=\overline{M}-\overline{L}$ so that $\Delta=M-L$ . We set

$$ c_{t}=\frac{L_{t}^{d-1}\cdot\Delta}{L_{t}^{d}} $$

so that if $\overline{D}_{t}=\overline{\Delta}-c_{t}\overline{L}_{t}$ , by definition we have $D_{t}\cdot L_{t}^{d-1}=0$ . Now given our $\overline{N}$ , we may assume that $L_{t}^{d-1}\cdot N=0$ by adding a multiple of $\overline{L}$ to $\overline{N}$ , which won’t change the quantity $\overline{L}^{d}\cdot\overline{N}$ and $\overline{M}^{d}\cdot\overline{N}$ .

Consider the quadratic form induced on the space of integrable adelic line bundles $\overline{N}$ , which satisfies $N\cdot L_{t}^{d-1}=0$ , by defining

$$ \langle\overline{N}_{1},\overline{N}_{2}\rangle_{t}:=\overline{L}_{t}^{d-1}\cdot\overline{N}_{1}\cdot\overline{N}_{2}. $$

Since $L_{t}$ is big and $\overline{L}_{t}$ is nef and semi-positive, by Proposition 7.1 it follows that $\langle\bullet,\bullet\rangle_{t}$ is negative semi-definite. Observe that $\langle\overline{D}_{t},\overline{D}_{t}\rangle_{t}=0,$ since $\overline{D}_{t}$ is a linear combination of $\overline{L},\overline{M},$ and all of the arithmetic intersections of these adelic line bundles are zero. Therefore, by negative semi-definiteness, it follows that $\langle\overline{D}_{t},\overline{N}\rangle_{t}=0$ . Expanding out, this gives us

$$ \overline{L}_{t}^{d-1}\cdot\overline{\Delta}\cdot\overline{N}=c_{t}\overline{L}_{t}^{d}\cdot\overline{N}. $$

We now set $A(t)=\overline{L}_{t}^{d}\cdot\overline{N}$ and $v(t)=L_{t}^{d}$ . We may compute that

$$ A^{\prime}(t)=d\overline{L}_{t}^{d-1}\overline{\Delta}\cdot\overline{N}=dc_{t}\overline{L}_{t}^{d}\cdot\overline{N}=dc_{t}A(t). $$

Similarly we have $v^{\prime}(t)=dc_{t}v(t)$ . Hence $A^{\prime}(t)v(t)=A(t)v^{\prime}(t)$ for all $t,$ and so

$$ \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{A(t)}{v(t)}\right)=0. $$

Evaluating at $t=0$ and $1$ gives us (7.3) as desired.

We now replace $X$ with a blowup, so that $D$ is a Cartier divisor. Then $L$ and $M$ are still geometrically semiample and big. Let $N=O(D)$ and give $\overline{N}$ an adelic metric so that it is integrable. We thus have

$$ \frac{\overline{L}^{d}\cdot\overline{N}}{\deg_{L}(X)}=\frac{\overline{M}^{d}\cdot\overline{N}}{\deg_{M}(X)}. $$

On the other hand, if $s$ is the canonical section of $O(D)$ , we have the formula

$$ h_{L}(D)=\widehat{\deg}(\overline{L}^{d}|_{D})=\overline{L}^{d}\cdot\overline{N}+\int_{\Omega_{K}}\left(\int_{X_{v}^{\an}}\log|s|_{v}dc_{1}(\overline{L})^{d}_{v}\right)d\nu(v). $$

and similarly for $M$ . Here, we let $c_{1}(\overline{L})^{d}_{v}$ be the un-normalized measure, i.e. it has total mass $\deg_{L}(X)$ . We now apply Proposition 4.9, which holds for geometrically semiample and big line bundles. We hence obtain that outside a set of measure zero, we have $\frac{c_{1}(\overline{L})_{v}^{d}}{\deg_{L}(X)}=\frac{c_{1}(\overline{M})_{v}^{d}}{\deg_{M}(X)}$ . Combining with (7.4) gives us $\frac{h_{L}(D)}{\deg_{L}(X)}=\frac{h_{M}(D)}{\deg_{M}(X)}$ as desired. ∎

## 8. Bogomolov Conjecture for Subvarieties over GVFs

In this section, we will turn to proving the Bogomolov conjecture over arbitrary GVFs. As the archimedean case was already proven by Chen–Moriwaki in [18], we only need to handle the non-archimedean case.

#### Theorem 8.1.

Let $K$ be a non-trivial non-archimedean GVF and let $k_{0}$ denote its height zero subfield. Let $A$ be an abelian variety over $K$ and assume that $\Tr_{\overline{K}/\overline{k_{0}}}(A_{\overline{K}})=0$ . Let $V$ be a positive dimensional subvariety of $A$ . Then

$$ \widehat{h}_{A}(V)=0\implies V=x+B $$

where $x$ is a point of $A$ and $B$ an abelian subvariety.

When $V$ is a divisor, this follows from the results of Section 6. The aim is to reduce the general subvariety case to the case of divisors. For instance, suppose $A$ is simple and $V=C$ is a curve. If $\widehat{h}_{A}(C)=0,$ then the divisor $D=\underbrace{C+C+\cdots+C}_{g-1\text{ times}}$ satisfies $\widehat{h}_{A}(D)=0,$ giving us a contradiction. In general, we can try to do an inductive argument similar to Xie–Yuan [72], whenever we have a $r>0$ so that the addition morphism $p:V^{r}\to A$ has a generic fiber of positive dimension, but of dimension strictly less than $V$ .

The first case not covered by this type of argument is when $V$ is a surface inside an abelian fourfold $A.$ In this case one expects $p:V\times V\to A$ to be a generically finite morphism, and hence the generic fiber is dimension zero. We now explain how to construct our desired height zero divisor $D$ in this case.

Now, assume first for simplicity that $p:V\times V\to A$ is a birational morphism. Then as it cannot be an isomorphism, a result of Kollar–Mori, [52, Corollary 2.63], implies that there must exist an exceptional divisor $E$ on $V\times V$ . Let $L$ be a symmetric ample line bundle on $A$ and let $\overline{L}$ be the canonical adelic line bundle. Let $\overline{P}=\pi_{1}^{*}\overline{L}+\pi_{2}^{*}\overline{L}$ and let $\overline{N}=\delta^{*}\overline{L}$ . Using Proposition 7.3, one obtains that

$$ h_{\overline{P}}(D)=h_{\overline{N}}(D) $$

for any geometrically integral divisor $D$ on $V\times V$ as a consequence of $\widehat{h}_{A}(V)=0$ . This step can be viewed as a refined version of equidistribution, which gives us information even when the measures are all trivial. Applying this to $E$ , we see that since $h_{\overline{N}}(E)=0$ by the projection formula as $\delta$ contracts $E$ . Hence $h_{\overline{P}}(E)=0$ , giving us our height zero divisor.

In general $p:V\times V\to A$ will not be birational. As it may however be finite, we switch to looking at $\delta:V\times V\to A$ given by $(x,y)\mapsto x-y$ . This map is expected to be generically finite, but not finite as the diagonal $\Delta$ is sent to $0$ under $\delta$ . We then use an algebraic geometry construction from [1], which was suggested by GPT6 Astra. Let $X=V\times V$ and view $K(X)$ as a finite extension of $K(A)$ using $\delta$ . For simplicity, let’s assume this extension is separable. We let $E/K(A)$ be the Galois closure of $K(X)/K(A)$ and we let $A^{\prime}$ be the normalization of $A$ in $E$ . Let $\sigma_{i}:K(X)\xhookrightarrow{}E$ for $i=1,\ldots,r$ be the different conjugate embeddings. Then we obtain rational maps $\tau_{i}:A^{\prime}\dashrightarrow{}X$ . Letting $X^{\prime}=\underbrace{X\times_{A}\times\cdots\times_{A}X}_{r\text{ times }}$ , we obtain a rational map $\tau:A^{\prime}\dashrightarrow{}X^{\prime}$ by combining the $\tau_{i}$ ’s.

We now let $Y$ be the closure of the graph of $\tau$ . This comes with projection maps $\pi_{i}:Y\to X$ and also maps $f:Y\to A$ given by $\delta\circ\pi_{i}$ . Furthermore, the Galois group $G=\Gal(E/K(A))$ acts on $Y$ . We now set $Z=Y/G$ . Then $f:Y\to A$ descends to $\tilde{f}:Z\to A$ as a projective birational morphism. This map $\tilde{f}$ cannot be an isomorphism as otherwise $f:Y\to A$ is a finite morphism, which cannot be because $\delta$ contracts the diagonal. This produces for us our exceptional divisor.

We now begin the proof of Theorem 8.1 in the general case. We first proceed by induction on $(\dim V,\dim A)$ , where if we are in the case of $(r,g)$ , we assume that the cases $(a,b)$ has been proven for all $a<r$ and all $a=r,b<g$ . Assume $V$ is a positive dimensional subvariety of $A$ with $\dim A=g$ , $\deg_{L}(V)=d$ and $\widehat{h}_{A,L}(V)=0$ . We may assume that $\Stab(V)$ is finite and that $V-V$ generates $A$ , as otherwise we are done by induction (namely, by either quotienting $A$ or considering the abelian subvariety generated by $V-V$ ). We may also assume that $K$ is countable, and is algebraically closed. Note that we may pass from $K$ to any other countable GVF extension $L$ which is algebraically closed, as the zero trace condition is maintained. Indeed if $k$ is the height zero subfield of $K$ and $k^{\prime}$ that of $L$ , then both $k^{\prime}$ and $k$ are algebraically closed too. Applying Theorem 6.4(3) and Theorem 6.8 of [22] gives us that $\Tr_{L/k^{\prime}}(A_{L})$ is still $0$ too.

The case of $\dim V=1$ can be deduced from the divisor case by the following argument. Let $B$ be the abelian subvariety that $C-C$ generates. After translating $C$ by a height zero point on $C$ , which exists after passing to some countable GVF extension, we may assume that $C\subseteq B$ . Then

$$ D=\underbrace{C+C+\cdots+C}_{\dim B-1\text{ times}} $$

is a divisor of $B$ with finite stabilizer and having canonical height $0$ . Then it must be the translate of some abelian subvariety of $B$ , contradicting the fact that $C$ generates $B$ .

#### Proposition 8.2.

For any abelian subvariety $B\subseteq A$ , let $q:A\to A/B$ be the quotient morphism. Then $q(V)=A/B$ .

#### Proof.

Assume otherwise that $q(V)$ is a proper subvariety of $A/B;$ we know by Lemma 6.4 that $q(V)$ also has height zero. Now by induction, we know that $q(V)=x+B^{\prime}$ for some abelian subvariety $B^{\prime}$ of $A/B$ . However $q(V)-q(V)$ must generate $A/B$ which is a contradiction unless $B^{\prime}=A/B$ . ∎

Proposition 8.2 implies that $V$ is geometrically non-degenerate in the sense of Debarre–Moonen [24, Definition 5.1]. Then [24, Corollary 5.6] implies that

$$ \dim(\underbrace{a_{1}V+\cdots+a_{m}V}_{m\text{ times }})=\min(g,m(\dim V)), $$

where $a_{1},\ldots,a_{m}$ are any positive integers. Let $m$ be the smallest positive integer so that $m(\dim V)\geq g$ and consider the addition map $f:V^{m}\to A$ .

#### Proposition 8.3.

We have the equality $m(\dim V)=g$ .

#### Proof.

Assume otherwise that $m(\dim V)>g$ . Then the generic fiber of $f:V^{m}\to A$ has dimension $r$ , where $0<r<\dim V$ . First, observe by Proposition 8.2 that $A$ cannot have an elliptic factor, as otherwise it is impossible for $q(V)=A/E$ since we may assume that $V$ is not a divisor by Theorem 6.1. Thus all effective divisors of $A$ have positive canonical height.

Now let $K^{\prime}=K(A)$ be the generic fiber of $A$ . We endow it with a polarized GVF structure [51, Definition 2.3.5] coming from the adelic line bundle $\overline{L}$ , i.e. the GVF structure denoted by $K(A,\overline{L},\ldots,\overline{L})$ . By definition, if $\overline{\mathcal{D}}$ is an adelic divisor on a birational model of $A$ , the GVF functional $\ell$ for the structure $K(A,\overline{L},\ldots,\overline{L})$ is defined by

$$ \ell(\overline{\mathcal{D}})=\widehat{\deg}(\overline{L}^{g}\cdot\overline{\mathcal{D}}). $$

#### Lemma 8.4.

The height zero subfield of $\overline{K^{\prime}}$ is still $k$ .

#### Proof.

This is [51, Lemma 5.4.3]. His proof uses the Bogomolov conjecture for divisors of $A$ which we already have. In general if $X$ is a normal projective variety and $\overline{L}$ an adelic line bundle on $X$ , the same proof shows that the polarized GVF structure on $K(X)$ still has the same height zero subfield as long as all prime divisors of $X$ have positive height with respect to $\overline{L}$ .

∎

Let $W$ be the generic fiber for $f:V^{m}\to A$ , so that $W$ can be viewed as a variety over $K^{\prime}$ . We may view it naturally as a subvariety of $A_{K^{\prime}}^{m}$ using the embedding induced by $V^{m}\xhookrightarrow{}A^{m}$ . We claim that $W$ has zero canonical height inside $A_{K^{\prime}}^{m}$ . Let $\overline{M}=\pi_{1}^{*}\overline{L}+\cdots+\pi_{m}^{*}\overline{L},$ with underlying line bundle $M.$ Then by definition,

$$ \widehat{h}_{K^{\prime}}(W)=\frac{\ell(\langle\overline{M},\ldots,\overline{M}\rangle_{V^{m}/A})}{M_{K^{\prime}}^{\dim W}(\dim W+1)}, $$

where $\langle\overline{M},\ldots,\overline{M}\rangle$ gives us an adelic line bundle on $A$ and hence can be evaluated by our GVF functional $\ell$ . We thus have

$$ \widehat{h}_{K^{\prime}}(W)=\frac{\widehat{\deg}_{K}(\langle\overline{M},\ldots,\overline{M}\rangle_{V^{m}/A}\cdot\overline{L}^{g})}{M_{K^{\prime}}^{\dim W}(\dim W+1)}, $$

where $\langle\overline{M},\ldots,\overline{M}\rangle_{V^{m}/A}\cdot\overline{L}^{g}$ is viewed as an adelic line bundle on $\Spec K$ . We now view the morphisms $V^{m}\to A\to\Spec K$ as $X\to Y\to S$ . We apply [78, Lemma 4.6.1, (1)], where after replacing $A$ with a Zariski open $U$ , we obtain that $(V^{m})_{U}\to U$ is flat. In this situation, we obtain an isomorphism

$$ \langle\overline{M},\ldots,\overline{M}\rangle_{(V^{m})_{U}/U}\cdot\overline{L}^{g}\simeq\langle\overline{M},\ldots,\overline{M},f^{*}\overline{L}^{g}\rangle_{(V^{m})_{U}/\Spec K}. $$

Now as $f^{*}\overline{L}\leq a\overline{M}$ for some $a>0$ by the ampleness of $\overline{M},$ it follows that

$$ \langle\overline{M},\ldots,\overline{M},f^{*}\overline{L}^{g}\rangle_{(V^{m})_{U}/\Spec K}\leq a^{\prime}\langle\overline{M},\ldots,\overline{M}\rangle_{(V^{m})_{U}/\Spec K} $$

for some $a^{\prime}>0$ . But the latter is $0$ as $\widehat{h}_{\overline{M}}(V^{m})=0$ . This proves that

$$ \widehat{h}_{K^{\prime}}(W)=0 $$

as desired. Now by induction, as the height zero subfield of $K^{\prime}$ is still $k_{0}$ and $\Tr_{\overline{K^{\prime}}/\overline{k_{0}}}(A_{K^{\prime}}^{m})=0$ , it follows that $W$ is a finite union of cosets of $A_{K^{\prime}}^{m}$ . In this case, since $W$ is irreducible (but not necessarily geometrically irreducible) as it is the fiber of the dominant morphism $f$ from an irreducible variety, the cosets forming $W$ must be translates of the same abelian subvariety $B$ . This follows from the fact that every abelian subvariety of $A_{K^{\prime}}$ is defined over $K$ . We may hence write $W=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i}+B)$ for $x_{i}\in A^{m}(\overline{K^{\prime}})$ . As the abelian subvariety $B$ descends to $K$ and and hence it follows that for a Zariski open $U\subseteq A$ , we must have $f^{-1}(y)=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i,y}+B)$ for all $y\in U$ , where $x_{i,y}$ are points of $V^{m}$ that can depend on $y$ . Then there is a Zariski open of $V^{m}$ which is stabilized by $B$ and hence $V^{m}$ has $B$ as a stabilizer, which contradicts $V$ having finite stabilizer. ∎

By Proposition 8.3, the morphism $f:V^{m}\to A$ is generically finite. We now consider the map $\delta:V^{m}\to A$ , given by $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m})\mapsto x_{1}+\cdots+x_{m-1}-[m-1]x_{m}$ . This is the Faltings–Zhang map, used by Zhang [82] in his proof of the Bogomolov conjecture over number fields. A similar map previously appeared in Faltings’ proof of the Mordell–Lang conjecture [34]. Then this map is still generically finite thanks to geometric non-degeneracy of $V$ (by [24, Corollary 5.6]), and the diagonal $\Delta$ is contracted. The following construction is due to GPT6 Astra.

#### Proposition 8.5.

Let $Y=V^{m}$ and consider it as a generically finite cover of $A$ by $\delta:Y\to A$ . Then there exists a projective variety $X$ over $K$ and positive integer $s$ such that there is a closed embedding $\iota:X\xhookrightarrow{}Y^{s}_{A}$ , where $Y_{A}^{s}:=\underbrace{Y\times_{A}Y\times_{A}\cdots\times_{A}Y}_{s\text{ times}},$ so that the induced map $f:X\to A$ is surjective, generically finite and has an exceptional divisor. Here, an effective divisor $D\subseteq X$ is exceptional for $f$ if $\codim f(D)\geq 2$ .

#### Proof.

Since $\delta:Y\to A$ is generically finite, we may view $K(Y)$ as a finite extension of $K(A)$ . Let’s first assume that $K(Y)/K(A)$ is a separable extension. Let $E$ be the Galois closure of $K(Y)$ over $K(A)$ . Let $\sigma_{i}:K(Y)\xhookrightarrow{}E$ be the different conjugate embeddings for $i=1,\ldots,r$ . This gives us an injection

$$ \Spec E\xhookrightarrow{}\Spec R=\Spec\underbrace{K(Y)\otimes_{K(A)}\cdots\otimes_{K(A)}K(Y)}_{r\text{ times }} $$

corresponding to the surjection $R\to E$ given by $x_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{r}\mapsto\prod_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_{i}(x_{i})$ . We now view $\Spec R$ as the generic fiber of the natural map $\delta:Y^{r}_{A}\to A$ . We let $\eta$ be the point corresponding to $\Spec E$ and we set $X$ to be the Zariski closure of $\eta$ inside $Y^{r}_{A}$ .

The Galois group $G=\Gal(E/K(A))$ naturally acts on $Y^{r}_{A}$ , by permuting the factors of the fiber product, i.e. $g\cdot(x_{1},\ldots,x_{r})=(x_{\pi_{g}^{-1}(1)},\ldots,x_{\pi_{g}^{-1}(r)})$ , where $\pi_{g}$ is the permutation on $(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{r})$ that the action of $g$ induces. This induces the usual action of $G$ on $\Spec E$ . Since $X$ is the Zariski closure of $\eta$ , it follows that $G$ acts on $X$ too. Observe that $\delta:X\to A$ is not a finite morphism as it factors through $X\to Y\to A$ for any of the projection maps $\pi_{i}:X\to Y$ , and the map $X\to Y$ is surjective while the map $\delta:Y\to A$ is contracts a positive dimensional subvariety.

We now have the map $\delta:X\to A$ so that $g\circ\delta=\delta$ for all $g\in G$ . Let $W=X/G$ be the finite quotient of $X$ by $G$ , which exists because $G$ is a finite group. Then we have an induced morphism $\tilde{\delta}:W\to A$ which is birational, as they both share the same function field. However it cannot be an isomorphism, as otherwise $\delta:X\to A$ is a finite morphism. We now apply [52, Corollary 2.63]. Since $A$ is smooth, it is $\mathbb{Q}$ -factorial and hence the corollary applies, giving us an exceptional divisor in $X$ as desired by pulling back the exceptional divisor in $W.$

If $K(Y)/K(A)$ is inseparable, we have to modify the argument as if we take the normal closure $E$ of $K(Y)/K(A)$ , then the invariant subfield of the Galois group $\Gal(E/K(A))$ for $E$ need not equal $K(A)$ . We remedy this by letting $E/K(A)$ be the Galois closure of the maximal separable subextension $F$ of $K(Y)/K(A)$ . We refer the readers to [67, Tag 09HD] for basic facts about purely inseparable extensions. We let $\sigma_{i}:F\xhookrightarrow{}E$ be the different conjugate embeddings for $i=1,\ldots,r$ . Since $K(Y)/F$ is purely inseparable, these extend to give $\sigma_{i}:K(Y)\xhookrightarrow{}\overline{E}$ . We set $E^{\prime}$ to be the compositum of the $\sigma_{i}(K(Y))$ ’s. Then $E^{\prime}/E$ is purely inseparable, the Galois group $G=\Gal(E/K(A))$ acts on $E^{\prime}$ and permutes the conjugate embeddings $\sigma_{i}$ ’s, and the fixed field $(E^{\prime})^{G}$ is purely inseparable over $K(A)$ .

We perform the same construction on $Y_{A}^{r}$ again, but this time with the point $\Spec E^{\prime}$ instead of $\Spec E$ . Taking the Zariski closure, we obtain a closed subvariety $X\subseteq Y_{A}^{r}$ such that $G$ acts on $X$ . Taking the quotient gives us a morphism $\tilde{\delta}:X\to A$ , which need not be birational as $K(X)=(E^{\prime})^{G}$ which could be larger than $K(A)$ .

We now take the normalization $A^{\prime}$ of $A$ in $K(X)$ and we replace $X$ with its normalization $X^{\prime}$ . Then $\tilde{\delta}:X^{\prime}\to A$ extends to $\tilde{\delta}:X^{\prime}\to A^{\prime}$ by [67, Tag 035H] as $X^{\prime}$ is normal. We have the following lemma regarding $\pi:A^{\prime}\to A$ .

#### Lemma 8.6.

The morphism $\pi:A^{\prime}\to A$ is finite and a universal homeomorphism. Hence $A^{\prime}$ is also $\mathbb{Q}$ -factorial.

#### Proof.

Since $A^{\prime}\to A$ is the normalization of $A$ over a finite extension, it follows that $A^{\prime}\to A$ is finite. To show its a universal homeomorphism, we let $U=\Spec C$ be an affine open of $A$ . As $K(A^{\prime})/K(A)$ is purely inseparable, there exists $e>0$ such that $x^{p^{e}}\in K(A)$ for all $x\in K(A^{\prime})$ . Let $B$ be the integral closure of $C$ inside $K(A^{\prime})$ . Then for all $b\in B,$ $b^{p^{e}}\in K(A)$ and is also integral over $C$ , implying that $b^{p^{e}}\in C$ as $A$ is normal. Thus $C\xhookrightarrow{}B$ satisfies the hypothesis of [67, Tag 0BRA] which implies that $\Spec B\to\Spec C$ is a universal homeomorphism. Hence $\pi:A^{\prime}\to A$ is a universal homeomorphism.

Now let $D^{\prime}\subseteq A^{\prime}$ be a prime Weil divisor. Then $\pi(D^{\prime})$ is also a prime Weil divisor on $A$ . Since $A$ is smooth, $\pi(D^{\prime})$ is Cartier. Now the pullback $\pi^{*}\pi(D^{\prime})$ is also Cartier, but $\pi^{*}\pi(D^{\prime})=eD^{\prime}$ for some positive integer $e>0$ . Hence $D^{\prime}$ is $\mathbb{Q}$ -Cartier and thu $A^{\prime}$ is $\mathbb{Q}$ -factorial. ∎

Applying [52, Corollary 2.63], as $A^{\prime}$ is still $\mathbb{Q}$ -factorial, we obtain an exceptional divisor on $X^{\prime}$ . Mapping it down to $X$ gives us the exceptional divisor we want, finishing the proof. ∎

Applying Proposition 8.5, we obtain an exceptional projective variety $X$ with a closed embedding into $Y^{s}_{A}$ and hence into $A^{s}$ , such that $f:X\to A$ is generically finite and has an exceptional divisor $D$ . Since the induced $f:X\to A$ is generically finite and surjective, so is the map $\pi_{i}:X\to Y$ . Now let $\overline{L}$ be the canonical adelic line bundle on $A$ . Recall that $Y=V^{m}$ which when viewed as a subset of $A^{m}$ , there is an adelic line bundle $\overline{L}^{\prime}$ given by pulling back and tensoring the different $\overline{L}$ ’s.

We let $\overline{M}=\pi_{1}^{*}\overline{L}^{\prime}+\cdots+\pi_{r}^{*}\overline{L}^{\prime}$ and let $\overline{N}=f^{*}\overline{L}$ . Then both $\overline{M}$ and $\overline{N}$ are nef, semipositive adelic line bundles, and are geometrically semiample and big. In fact, $\overline{M}$ is geometrically ample since $\iota:X\xhookrightarrow{}Y^{s}_{A}$ is a closed immersion and so if $p_{i}:Y^{r}_{A}\xhookrightarrow{}Y^{r}\to Y$ are the projection maps, then

$$ \overline{M}=\iota^{*}(p_{1}^{*}\overline{L}^{\prime}+\cdots+p_{r}^{*}\overline{L}^{\prime}) $$

and each $\overline{L}^{\prime}$ is geometrically ample, giving us that $\overline{M}$ is geometrically ample.

The morphism $f:X\to A$ commutes with composing $\delta:V^{m}\to A$ with $\pi_{i}:X\to Y$ .

#### Proposition 8.7.

There exists $a>0$ such that both $a\overline{L}^{\prime}-\delta^{*}\overline{L}$ and $a\overline{M}-\overline{N}$ is nef on $Y$ and $X$ respectively.

#### Proof.

It suffices to find $a>0$ such that $a\overline{L}^{\prime}-\delta^{*}\overline{L}$ is nef on $Y=V^{m}$ . Let $p_{i}:V^{m}\to V$ be the different coordinate projections. Then $\overline{L}^{\prime}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_{i}^{*}\overline{L}$ . Now by the theorem of the cube [7, Theorem 8.6.11], the function $q(\alpha)=\alpha^{*}L$ for $\alpha\in\Hom(A^{m},A)$ is quadratic if $L$ is symmetric. We hence obtain the identity

$$ m(m-1)\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_{i}^{*}L-\delta^{*}L=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq m-1}(p_{i}-p_{j})^{*}L+\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}((m-1)p_{i}+p_{m})^{*}L, $$

coming from the general identity for quadratic forms

$$ \left(\sum_{i}c_{i}^{2}\right)\sum_{i}q(x_{i})-q(\sum c_{i}x_{i})=\sum_{i<j}q(c_{j}x_{i}-c_{i}x_{j}), $$

where we take $c_{1}=\cdots=c_{m-1}=1$ and $c_{m}=-(m-1)$ . As $\overline{L}$ has the canonical metric, it is compatible with the theorem of the cube and hence (8.1) holds with $\overline{L}$ replacing $L$ , proving that $m(m-1)\overline{L}^{\prime}-\delta^{*}\overline{L}$ is nef as desired. ∎

#### Proposition 8.8.

We have $\overline{M}\cdot\overline{N}^{g}=0$ where $g=\dim A$ . Hence $\overline{M}^{g+1}=\overline{N}^{g+1}=0$ .

#### Proof.

Since $a\overline{L}^{\prime}-\delta^{*}\overline{L}$ is nef and $(\overline{L}^{\prime})^{g+1}=0$ , it follows that all mixed intersections between $\overline{L}^{\prime}$ and $\delta^{*}\overline{L}$ vanish. Hence we have $\overline{L}^{\prime}(\delta^{*}\overline{L})^{g}=0$ . By the projection formula, we have $\pi_{i}^{*}\overline{L}^{\prime}(f^{*}\overline{L})^{g}=0$ for each $i=1,\ldots,r$ . Hence $\overline{M}\cdot\overline{N}^{g}=0$ .

By the projection formula, we know that $\overline{N}^{g+1}=0$ . We now apply Proposition 7.2. As $\overline{M}$ and $\overline{N}$ are nef, we obtain $\overline{M}^{g+1}=0$ as desired. ∎

We now apply Proposition 7.3. Let $D$ be an exceptional divisor for $f:X\to A$ . It follows that

$$ h_{\overline{M}}(D)=h_{\overline{N}}(D). $$

However, $\overline{N}=f^{*}\overline{L}$ . As $\codim f(D)\geq 2$ , the projection formula implies that $h_{\overline{N}}(D)=0$ . Thus $h_{\overline{M}}(D)=0$ . Using our closed embedding $\iota:X\xhookrightarrow{}Y_{A}^{s}\xhookrightarrow{}Y^{s}$ , we obtain a subvariety $D$ of $Y^{s}=V^{ms}$ with dimension $g-1$ with zero canonical height.

We now apply the same argument as in Proposition 8.3 to arrive at a contradiction through the following proposition.

#### Proposition 8.9.

Let $K$ be a countable GVF and $A$ an abelian variety over $K$ which satisfies $\Tr_{\overline{K}/\overline{k_{0}}}(A_{\overline{K}})=0$ where $k_{0}$ is the height zero subfield of $K$ . Assume that $V\subseteq A$ is a height zero subvariety which is not a coset. Furthermore assume that $(\dim V,\dim A)$ is minimal among all counterexamples. Let $D\subseteq V^{r}$ be a positive dimensional subvariety of height zero. Then $\gcd(\dim D,\dim V)>1$ .

#### Proof.

We proceed by induction on $\dim D$ . First, observe that the image of $D$ to any $V$ must be either a point or the entire $V$ . Indeed otherwise the image of $D$ is a positive dimensional subvariety of $V$ with canonical height zero, just as in the proof of Proposition 8.2. By minimality of $V$ , the image of $D$ must be a coset, say $x+B$ . By Proposition 8.3, we know that $\dim A\geq 2\dim V$ . This implies that

$$ \dim(A/B)=\dim A-\dim B\geq 2\dim V-\dim B>2\dim V-\dim V=\dim V. $$

In particular, we cannot have $q(V)=A/B$ which contradicts Proposition 8.2.

Now let’s assume that $\pi:D\to V$ is surjective where $\pi$ is the first projection. We let $\nu:V^{\prime}\to V$ be the normalization of $V$ inside $K(V)$ and endow $K(V)$ with the polarized GVF structure $(K(V),\nu^{*}\overline{L},\ldots,\nu^{*}\overline{L})$ . As all prime divisors of $V$ have canonical height $>0$ by assumption of minimality, it follows by the proof of Lemma 8.4 that $A_{K(V)}$ remains traceless over the height zero subfield.

Now as in the proof of Proposition 8.3, it follows that $D_{K(V)}$ has height zero and lies inside $V_{K(V)}^{r-1}$ . But $V_{K(V)}$ and $A_{K(V)}$ is still a minimal counterexample in terms of $(\dim V,\dim A)$ whereas $\dim D_{K(V)}=\dim D-\dim V$ . Hence either $\dim D-\dim V=0,$ or we can apply induction. Either way, we find that

$$ \gcd(\dim D-\dim V,\dim V)>1\implies\gcd(\dim D,\dim V)>1 $$

as desired. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 8.1.

Combining $\dim D=g-1$ combined with Proposition 8.9 gives us a contradiction, since we know from Proposition 8.3 that $\dim V$ divides $g=\dim A.$ Thus the Bogomolov for traceless GVFs must be true, proving Theorem 8.1.

∎

It is now straightforward to conclude the Bogomolov conjecture over GVFs where $A$ may not have trivial trace.

#### Theorem 8.10.

Let $K$ be a countable non-archimedean GVF and let $k$ be the height zero subfield. Assume both $K$ and $k$ are algebraically closed. Let $A/K$ be an abelian variety and let $B=\Tr_{K/k}(A)$ be its trace with the trace morphism $\Tr:B_{K}\to A$ . Then if $V\subseteq A$ has canonical height zero, $V$ must be of the form $x+B+\Tr(W_{K})$ where $x$ is a point of height zero, $B$ is an abelian subvariety, and $W\subseteq B$ a subvariety defined over $k_{0}$ .

#### Proof.

By [51, Lemma 5.0.3] (and noting that images of cosets are still images of cosets), it suffices to prove the conjecture for any isogenous abelian variety. There exists an abelian variety $C/K$ with $\Tr_{K/k}(C)=0$ and an isogeny $B\times C\to A$ . Hence it suffices to prove it for $B\times C$ . As we know the Bogomolov conjecture for $C$ and $B$ is defined over $k$ , [51, Lemma 5.4.6] shows that the Bogomolov conjecture for $B\times C$ follows as desired. ∎

## 9. Uniform Height Gaps for Subvarieties in Positive Characteristic

We now explain how to prove uniform height gaps for subvarieties in positive characteristic by using Theorem 8.10. Already in [51, §4.2], Hultberg showed that Theorem 8.10 implies the new gap principle for subvarieties over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , and also over function fields of characteristic zero (see also [60]). We show that Theorem 8.10 also implies a new gap principle for subvarieties in positive characteristic. The main difficulty in the positive characteristic situation is that an abelian variety $A$ can be non-isotrivial but isogeneous to an isotrivial abelian variety $B$ . To handle this, we will use the theory of $p$ -divisible groups. We begin by reviewing some results on $p$ -divisible groups by Lau–Nicole–Vasiu [54].

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $D$ be a $p$ -divisible group over $k$ . The isomorphism number $n_{D}$ is the smallest $n$ such that $D[p^{n}]$ determines $D$ , i.e. if $E$ is another $p$ -divisible group with $E[p^{n}]\simeq D[p^{n}]$ , then $E\simeq D$ . The distance $q_{D,E}$ between two $p$ -divisible groups $D$ and $E$ is the minimal non-negative integer $m$ for which there exists an isogeny $\pi:D\to E$ with kernel killed by $p^{m}$ . We say that $D$ is a minimal $p$ -divisible group if $n_{D}=1$ and we define the minimal height of $D$ to be $q_{D,D_{0}}$ where $D_{0}$ is the unique minimal $p$ -divisible group in the isogeny class of $D$ .

Let $K=\overline{k(C)}$ be the algebraic closure of a function field of a curve $C$ over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic $p$ and let $A/K$ be an abelian variety. Then $D_{A}=A[p^{\infty}]$ defines for us a $p$ -divisible group. We want to understand the minimal degree of an isogeny $\pi:A\to B$ such that $D_{B}$ is minimal.

#### Proposition 9.1.

There exists an isogeny $\pi:A\to B$ , with $\ker(\pi)\subseteq A[p^{2g}]$ , so that $D_{B}$ is minimal.

#### Proof.

Let $D_{A}=A[p^{\infty}]$ . By [54, Theorem 1.5], we know that $q_{D_{A}}\leq\lfloor\nu(c)\rfloor$ , where $\nu:[0,c+d]\to\mathbb{R}$ is the Newton polygon for $D_{A}$ , with $d$ denoting the dimension and $c$ the codimension, where $c+d$ adds up to the height of $D_{A}$ which is $2g$ . As noted by the discussion after [54, Theorem 1.2], we have

$$ \nu(c)\leq\frac{cd}{c+d}\leq\frac{(c+d)^{2}}{(c+d)}=2g. $$

Hence we can find $\pi:D_{A}\to D_{0}$ , with $D_{0}$ minimal and $\ker(\pi)\subseteq D_{A}[p^{2g}]$ . Let $H=\ker(\pi)$ . Then taking $B=A/\ker(\pi)$ gives us an isogenous abelian variety with $D_{B}\simeq D_{0}$ which is minimal as desired. ∎

If $A/K$ is an abelian variety with $D_{A}$ minimal, then if $A$ is isogenous to an abelian variety over $k$ , it follows that $A$ itself is also defined over $k$ . This resolves the issue noted at the beginning of the section: a non-isotrivial abelian variety $A$ may be isogenous to an isotrivial abelian variety $B$ .

#### Proposition 9.2.

Let $A/K$ be an abelian variety with $D_{A}$ minimal, and assume there exists $B/k$ so that there is an isogeny $\pi:B_{K}\to A$ . Then $A$ itself is defined over $k$ .

#### Proof.

Let $H=\ker(\pi)$ , which is a finite flat group subscheme over $K$ . We want to prove that $H$ descends to $H^{\prime}$ over $k$ , in which then $A\simeq(B/H^{\prime})_{K}$ and hence $A$ is constant. We split $H$ to its $p$ -part and $p$ -primary part, giving us a decomposition $H=H_{p}\times H_{0}$ , where $H_{p}$ is a finite flat $p$ -group scheme and $H_{0}$ is finite and etale. Then $H_{0}$ automatically descends to $k$ and by quotienting out $H_{0}$ , we may assume that $\pi$ is a $p$ -primary isogeny.

We first note that any minimal $p$ -divisible group $D$ over $K$ , must have already been defined over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ . Indeed, choose a $p$ -divisible group $D^{\prime}$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ with the same Newton polygon as $D$ . After base changing to $k$ , the group $D^{\prime}_{K}$ lies in the same isogeny class as $D$ . But both $D^{\prime}_{K}$ and $D$ are minimal [54, Corollary 4.9] and hence must be isomorphic to each other.

We now choose $D^{\prime}_{A}$ over $k$ so that $D^{\prime}_{A,K}\simeq D_{A}$ . Let $D_{B}$ be the $p$ -divisible group of $B$ over $k$ . The isogeny $\pi:B_{K}\to A$ gives us an isogeny $\pi_{D}:D^{\prime}_{B,K}\to D^{\prime}_{A,K}$ . By [54, Lemma 2.8],

$$ \Hom(D_{B},D^{\prime}_{A})\simeq\Hom(D_{B,K},D^{\prime}_{A,K}), $$

the isogeny $\pi$ descends to $\pi^{\prime}_{D}:D_{B}\to D^{\prime}_{A}$ and hence $\ker(\pi_{D})$ also descends to $\ker(\pi^{\prime}_{D})$ which is defined over $k$ . But $\ker(\pi)=\ker(\pi_{D})$ and so $\ker(\pi)$ descends over $k$ as desired. ∎

We also have to understand the locus of abelian varieties whose $p$ -divisible groups are minimal. Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a $p$ -divisible group over a $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ -scheme $S$ . We have the following result.

#### Theorem 9.3.

Assume that $\mathcal{D}$ has constant Newton polygon. Then the locus of $s\in S$ where the geometric fiber $\mathcal{D}_{\overline{s}}$ is minimal is closed in $S$ .

#### Proof.

This follows from [54, Theorem 1.1]. ∎

Now consider the moduli space $\mathcal{A}_{g,n}$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ . For each possible Newton polygon, there is a locally closed subscheme $\mathcal{A}_{g,n}^{\nu}$ of $\mathcal{A}_{g,n}$ , consisting of points whose $p$ -divisible group has Newton polygon $\nu$ by [54, Lemma 4.8]. Then the minimal locus $\mathcal{A}_{g,n}^{\nu,\min}$ is closed inside $\mathcal{A}_{g,n}^{\nu}$ by [54, Theorem 1.1] and hence is locally closed inside $\mathcal{A}_{g,n}$ . Note that if $K$ is any field and $A/K$ an abelian variety that maps to $\mathcal{A}_{g,n}^{\nu,\min}$ , then the $p$ -divisible group of $A$ is minimal.

We are now ready to begin the proof of our new gap principle in positive characteristic.

#### Theorem 9.4.

Let $K=k(B)$ be a function field for a curve of characteristic $p$ . Let $A$ be an abelian variety over $K$ and $L$ a symmetric ample line bundle. Let $V\subseteq A_{\overline{K}}$ be a subvariety such that $\Stab(V)$ is finite and $V-V$ generates $A$ . Then there exists $c=c(\dim A,\deg_{L}(V))>0$ and $M=M(\dim A,\deg_{L}(V))$ , such that

$$ \widehat{h}_{A,L}(V)\geq ch_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A_{0}) $$

where $A_{0}$ is an abelian variety with an isogeny $\pi:A\to A_{0}$ of degree at most $M$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\deg_{L}(V)=d$ . Then as $V-V$ generates $A$ , it follows from [36, Lemma 2.5] that $\deg_{L}(A)$ is bounded in terms of $d$ . Applying [36, Lemma 2.2(iv)] allows us to assume that $(A,L)$ is a principal polarization by passing to an isogeneous abelian variety (whose degree is bounded by the lemma).

Now, fix some $n\geq 3$ not divisible by $p$ . Consider the Hilbert scheme of the universal abelian variety $\mathfrak{A}/\mathcal{A}_{g,n}.$ Since $\deg_{L}(V)$ is bounded, we may restrict to a finite type scheme $\mathbb{H}$ for which all such $(A,V)$ ’s appear as a point on $\mathbb{H}/\mathcal{A}_{g,n}$ . We further pass to a Zariski open $\mathbb{H}^{\circ}$ that parametrizes geometrically integral subvarieties $V$ , with $\Stab(V)$ finite and $V-V$ generating $A$ , and we give $\mathbb{H}^{\circ}$ the reduced scheme structure.

Now let $T\subseteq\mathbb{H}^{\circ}$ be an irreducible component. Then we have a principally polarized abelian scheme $\mathcal{A}$ over $T$ and a flat family of geometrically integral subvarieties $\mathcal{V}\subseteq\mathcal{A}$ . We may find a symmetric line bundle $\mathcal{L}$ on $\mathcal{A}$ inducing twice the polarization and then endow $\mathcal{L}$ with a canonical adelic metric $\overline{\mathcal{L}}$ . Since $\mathcal{V}$ is integral, we can form the Deligne pairing

$$ \overline{M}=\langle\overline{\mathcal{L}},\ldots,\overline{\mathcal{L}}\rangle_{\mathcal{V}/\mathbb{H}^{\circ}}. $$

Then for any GVF field $K$ , a GVF-valued point $s\in\mathbb{H}^{\circ}(K)$ corresponding to the pair $(A,V)$ satisfies

$$ h_{\overline{M}}(s)=a\widehat{h}_{A,L}(V) $$

for some fixed constant $a>0$ depending only on $\deg_{L}(V).$

Now assume for the sake of contradiction that our theorem is false. By Proposition 9.1, we may assume $A$ has minimal $p$ -divisible group by taking an isogeny of degree dividing $p^{2g}$ from the original $A$ to an abelian variety $A^{\prime}$ with minimal $p$ -divisible group and replacing $V$ with its image in $A^{\prime}$ .

Hence we may find a sequence of abelian varieties $A_{n}/K_{n}$ , with minimal $p$ -divisible group, and subvarieties $V_{n}$ with $(A_{n},V_{n})$ lying in $T$ , such that

$$ \widehat{h}_{A_{n},L}(V_{n})<\frac{1}{n}h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A_{n}). $$

Since there are only finitely many Newton polygons, we may assume that $A_{m}\in\mathcal{A}_{g,n}^{\nu,\min}(K_{n})$ for the same $\nu$ . Now cover $\mathcal{A}_{g,n}$ with finitely many affine opens $U_{i}$ . We may assume all the $A_{m}$ ’s lie in the same open, say $U_{1}$ . Using $\mathcal{L}^{4}$ , we may embed $\mathfrak{A}_{U_{i}}\xhookrightarrow{}\mathbb{P}^{N}$ . Now by [60, Theorem 1.1], combining with Zhang’s fundamental inequality, there exists some $C=C(\dim A,\deg_{L}(V))>0$ such that

$$ \widehat{h}(\iota(V_{n}))\leq Ch_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A_{n}) $$

where $\widehat{h}(\iota(V))$ denotes the Weil height of $\iota(V)$ inside $\mathbb{P}^{N}$ .

Fix an ample line bundle $\overline{M}$ on $T$ .
