We degenerate using $\varepsilon_{n}=h_{\overline{M}}(x_{n})$ , where we may assume that $h_{\overline{M}}(x_{n})>0$ where $x_{n}=[(A_{n},V_{n})]$ , as otherwise $h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A_{n})=0$ . Applying Proposition 4.4 to the sequence $([A_{n},V_{n}],K_{n}[\varepsilon_{n}])$ , we obtain an ultrafilter limit $x_{\omega}=[A_{\omega},V_{\omega}]$ over $K_{\omega}$ that lies in $T(K_{\omega})$ . Then by definition, we have $h_{\overline{M}}(x_{\omega})=1>0$ .

We first claim that $h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A_{\omega})>0$ . Indeed let’s assume that $h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A_{\omega})=0$ . Then by (9.1), we also have $\widehat{h}(\iota(V_{\omega}))=0$ . Let $k_{\omega}$ be the height zero subfield of $K_{\omega}$ . Then $\widehat{h}(\iota(V_{\omega}))=0$ and $h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A_{\omega})=0$ implies that both $A_{\omega}$ and $V_{\omega}$ are defined over $\overline{k_{\omega}}$ . Hence $x_{\omega}\in T(\overline{k_{\omega}})$ , but this contradicts $h_{\overline{M}}(x_{\omega})>0$ . Hence $h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A_{\omega})>0$ .

Now as each $A_{n}$ lie in $\mathcal{A}_{g,3}^{\nu,\min}$ , it follows that $A_{\omega}$ also does. Now we have $\widehat{h}_{A_{\omega},L}(V_{\omega})=0$ . Using Theorem 8.10, it follows that

$$ V_{\omega}=a+B_{\omega}+\Tr(W_{K_{\omega}}) $$

where $B_{\omega}$ is an abelian subvariety of $A_{\omega}$ , and $W$ is a subvariety of $\Tr_{\overline{K_{\omega}}/\overline{k_{\omega}}}(A_{\omega})$ where $k_{\omega}$ is the height zero subfield of $K_{\omega}$ . As $\Stab(V_{\omega})$ is finite, $B$ must be zero. Then as $V-V$ generates $A$ , it follows that the image of $W_{K_{\omega}}-W_{K_{\omega}}$ generates $A$ and hence we must have $\Tr_{\overline{K_{\omega}}/\overline{k_{\omega}}}(A_{\omega})$ being full dimensional.

We now apply Proposition 9.2. As $A_{\omega}$ has minimal $p$ -divisible subgroup, it follows that $A_{\omega}$ is defined over $\overline{k_{\omega}}$ . Then $h_{\operatorname{Fal}}(A_{\omega})=0$ , which is a contradiction. This finishes our proof, where we obtain uniform constants that may depend on the characteristic of $k$ .

Finally for sufficiently large positive characteristic, as already noted by Hultberg [51, Theorem 4], the Bogomolov conjecture for GVFs in characteristic zero gives a uniform height gap for all sufficiently large positive characteristic. This removes the dependence on the characteristic $p$ . ∎

# Non-Archimedean Rigidity and the Uniform Dynamical Manin–Mumford for $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$

**Authors:** Zhuchao Ji Address: Institute for Theoretical Sciences, Westlake University, 600 Dunyu Road, Hangzhou, Zhejiang 310030, China Email address: jizhuchao@westlake.edu.cn and Jit Wu Yap Address: Department of Mathematics, National University of Singapore, 10 Lower Kent Ridge Road, Singapore 119076 Email address: yapjitwu@nus.edu.sg

## Abstract

We prove a uniform form of the dynamical Manin–Mumford conjecture for split endomorphisms $\Phi=\left(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\right):\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}\to\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ over $\mathbb{C}$ , where each $f_{i}$ has degree $d\geq 2$ and at most one $f_{i}$ is exceptional. Specifically, we bound the number of irreducible components of $\overline{\operatorname{Prep}\left(\Phi\right)\cap V\left(\mathbb{C}\right)}^{\mathrm{Zar}}$ uniformly, depending only on $\left(n,d,\deg V\right)$ . We also obtain uniform statements for the dynamical Bogomolov conjecture. Our approach combines a degeneration argument via ultrafilters with a new non-archimedean rigidity theorem, along with the quantitative dynamical Zhang’s inequality by Mavraki and the second author.

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1. The main results

Let $\Phi=\left(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\right):\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}\to\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ be a split endomorphism of $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ over $\mathbb{C}$ with $\deg f_{i}=d\geq 2$ . Assume that at most one of the maps $f_{i}$ is exceptional. Here non-exceptional means not conjugate to a monomial, Chebyshev or Lattès map. Then the dynamical Manin–Mumford conjecture [92, 48], proven in this setting by Ghioca–Nguyen–Ye [47, 46], with a gap fixed by Mavraki–Schmidt–Wilms [67], states that any subvariety $V\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ with a Zariski dense set of preperiodic points for $\Phi$ must itself be preperiodic for $\Phi$ . The reader may also see [29, 31] for some cases of the dynamical Manin–Mumford conjecture for maps over $\mathbb{P}^{2}$ .

Ghioca–Nguyen–Ye’s proof follows the strategy introduced by Ullmo [82] and Zhang [91] in their proofs of the Bogomolov conjecture. Applying Yuan’s equidistribution theorem for small points [89], they show that if $C\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{2}$ is a curve with infinitely many preperiodic points, then

$$ \left(\deg\pi_{2}\right)\pi_{1}^{*}\mu_{f_{1}}=\left(\deg\pi_{1}\right)\pi_{2}^{*}\mu_{f_{2}} $$

as measures on $C\left(\mathbb{C}\right)$ , where $\mu_{f_{i}}$ is the equilibrium measure of $f_{i}$ . The proof is then completed by establishing that equality of measures forces $C$ to be preperiodic under $\left(f_{1},f_{2}\right)$ . This is a rigidity statement for the equilibrium measures $\mu_{f_{1}},\mu_{f_{2}}$ , belonging to a wider class of rigidity phenomena studied by various authors [32, 60, 61, 28, 86, 30, 56, 68].

Our first main result is a non-archimedean analogue of Ghioca–Nguyen–Ye’s rigidity theorem.

#### Theorem 1.1.

Let $f,g:\mathbb{P}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be two rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$ defined over $K$ where $K$ is an algebraically closed complete valued non-archimedean field of residue characteristic $0$ . Let $C\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be an irreducible curve over $K$ that projects dominantly to both coordinates. Assume that $\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f\right)>0$ . Then if $\left(\deg\pi_{2}\right)\pi_{1}^{*}\mu_{f}=\left(\deg\pi_{1}\right)\pi_{2}^{*}\mu_{g}$ , the curve $C$ must be preperiodic for $\left(f,g\right)$ .

In fact, we prove a stronger statement in Theorem 4.1: the assumption $\deg f=\deg g$ is unnecessary, and it suffices that $\pi_{1}^{*}\mu_{f}$ and $\pi_{2}^{*}\mu_{g}$ are proportional on an open subset $U\subseteq C^{\operatorname{an}}$ with $\left(\pi_{1}^{*}\mu_{f}\right)\left(U\right)>0$ . The conclusion is that $C$ is preperiodic under $\left(f^{a},g^{b}\right)$ for some positive integers $a,b$ satisfying $\left(\deg f\right)^{a}=\left(\deg g\right)^{b}$ .

The condition that $\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f\right)>0$ is necessary for Theorem 1.1. If $\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f\right)=0$ , and $C=\Delta$ is the diagonal, the classification in [38] imply that any $g$ which is small enough perturbation of $f$ will satisfy $\mu_{f}=\mu_{g}$ .

When $f$ and $g$ are polynomials and $C=\Delta$ , Theorem 1.1 was recently proved by Chen Gong and the second-named author [50] using a relatively elementary argument based on a non-archimedean analogue of the polynomial trees constructed by DeMarco and McMullen [20]. Our approach is different: it relies on ergodic properties of the equilibrium measures $\mu_{f},\mu_{g}$ which were established recently only by Favre and Rivera-Letelier [38].

A non-archimedean dynamical rigidity theorem for a place $v$ may be viewed as a rigidity theorem for families of dynamical systems, when viewed through the local geometry determined at $v$ . Using ultrafilter degeneration techniques by Luo [64, 65] and Favre–Gong [34], we show that Theorem 1.1 implies the uniform dynamical Manin-Mumford conjecture for $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{2}$ .

#### Theorem 1.2.

Let $f,g:\mathbb{P}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be two rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$ over $\mathbb{C}$ and let $C\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{2}$ be an irreducible curve of degree $D$ . Then there exists a constant $B=B\left(d,D\right)>0$ so that either

$$ C\text{ is }\left(f,g\right)\text{-special or }\left|\operatorname{Prep}\left(f,g\right)\cap C\right|\leq B. $$

When $f,g$ are non-exceptional, special curves are simply the preperiodic curves. The definition of an $\left(f,g\right)$ -special curve is given in Definition 9.6. Under the same philosophy, in the polynomial case, Gong–Yap [50] showed that their non-archimedean rigidity theorem implies a uniform bound on the number of common preperiodic points.

Taking $C$ to be the diagonal in Theorem 1.2, we resolve the conjecture of DeMarco–Krieger–Ye [22, Conjecture 1.4] on a uniform bound for common preperiodic points.

#### Theorem 1.3.

For every integer $d\geq 2$ , there exists a constant $B=B(d)>0$ such that, for any two rational maps $f,g:\mathbb{P}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}$ of degree $d$ over $\mathbb{C}$ , either

$$ \operatorname{Prep}(f)=\operatorname{Prep}(g)\quad\text{or}\quad\left|\operatorname{Prep}(f)\cap\operatorname{Prep}(g)\right|\leq B. $$

Using ideas of David–Philippon [14] in the setting of $\mathbb{G}_{m}^{n}$ and specialization arguments by Mavraki–Yap [69], we can extend Theorem 1.2 to the case of $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ for general $n\geq 2$ . This gives us the following theorem, which can be viewed as a uniform dynamical Manin–Mumford on $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ for general $n\geq 2$ , allowing at most one exceptional coordinate map.

#### Theorem 1.4.

Let $\Phi=\left(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\right)$ be a split endomorphism of $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ defined over $\mathbb{C}$ such that each $f_{i}$ is of the same degree $d\geq 2$ . Assume that at most one of the maps $f_{i}$ is exceptional. Let $V\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ be an irreducible subvariety, defined over $\mathbb{C}$ , of degree $D$ . Then there exists $N=N\left(n,d,D\right)>0$ such that

$$ \overline{\operatorname{Prep}\left(\Phi\right)\cap V\left(\mathbb{C}\right)}^{\operatorname{Zar}}\text{ is a union of at most }N\text{ irreducible preperiodic subvarieties.} $$

As is the usual case with Arakelov-theoretic methods, we obtain analogous uniform Bogomolov statements. In particular, we obtain a uniform height gap for hypersurfaces $H\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ , analogous to the new gap principle by Gao–Ge–Kühne [41]. Given a split endomorphism $\Phi:\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}\to\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ of rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$ , we say that $V$ is weakly $\Phi$ -special if any of the following holds:

- (1) $V$ is preperiodic for $\Phi$ ;

- (2) $V$ does not project dominantly to one of the coordinates;

- (3) $V$ is of the form $\pi^{-1}\left(W\right)$ where $\pi:\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}\to\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n-1}$ is the projection away from a coordinate and $W$ a closed subvariety of $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n-1}$ .

#### Theorem 1.5.

Let $\Phi=\left(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\right)$ be a split endomorphism of $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ such that each $f_{i}$ has degree $d\geq 2$ and at least one $f_{i}$ is non-exceptional. Let $H\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ be an irreducible hypersurface of degree $D$ which is not weakly $\Phi$ -special that is defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Then there exists $c=c\left(n,d,D\right)>0$ such that

$$ \widehat{h}_{\Phi}\left(H\right)\geq c\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\Phi\right),1\right\}. $$

Here, $\widehat{h}_{\Phi}$ denotes the canonical height of $\Phi$ with respect to the line bundle $L$ and $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\Phi\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f_{i}\right)$ , where by abuse of notation $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}$ is a Weil height for the moduli space $\operatorname{rat}_{d}$ of degree $d$ rational maps up to equivalence [79].

#### Remark 1.6.

Shortly after we proved Theorem 1.1, DeMarco and Mavraki [25] informed us that they have a strategy to deduce non-degeneracy results from our non-archimedean rigidity theorem, and in particular obtain different proofs of Theorems 1.2 and 1.4, as well as relative versions. As our strategies for obtaining uniformity is different from theirs, we decided to write our results separately.

#### Remark 1.7.

One major technical difficulty in implementing the strategy of [50] to the setting of Theorem 1.2 is the lack of understanding of the loci of triplets $\left(f,g,C\right)$ where $C$ is preperiodic for $\left(f,g\right)$ . In [50], the authors only deal with the case where $(f,g)$ are polynomials and $C=\Delta$ is the diagonal, and in particular this loci is known to be almost always a Zariski closed set. However in our setting, we a priori only know that it is a countable union of Zariski closed sets. This makes the ultrafilter degeneration method much more technical. In [25], DeMarco and Mavraki are able to use their non-degeneracy results to characterize the loci [26, Theorem 1.1]. As an example, [25, Theorem 1.2] states that the loci of pairs of non-exceptional rational maps $(f,g)$ in $\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times\operatorname{Rat}_{d}$ such that $\operatorname{Prep}(f)=\operatorname{Prep}(g)$ is Zariski closed.

### 1.2. Proof Strategy for Theorem 1.3

There have been many partial results towards Theorem 1.4. The case of $n=2$ and $V$ being the diagonal $\Delta\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{2}$ was first studied by DeMarco–Krieger–Ye [21, 22] for the quadratic unicritical family and the Legendre family of Lattès maps. Poineau [76, 77] subsequently extended their results to cover all pairs of Lattès maps. In this case, one is looking for a uniform bound on the size of $\operatorname{Prep}\left(f,g\right)\cap\Delta=\operatorname{Prep}\left(f\right)\cap\operatorname{Prep}\left(g\right)$ . For general families of rational maps, DeMarco–Mavraki [24] showed the existence of a Zariski open $U\subseteq\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times\operatorname{Rat}_{d}$ and $N=N\left(d\right)>0$ depending only on $d$ so that $\left|\operatorname{Prep}\left(\Phi\right)\cap\Delta\right|\leq N$ for all $\Phi\in U$ . Gauthier [45] extended DeMarco–Mavraki results to the case of different degrees. For one-parameter families and $n=2$ , Theorem 1.4 was proven by Mavraki–Schmidt [68].

Among these previous results, one can summarize two different approaches to proving cases of Theorem 1.4 when $n=2$ . By a specialization argument following Mavraki and the second author [69] (see Section 9), it suffices to handle the case where $\Phi$ and $C$ are defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . The first is to study an adelic energy pairing $\left(f,g\right)$ between two rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , first defined by Favre–Rivera-Letelier [36], see also Fili [40]. The adelic energy pairing $\left(f,g\right)$ can be written as a sum of local energy pairings

$$ \left(f,g\right)=\sum_{v\in M_{K}}n_{v}\left(f,g\right)_{v} $$

where $K$ is a number field where $f,g$ are defined over and $n_{v}=\left[K_{v}:\mathbb{Q}_{p}\right]/\left[K:\mathbb{Q}\right]$ . The local energy pairing $\left(f,g\right)_{v}$ is non-negative and is zero if and only if $\mu_{f,v}=\mu_{g,v}$ , where $\mu_{f,v},\mu_{g,v}$ are the equilibrium measure of $f$ and $g$ , supported on $\mathbb{P}_{v}^{1,\operatorname{an}}$ , see [3] and [5] for more details of dynamics on $\mathbb{P}^{1,\operatorname{an}}_{v}$ and this measure.

By the work of DeMarco–Krieger–Ye [21, 22], generalized by Gauthier [45] and Ang–Yap [2], it is known that to obtain uniform bounds on $\left|\operatorname{Prep}\left(f\right)\cap\operatorname{Prep}\left(g\right)\right|$ , it suffices to prove that if $\left(f,g\right)\not=0$ , then

$$ \left(f,g\right)\geq c\max\left\{h\left(f,g\right),1\right\} $$

for some $c=c\left(d\right)>0$ depending only on the degree $d$ . Here, $h\left(f,g\right)$ can be taken as $h\left(f\right)+h\left(g\right)$ for an ample Weil height $h$ on $\operatorname{Rat}_{d}$ . DeMarco–Krieger–Ye shows that (1.1) holds if $\left(f,g\right)$ belong to the quadratic unicritical family [22], or to the family of Lattès map associated to the Legendre family [21]. This is also the approach taken by Poineau [76, 77] for the case of general Lattès maps $\left(f,g\right)$ .

The second approach is to study the non-degeneracy of subvarieties with respect to a bifurcation current. Given a family of polarized dynamical systems $\left(X\to S,\Phi,\cal{L}\right)$ and a closed subvariety $Y\subseteq X$ of codimension $r$ that defines a flat family over $S$ , we say that the triple $\left(X,Y,\Phi\right)$ is non-degenerate if we have the non-vanishing

$$ \hat{T}_{\Phi}^{k-r+\dim S}\wedge\left[Y\right]\not=0 $$

where $\hat{T}_{\Phi}$ is a dynamical $\left(1,1\right)$ -current associated to our family. One may consult [24, Section 4] for more details. Studying and proving instances of non-degeneracy has been very successful in resolving the uniform Mordell–Lang conjecture [42, 27, 58, 41] and also in dynamical settings [44, 24, 23, 68, 1].

We follow the first approach in directly establishing uniform lower bounds for the global energy pairing $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle$ . In the more general setting of bounding $\left|\operatorname{Prep}\left(f,g\right)\cap C\right|$ , we may define a generalization of the adelic energy pairing using the notion of a flat metric [87]. We write it as $\left(f,g\right)_{C}$ and there is also a local decomposition

$$ \left(f,g\right)_{C}=\sum_{v\in M_{K}}n_{v}\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,v}. $$

Then using the quantitative dynamical Zhang’s inequality by Mavraki–Yap [69], if $C$ is of bidegree $\left(d_{1},d_{2}\right)$ , it suffices to prove the existence of $c=c\left(d_{1},d_{2},d\right)>0$ depending only on $\left(d_{1},d_{2},d\right)$ such that

$$ \left(f,g\right)_{C}\geq c\max\left\{h\left(f,g\right),1\right\}. $$

Observe that the quantitative Zhang’s inequality is essential in our approach as we do not establish any form of bigness for the associated line bundles. This is because we are unable to understand when does the exceptional locus, where $C$ is preperiodic for $\left(f,g\right)$ , lie in a proper Zariski closed set. In particular, we are unable to apply the height inequalities or equidistribution results from Yuan–Zhang [88] to deduce uniformity. Instead, we have to rely on a pointwise approach which can be handled by the quantitative Zhang’s inequality. This is also why we only obtain uniform bounds and not any sort of relative results as in [68] and [25].

### 1.3. Degenerations and Non-Archimedean Rigidity

To prove uniform lower bounds on $\left(f,g\right)_{C}$ , we will prove uniform lower bounds on the local energy pairing $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,v}$ . Let $S$ be a quasi-projective variety over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ parametrizing a family of triples $\left(f,g,C\right)$ where $f,g$ are rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$ and $C$ is a degree $\left(d_{1},d_{2}\right)$ curve. In Section 5, we prove that the local energy pairing $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,s}$ defines a function

$$ \left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,s}:S^{\operatorname{an}}\setminus S^{\operatorname{triv}}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} $$

where $S^{\operatorname{an}}$ is the Berkovich analytification of $S$ and $S^{\operatorname{triv}}$ is the set of points $s\in S^{\operatorname{an}}$ whose residue field $\cal{H}\left(s\right)$ is trivially valued. Furthermore using properties of the Deligne pairing [88, Section 4], the function $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,s}$ is continuous under some technical hypothesis which we are able to assume in our argument. Now, the locus of points $\left(f,g,C\right)\in S$ for which $C$ is preperiodic for $\left(f,g\right)$ can be given by a countable union of closed subvarieties $V_{1},V_{2},\ldots$ . Ideally, this should be contained in a proper Zariski closed subvariety but it is not clear a priori. This makes the argument more technical than in [50].

We now let $\lambda_{V_{i}}$ be local height functions for $V_{i}$ (see Section 3.2). Let $\lambda_{\partial S}$ be a local height function for the boundary of $S$ and let $\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f\right)$ be the Lyapunov exponent of $f$ , which is well-defined for any rational map $f$ of degree $d\geq 2$ over a non-trivially valued field $K$ . We then have the following uniform bound (Proposition 6.3):

#### Proposition 1.8.

Assume that the local energy pairing $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,s}$ is continuous on $S^{\operatorname{an}}\setminus S^{\operatorname{triv}}$ . Let $\left(K,\left|\cdot\right|\right)$ be an complete non-trivially valued field of characteristic $0$ . Let $\delta,c_{1},c_{2},\ldots$ be positive constants. Then there exists constants $N>0$ and $c>0$ depending on $K,\delta,c_{1},c_{2},\ldots$ such that if $s=\left(f,g,C\right)\in S\left(K\right)$ satisfies:

- (1) $\lambda_{V_{i}}\left(s\right)\leq c_{i}\lambda_{\partial S}\left(s\right)$ for all $i\geq 1$ ;

- (2) $\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f\right)\geq\delta\lambda_{\partial S}\left(s\right)$ ;

- (3) $\lambda_{\partial S}\left(s\right)\geq N$ .

Then we have the uniform lower bound

$$ \left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C}\geq c\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right). $$

To prove Proposition 1.8, we use a degeneration arguments by ultrafilters, see Section 3.3. Degeneration arguments have been previously used to prove uniform bounds in [21] and [77]. We remark the methods of Poineau [76, 77] allow for an alternative way to obtain Proposition 1.8 given Theorem 1.1. The second author thanks Poineau for sharing this with him. Degenerations of rescaling limits by ultrafilters was first introduced in complex dynamics by Luo [64, 65] and formalized using Berkovich spaces by Favre–Gong [34]. The second author has also used these technique to obtain uniform bounds on $K$ -rational small points for both dynamical systems and abelian varieties [85, 63]. After degenerating, it suffices to prove the following non-archimedean rigidity statement. We note that using non-archimedean/tropical objects to understand degenerations has shown up in various settings in both dynamics and Diophantine geometry, for example [18, 57, 19, 17, 39, 33, 83].

The archimedean analogue of Theorem 1.1 was proven by Mavraki–Schmidt [68], building on ideas of Levin–Przytycki [61]. A weaker version played a crucial role in the proof of dynamical Manin–Mumford for $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ by Ghioca–Nguyen–Ye [47, 46]. However there are significant difficulties in adapting the archimedean proof to the non-archimedean setting due to the failure of Montel’s theorem, see [35] for more details. We are able to overcome this in Section 4, adapting the proof of Ji–Xie [56] in the archimedean case. On the way, we have to use many facts about non-archimedean dynamics which were recently proven by Favre and Rivera-Letelier [38].

Using Proposition 1.8 and other similar inequalities, we establish Theorem 1.5 for $n=2$ in Section 7 and deduce Theorem 1.2 in Section 9. One crucial ingredient is Ingram’s result [55] that critical heights are comparable to an ample height on $\operatorname{rat}_{d}$ outside the Lattès locus. This result relies on McMullen’s rigidity theorem [70] that multipliers of periodic points give rise to a finite morphism of $\operatorname{rat}_{d}$ to affine space outside of the Lattès locus. As a consequence, we are able to prove that the Lyapunov exponents cannot be too small for non-Lattès maps, see Theorem 7.3. Having such a lower bound on the Lyapunov exponents is necessary for us as Theorem 1.1 only applies to maps with positive Lyapunov exponent.

To obtain Theorem 1.5 for $n>2$ , we will rely on a method used by David–Philippon in their work for uniform bounds on $\mathbb{G}_{m}^{n}$ and $E^{g}$ [15, 16] that allows us to reduce Theorem 1.5 to the case of $n=2$ . This is carried out in Section 8 and relies on the arithmetic Bézout theorem. An argument with the quantitative dynamical Zhang’s inequality [69] gives us Theorem 1.4 over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . To obtain the case of $\mathbb{C}$ , we follow the specialization strategy in [69] that was used to deduce the geometric uniform Bogomolov in characteristic $0$ from the case of number fields. This is carried out in Section 9 and finishes the proof of Theorem 1.4.

#### Remark 1.9.

We make a remark that there is a theory of globally valued fields [81, 84] that axiomatizes the notion of a field $K$ with a global height function for which $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ with the absolute Weil height is an example of. This is related to the theory of adelic curves of Chen–Moriwaki [11, 12] and also to the theory of Yuan–Zhang [88]. The theory of globally valued fields allows one to degenerate via ultrafilters on sequences of globally valued fields, similar to how we degenerate on sequences of valued fields. The reader may see [53, 62] for applications to (semi)-abelian varieties. One can use this theory to obtain an alternative argument for Theorem 1.5 in the case of $n=2$ using Theorem 1.1 through the theory of adelic curves and globally valued fields.

### 1.4. Organization of the paper

In Section 2, we recall canonical heights of subvarieties and the quantitative dynamical Zhang inequality. In Section 3, we recall local height functions and degenerations by using ultrafilter. In Section 4, we prove the non-archimedean rigidity theorem, including the stronger local form in Theorem 4.1, and deduce Theorem 1.1. In Section 5, we construct flat metrics in families and establish continuity of local energy pairings. In Section 6, we prove uniform local energy bounds, including Proposition 1.8. In Section 7, we establish the height gap for curves in Theorem 7.2. In Section 8, we prove Theorem 1.5 and deduce uniform dynamical Manin–Mumford over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . In Section 9, we use a specialization argument to prove Theorem 1.4, and then deduce Theorems 1.2 and 1.3.

## 2. Canonical Heights of Subvarieties

Let $K$ be a number field and let $X$ be a projective variety over $K$ . Let $L$ be an ample line bundle on $X$ and $f:X\to X$ an endomorphism such that $f^{*}L\simeq L^{d}$ for some $d\geq 2$ . Then $\left(X,f,L\right)$ is a polarized dynamical system and hence by [95, Section 2], there exists an adelic line bundle $\overline{L}_{f}$ with underlying line bundle $L$ such that $f^{*}\overline{L}_{f}\simeq\overline{L}_{f}^{d}$ .

Using the arithmetic intersection theory of Gillet–Soulé [49], we can define the canonical height of any irreducible subvariety $V\subseteq X_{\overline{K}}$ as follows. Let $K^{\prime}$ be any finite extension such that $V$ is well-defined over, and view $\overline{L}_{f}$ as an adelic line bundle over $K^{\prime}$ . We then set

$$ h_{f}\left(V\right)=\frac{\overline{L}_{f}^{\dim V+1}\cdot V}{\left[K^{\prime}:\mathbb{Q}\right]}\in\mathbb{R} $$

and the normalized canonical height as

$$ \widehat{h}_{f}\left(V\right)=\frac{h_{f}\left(V\right)}{\deg_{L}\left(V\right)}. $$

This quantity is well-defined independent of the finite extension $K^{\prime}$ . Another way to define $\widehat{h}_{f}\left(V\right)$ is to let $V_{\operatorname{gal}}$ be the closed subvariety of $X_{K}$ corresponding to $V$ . We then set

$$ \widehat{h}_{f}\left(V\right)=\frac{1}{\left[K:\mathbb{Q}\right]}\frac{\overline{L}_{f}^{\dim V+1}\cdot V_{\operatorname{gal}}}{\deg_{L}\left(V_{\operatorname{gal}}\right)}. $$

When $V=x\in X\left(\overline{K}\right)$ is a point, this recovers the usual definition of the canonical height [10] given by

$$ \widehat{h}_{f}\left(x\right)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{h_{L}\left(f^{n}\left(x\right)\right)}{d^{n}} $$

where $h_{L}$ is an absolute Weil height for our ample line bundle $L$ , Hence we may call the quantity $\widehat{h}_{f}\left(V\right)$ the canonical height of $V$ . It satisfies the formula $\widehat{h}_{f}\left(f\left(V\right)\right)=d\widehat{h}_{f}\left(V\right)\text{ and }\widehat{h}_{f}\left(V\right)=0\text{ if }V\text{ is preperiodic.}$

There is also an alternative way to define heights using Chow forms instead of arithmetic intersection theory, developed by Philippon [73, 74, 75]. We refer readers to [69, Section 2.2] for a summary of the theory. When $X=\mathbb{P}^{n}$ is projective space, we let $h_{\operatorname{Ph}}\left(V\right)$ denote the Philippon height of the subvariety $V$ and

$$ \widehat{h}_{\operatorname{Ph}}\left(V\right)=\frac{h_{\operatorname{Ph}}\left(V\right)}{\deg V} $$

be the normalized Philippon height. If $f:\mathbb{P}^{n}\to\mathbb{P}^{n}$ is an endomorphism of degree $d\geq 2$ defined over $K$ , then it polarizes $L=O\left(1\right)$ and we obtain a canonical height $\widehat{h}_{f}$ . Then [69, Equation (2.8) and Proposition 4.1] imply that for any subvariety $V$ of $\mathbb{P}^{n}$ , we have

$$ \left|\widehat{h}_{f}\left(V\right)-\widehat{h}_{\operatorname{Ph}}\left(V\right)\right|\leq c\left(\dim V+1\right) $$

for some $c=c\left(f\right)>0$ depending only on $f$ . If $V$ is not geometrically irreducible, we define $h_{\operatorname{Ph}}\left(V\right)$ to be the sum of the heights of its geometrically irreducible components. Similarly $h_{f}\left(V\right)$ extends to a general subvariety $V$ and (2.1) still holds.

As the unnormalized canonical height $h_{f}$ comes from an adelic line bundle $\overline{L}_{f}$ , it satisfies Zhang’s fundamental inequality [93, 94, 95]. For an irreducible subvariety $V\subseteq X_{\overline{K}}$ , we let $e_{1}(\widehat{h}_{f},V)$ denote Zhang’s first essential minimum with respect to $\widehat{h}_{f}$ , i.e.

$$ e_{1}({\widehat{h}_{f}},V)\;=\;\sup_{U\subseteq V}\;\inf_{x\in U(\overline{K})}\widehat{h}_{f}(x), $$

where we take the supremum over all nonempty Zariski open subsets $U$ of $V$ . Then we have the inequality

$$ e_{1}(\widehat{h}_{f},V)\geq\frac{1}{\dim V+1}\widehat{h}_{f}(V), $$

i.e. for any $0<\delta<\frac{1}{\dim V+1}$ , the set of points

$$ \{x\in V(\overline{K})\mid\widehat{h}_{f}(x){<}\delta\widehat{h}_{f}(V)\} $$

is contained in a proper Zariski closed subset $W$ of $V$ . The main result of [69] is to give quantitative control of $\deg\left(W\right)$ in terms of the ratio $\frac{\widehat{h}_{f}\left(V\right)}{\max\left\{h\left(f\right),1\right\}}$ , where $h\left(f\right)$ is some Weil height function on $f$ . To be precise, we may assume that $X$ embeds into $\mathbb{P}^{N}$ via $L$ and $f$ extends to an endomorphism $f:\mathbb{P}^{N}\to\mathbb{P}^{N}$ of degree $d\geq 2$ . Then we let $h\left(f\right)$ be the standard Weil height on $\operatorname{End}^{N}_{d}$ . We have the following uniform control which can be deduced from [69, Theorem 1.1].

#### Theorem 2.1.

Let $\delta>0$ be a constant so that

$$ \widehat{h}_{f}\left(V\right)\geq\delta\max\left\{h\left(f\right),1\right\}. $$

Then there exists a constant $M=M\left(\delta,N,d,\deg V\right)$ and $\varepsilon=\varepsilon\left(\delta,N,d,\deg V\right)$ such that the set of points

$$ \left\{x\in V\left(\overline{K}\right)\mid\widehat{h}_{f}\left(x\right)<\varepsilon\widehat{h}_{f}\left(V\right)\right\} $$

is contained in a proper Zariski closed subvariety $W$ of degree at most $M$ .

We remark that the cases of $\mathbb{G}_{m}^{n}$ and abelian varieties were due to David and Philippon [14, 15]. For split endomorphisms $(f,g)$ on $(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{2}$ and $V=\Delta$ is the diagonal, such results can be deduced from Favre–Rivera-Letelier’s quantitative equidistribution framework [36], for example see the paper of Ang and the second author [2] or of Gauthier [45].

## 3. Local Height Functions and Degenerations

We will develop a theory of local height functions for closed subschemes on $X^{\operatorname{an}}$ when $X$ is a quasi-projective variety over a number field $K$ . For function fields, this was developed in [63, Section 2]. The same arguments largely port over, except we have to be a little more careful when dealing with errors caused by different choices in constructing the local height functions.

### 3.1. Berkovich Spaces

Let $\left(B,\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert\right)$ be a commutative Banach ring, i.e. $B$ is a commutative ring with unity $1$ and $\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert:B\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ a norm for which $B$ is complete. Furthermore, we have the triangle inequality $\left\lVert a+b\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert a\right\rVert+\left\lVert b\right\rVert$ and we will assume that our norm $||\cdot||$ is multiplicative.

A multiplicative seminorm $\left|\cdot\right|:B\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ is said to be bounded if $\left|b\right|\leq\left\lVert b\right\rVert$ for all $b\in B$ . We define the Berkovich spectrum $\cal{M}\left(B\right)$ to be the set of all bounded multiplicative seminorms on $B$ . We endow $\cal{M}\left(B\right)$ with the Gelfand topology, which is the weakest topology such that for all $b\in B$ , the function $\left|b\right|:\cal{M}\left(B\right)\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ is continuous.

Now given a scheme $X$ over $k$ , not necessary of finite type, we may define $X^{\operatorname{an}}$ following [88, Section 3.1.1]. If $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ is affine, then we define $X^{\operatorname{an}}$ as $\cal{M}\left(A/B\right)$ , the set of multiplicative seminorms on $A$ that restricts to an element of $\cal{M}\left(B\right)$ on $B$ . In general if $X$ is given by an open cover $U_{i}=\operatorname{Spec}A_{i}$ , we may glue $U_{i}^{\operatorname{an}}$ to obtain $X^{\operatorname{an}}$ .

In our setting, we will take our base Banach ring to be $\left(\mathbb{Z},\left|\cdot\right|_{\infty}\right)$ , where $\left|\cdot\right|_{\infty}$ is the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb{Z}$ . The description of $\cal{M}\left(\mathbb{Z}\right)$ is given in [6, 1.4.3]. Then any scheme $X$ can be viewed canonically as a scheme over $\mathbb{Z}$ and we define $X^{\operatorname{an}}$ as the Berkovich analytification over $\left(\mathbb{Z},\left|\cdot\right|_{\infty}\right)$ .

If $X$ is an irreducible scheme, then any rational function $f$ on $X$ induces a continuous function $f:X^{\operatorname{an}}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\left\{\pm\infty\right\}$ .

### 3.2. Local Height Functions

Let $X$ be an irreducible projective variety over a number field $K$ and let $Z$ a closed subscheme of $X$ . Following Silverman [78, Theorem 2.1] (see also Matsuzawa [66]), we will define a local height function $\lambda_{Z}:X^{\operatorname{an}}\setminus Z^{\operatorname{an}}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\left\{+\infty\right\}$ . These functions will be well-defined up to a function that is bounded above by $\log^{+}\max\left\{\left|p_{1}\right|,\ldots,\left|p_{m}\right|\right\}$ for some $p_{i}\in K^{\times}$ .

First, let $D$ be a Cartier divisor of $X$ . Let $L,M$ be basepoint free line bundles on $X$ for which $\mathcal{O}\left(D\right)\simeq L\otimes M^{-1}$ . Fix a meromorphic section $s_{D}$ of $\mathcal{O}\left(D\right)$ . Picking bases of global sections $s=\left\{s_{0},\ldots,s_{n}\right\}$ for $L$ and $t=\left\{t_{0},\ldots,t_{m}\right\}$ for $M$ , we may define the local height $\lambda_{D}:X^{\operatorname{an}}\to$ relative to the presentation $\cal{D}=\left(s_{D},L,s,M,t\right)$ to be

$$ \lambda_{\cal{D}}\left(p\right)=\max_{k}\min_{l}\log\left|\frac{s_{k}}{t_{l}s_{D}}\left(p\right)\right| $$

where $\frac{s_{k}}{t_{l}s_{D}}$ is a rational function on $X$ . This gives us a well-defined continuous function $\lambda_{\cal{D}}:X^{\operatorname{an}}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\left\{+\infty\right\}$ . If $D$ is an effective Cartier divisor, then this is real-valued if $x\in X^{\operatorname{an}}\setminus D^{\operatorname{an}}$ .

For an affine variety $U$ with an embedding $\iota:U\xhookrightarrow{}\mathbb{A}^{M}$ , we say that a point $x\in U\left(K\right)$ has coordinates all $\leq 1$ if $x=\left(x_{1},\ldots,x_{M}\right)$ with $\left|x_{i}\right|\leq 1$ under the embedding $\iota$ .

#### Proposition 3.1.

There exists a finite collection of affine opens $U_{1},\ldots,U_{m}$ with embeddings $\iota_{i}:U_{i}\xhookrightarrow{}\mathbb{A}^{M_{i}}$ such that for any $x\in X\left(K\right)$ for a valued field $K$ , there exists $i$ such that the coordinates of $x$ in $U_{i}$ are all $\leq 1$ .

#### Proof.

Embedding $X$ into $\mathbb{P}^{N}$ , it suffices to prove it for $\mathbb{P}^{N}$ . In this case, if $U_{0},\ldots,U_{N}$ are the $N+1$ basic affine opens where $U_{i}$ is given by $\left(\frac{z_{0}}{z_{i}},\frac{z_{1}}{z_{i}},\ldots,\frac{z_{N}}{z_{i}}\right)$ , then the coordinates of $x=\left[x_{0}:\cdots:x_{N}\right]$ in $U_{i}$ are $\leq 1$ if $\left|x_{i}\right|$ is maximal. Since $\left|x_{i}\right|$ will be maximal for some $0\leq i\leq N$ , we are done. ∎

This implies the following.

#### Proposition 3.2.

Let $\cal{D}$ and $\cal{D}^{\prime}$ be two presentations of $D$ , Then there exists $p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}\in K^{\times}$ so that

$$ \left|\lambda_{\cal{D}}-\lambda_{\cal{D}^{\prime}}\right|\leq\log^{+}\max\left\{\left|p_{1}\right|,\ldots,\left|p_{m}\right|\right\} $$

on $X^{\operatorname{an}}$ .

#### Proof.

This follows from the proof of [7, Theorem 2.2.11 and Remark 2.2.13]. ∎

We also have a formula for $\lambda_{\cal{D}}$ when $D$ is locally cut out by a function $f$ .

#### Proposition 3.3.

Let $U$ be an affine open and assume that $D=\operatorname{div}\left(f\right)$ locally on $U$ . Let $\cal{D}$ be a presentation for $D$ , where we set $D\simeq L\otimes M^{-1}$ . Fix an embedding $U\xhookrightarrow{}\mathbb{A}^{N}$ . Then there exists $p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}\in K^{\times}$ and $A>0$ so that for any $x\in X^{\operatorname{an}}$ with coordinates $\left|x_{i}\right|\leq 1$ in $U$ , we have

$$ \left|\log\left|f\left(x\right)\right|^{-1}-\lambda_{\cal{D}}\left(x\right)\right|\leq A\log^{+}\max\left\{\left|p_{1}\right|,\ldots,\left|p_{m}\right|\right\}. $$

#### Proof.

Let $D\simeq L\otimes M^{-1}$ be the line bundles used for the presentation for $\cal{D}$ . If $L$ and $M$ are both trivial on $U$ , then this follows from the proof of [66, Lemma 4.2.4]. Note that we obtain the analogous statement if we look at points with affine coordinates $\leq C$ instead of just $\leq 1$ , where the data of $\left\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}\right\}$ and $A$ will be allowed to depend on $C$ too.

In general, we replace $U$ with a finite affine open cover $U_{1},\ldots,U_{n}$ with $U_{i}=\operatorname{div}\left(f_{i}\right)$ where each $L$ and $M$ are trivial on $U_{i}$ . Note that if $\left(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}\right)$ are affine coordinates for $U$ , then $\left(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N},f_{i}^{-1}\right)$ may serve as affine coordinates for $U_{i}$ . As the $U_{i}$ ’s cover $U$ , we may find $c_{1},\ldots,c_{n}\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ so that

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}f_{i}=1 $$

on $U$ . Then is some $\delta>0$ , depending only on $m$ and $c_{i}$ ’s, so that $\left|f_{i}\left(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}\right)\right|\leq\delta$ for at least one $i$ . Then for $U_{i}$ our affine coordinates are bounded above by $\max\left\{1,\delta^{-1}\right\}$ , which imply that $\left|\log\left|f\left(x\right)\right|^{-1}-\lambda_{\cal{D}}\left(x\right)\right|\leq A\log^{+}\max\left\{\left|p_{1}\right|,\ldots,\left|p_{m}\right|\right\}$ with the $p_{i}$ ’s and $A>0$ depending only on our affine open cover as desired. ∎

Now let $Z$ be a closed subscheme of $X$ . Let $D_{i}$ be Cartier divisors and let $\cal{D}_{i}$ be presentations of each $D_{i}$ . We say that $\cal{Z}=\left\{\cal{D}_{1},\ldots,\cal{D}_{m}\right\}$ is a presentation of $Z$ if $\cap_{i=1}^{m}D_{i}=Z$ as closed subschemes of $X$ . We then define

$$ \lambda_{\cal{Z}}=\min\left\{\lambda_{\cal{D}_{1}},\ldots,\lambda_{\cal{D}_{m}}\right\}. $$

This is a continuous real valued function on $X^{\operatorname{an}}\setminus Z^{\operatorname{an}}$ . We have the following analogues of Propositions 3.2 and 3.3. They both follow from the proof of [66, Proposition 4.25].

#### Proposition 3.4.

Let $\cal{Z},\cal{Z}^{\prime}$ be two presentations for $Z$ . Then there exists $p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}\in K^{\times}$ such that

$$ \left|\lambda_{\cal{Z}}-\lambda_{\cal{Z}^{\prime}}\right|\leq\log^{+}\max\left\{\left|p_{1}\right|,\ldots,\left|p_{m}\right|\right\}. $$

#### Proposition 3.5.

Let $U$ be an affine open of $X$ and let the ideal of $Z$ be given by $\left\{f_{1},\ldots,f_{k}\right\}$ . Let $\cal{Z}$ be a presentation for $Z$ . Fix an embedding $U\xhookrightarrow{}\mathbb{A}^{N}$ . Then there exists $p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}\in K^{\times}$ and $A>0$ so that

$$ \left|\log\min\left\{\left|f_{1}\left(x\right)\right|^{-1},\ldots,\left|f_{k}\left(x\right)\right|^{-1}\right\}-\lambda_{\cal{Z}}\right|\leq A\log^{+}\max\left\{\left|p_{1}\right|,\ldots,\left|p_{m}\right|\right\} $$

for all $x\in U\left(K\right)$ with coordinates $\leq 1$ .

The above propositions imply that for each closed subscheme $Z$ , we can define a local height function $\lambda_{Z}$ on $X^{\operatorname{an}}$ that is well-defined up to an error of $\log^{+}\max\left\{\left|p_{1}\right|,\ldots,\left|p_{m}\right|\right\}$ for a finite set of elements $p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}\in K^{\times}$ . We will now consider our local height functions up to such equivalence. This is essentially equivalent to considering functions up to $M_{K}$ -constants in the usual context of local height functions over global fields.

#### Proposition 3.6.

We have the following properties.

- (1) Let $Z\subseteq Y$ . Then $\lambda_{Z}\leq\lambda_{Y}$ .

- (2) If $\operatorname{Supp}Z\subseteq\operatorname{Supp}Y$ , then there is a constant $c>0$ such that $\lambda_{Z}\leq c\lambda_{Y}$ .

- (3) Let $\varphi:X\to X^{\prime}$ be a morphism of projective varieties over $\mathbb{C}$ . Let $Y$ be a closed subscheme of $X^{\prime}$ . Then $\lambda_{\varphi^{*}Y}=\lambda_{Y}.$

- (4) Let $U\subseteq X$ be an open set and let $W\subseteq X$ be the complement of $U$ . If $Z|_{U}\subseteq Y|_{U}$ , then there exists a constant $c>0$ such that $\lambda_{Z}\leq\lambda_{Y}+c\lambda_{W}$ .

#### Proof.

The proof is analogous to that of [78, Theorem 2.1]. ∎

We now let $X$ be a quasi-projective variety. Fix a compactification $\overline{X}$ of $X$ . We thus obtain a local height function for the boundary $\lambda_{\partial X}$ where we set $\partial X=\overline{X}\setminus X$ . A priori this depends on the choice of compactification.

#### Proposition 3.7.

Let $\overline{X}$ and $\overline{X}^{\prime}$ be two compactifications of $X$ and let $\lambda_{\partial X},\lambda^{\prime}_{\partial X}$ be the two local height functions for the boundary. Then there exists a constant $c>0$ such that

$$ c^{-1}\lambda_{\partial X}^{\prime}\leq\lambda_{\partial X}\leq c\lambda_{\partial X}^{\prime}. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is analogous to that of [78, Theorem 5.1]. ∎

Now let $Z$ be a closed subscheme of $X$ . If we fix a compactification $\overline{X}$ and replace $Z$ with $Z\cup\left(\overline{X}\setminus X\right)$ , we thus obtain a well-defined $\lambda_{Z}$ up to a multiple of $\lambda_{\partial X}$ .

We now move to the setting of global heights oveer a number field $K$ . After fixing a compactification and a presentation for $\overline{X}\setminus X$ , we define

$$ h_{\partial X}\left(x\right)=\sum_{v\in M_{K}}n_{v}\lambda_{\partial X,v}\left(x\right)\text{ for all }x\in X\left(K\right) $$

where $\lambda_{\partial X,v}$ is the local height function restricted to $X_{v}^{\operatorname{an}}$ . This is invariant under finite extensions and we get a function on $X\left(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\right)$ . If $h^{\prime}_{\partial X}$ is the function coming from another choice of data, then

$$ h_{\partial X}\leq c_{1}h^{\prime}_{\partial X}+c_{2} $$

for some $c_{1},c_{2}>0$ . Now for a closed subscheme $Z$ of $X$ , we may fix a presentation $\cal{Z}$ for $Z\cup\left(\overline{X}\setminus X\right)$ which gives us a local height function $\lambda_{Z}$ . We can now define

$$ h_{Z}\left(x\right)=\sum_{v\in M_{K}}n_{v}\lambda_{\cal{Z},v}\left(x\right)\text{ for all }x\in\left(X\setminus Z\right)\left(K\right). $$

Again, this quantity is invariant under finite extensions and so we obtain a well-defined function on $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . If $h^{\prime}_{Z}$ is the global height function for another compactification and presentation, we obtain

$$ \left|h_{Z}-h^{\prime}_{Z}\right|\leq c_{1}h_{\partial X}+c_{2} $$

for some $c_{1},c_{2}>0$ . One fact that we will need is the following.

#### Proposition 3.8.

Let $h_{L}$ be an ample height function on $X\left(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\right)$ . Then there exists $c_{1},c_{2}>0$ so that

$$ h_{Z}\leq c_{1}h_{L}+c_{2}. $$

#### Proof.

See [78, Proposition 4.2]. ∎

### 3.3. Degenerations with Ultrafilters

We state and explain some basic general facts about degenerating via ultrafilters. For more details, the readers may consult [34], [85] or [50]. Let $X$ be a quasi-projective variety over a number field $K$ which is irreducible. Let $\left(K_{n}\right)$ be a sequence of complete valued fields with norm $\left|\cdot\right|_{n}$ that contains $K$ .

We define

$$ A^{\varepsilon}=\{(x_{n})\in\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}K_{n}\mid|x_{n}|^{\varepsilon_{n}}\text{ is bounded}\}. $$

This is a Banach ring under the supremum norm $\left|\left(x_{n}\right)\right|=\sup_{n}\left|x_{n}\right|^{\varepsilon_{n}}$ . We have natural projection maps $\pi_{n}:A^{\varepsilon}\to K_{n}$ which induce projections $\pi_{n}:X\left(A^{\varepsilon}\right)\to X\left(K_{n}\right)$ . The Berkovich spectrum $\cal{M}\left(A^{\varepsilon}\right)$ is isomorphic to $\beta\mathbb{N}$ , the set of ultrafilters on $\mathbb{N}$ , via the bijection

$$ \omega\mapsto\left|\left(x_{n}\right)\right|_{\omega}=\lim_{\omega}\left|x_{n}\right|^{\varepsilon_{n}} $$

where $\omega\in\beta\mathbb{N}$ is an ultrafilter on $\mathbb{N}$ (see [13] for the basics of ultrafilters).

#### Definition 3.9.

Let $x_{n}\in X\left(K_{n}\right)$ be a sequence of points. An $\left(\varepsilon_{n}\right)$ -degeneration of $\left(x_{n}\right)$ is a point $x\in X\left(A^{\varepsilon}\right)$ such that $\pi_{n}\left(x\right)=x_{n}$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ .

If an $\left(\varepsilon_{n}\right)$ -degeneration exists, it is necessarily unique.

#### Proposition 3.10.

There exists at most one $\left(\varepsilon_{n}\right)$ -degeneration of $\left(x_{n}\right)$ .

#### Proof.

Let $Y=\bigsqcup_{n\geq 1}\operatorname{Spec}K_{n}$ . Each projection $\pi_{n}\colon A^{\varepsilon}\to K_{n}$ induces

$$ \operatorname{Spec}\left(\pi_{n}\right)\colon\operatorname{Spec}K_{n}\to\operatorname{Spec}A^{\varepsilon}, $$

and these glue to a single morphism

$$ f\colon Y\to\operatorname{Spec}A^{\varepsilon}. $$

We claim that $f$ is an epimorphism in the category of separated, reduced schemes. Indeed given $g,h:\operatorname{Spec}A^{\varepsilon}\to X$ such that $g\circ f=h\circ f$ , we can consider the diagonal embedding $\Delta:X\to X\times X$ , which is a closed immersion by separatedness of $X$ . Pulling back $\Delta\left(X\right)$ via $\left(g,h\right):\operatorname{Spec}A^{\varepsilon}\to X\times X$ gives us a closed subscheme $Z$ of $\operatorname{Spec}A^{\varepsilon}$ and the map $f:Y\to\operatorname{Spec}A^{\varepsilon}$ must factor through $Z$ since $g\circ f=h\circ f$ .

We now claim that $f$ is dominant. Indeed, the image of $f$ consists of the kernels of the projection maps $\pi_{n}:A^{\varepsilon}\to K_{n}$ . Given any non-zero $a\in A^{\varepsilon}$ with $a=\left(a_{n}\right)$ , there must exist some $a_{n}\not=0$ and so $\pi_{n}\left(a\right)\not=0$ , which implies that $\ker\left(\pi_{n}\right)\in D\left(a\right)$ . Since distinguished opens form a basis, it follows that $f\left(Y\right)$ is dense and hence $f$ is dominant as desired. Now as $f$ is dominant and factors through $Z$ , we must have $Z$ be dense in $\operatorname{Spec}A^{\varepsilon}$ and as $\operatorname{Spec}A^{\varepsilon}$ is reduced, we must have $Z=\operatorname{Spec}A^{\varepsilon}$ and hence $g=h$ as desired.

Now the points $x_{n}\in X\left(K_{n}\right)$ define maps $\operatorname{Spec}K_{n}\to X$ which glue to

$$ g\colon Y\to X. $$

and $g$ is clearly unique. By definition an $\left(\varepsilon_{n}\right)$ -degeneration is a morphism

$$ \tilde{x}\colon\operatorname{Spec}A^{\varepsilon}\to X $$

with $\tilde{x}\circ f=g$ . Given two such lifts $\tilde{x}_{1},\tilde{x}_{2}$ , we have $\tilde{x}_{1}\circ f=\tilde{x}_{2}\circ f$ . Since $f$ is an epimorphism of reduced, separated schemes, post-composition with $f$ is injective on morphisms. It follows that $\tilde{x}_{1}=\tilde{x}_{2}$ , proving uniqueness. ∎

Clearly an $\left(\varepsilon_{n}\right)$ -degeneration need not always exist. For example if $\varepsilon_{n}=1$ and $X=\mathbb{A}^{1}$ , then $x_{n}$ corresponds to an element of $K_{n}$ and an $\left(\varepsilon_{n}\right)$ -degeneration exists if and only if $\left|x_{n}\right|$ is bounded from above. However if $X$ is a projective variety, then an $\left(\varepsilon_{n}\right)$ -degeneration always exists.

#### Proposition 3.11.

Assume that $X$ is a projective variety over $K$ . Let $x_{n}\in X\left(K_{n}\right)$ for all $n$ . Then an $\left(\varepsilon_{n}\right)$ -degeneration of $\left(x_{n}\right)$ always exists.

#### Proof.

Let $\left\{U_{1},\ldots,U_{n}\right\}$ be an affine open cover for $X$ and let $Y=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{n}U_{i}$ . Then we have a natural morphism $\pi:Y\to X$ and $Y$ is affine. Let $x_{n}\in X\left(K_{n}\right)$ . Then since $X$ is projective, $x_{n}$ lifts to $\tilde{x}_{n}\in X\left(R_{n}\right)$ where $R_{n}$ is the valuation ring of $K_{n}$ . Hence we have an induced morphism $\tilde{x}_{n}:\operatorname{Spec}R_{n}\to X$ . Since $\left\{U_{i}\right\}$ is an open cover and $R_{n}$ is a valuation ring, if $\tilde{x}_{n}^{-1}\left(U_{i}\right)$ contains the maximal ideal of $R_{n}$ then it contains the entire $\operatorname{Spec}R_{n}$ . Thus $\tilde{x}_{n}\in U_{i}\left(R_{n}\right)\subseteq Y\left(R_{n}\right)$ .

Since $Y$ is affine, we may let $x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}$ be a choice of affine coordinates for $Y$ over $K$ . Then $\tilde{x}_{n}$ has affine coordinates $a_{n,1},\ldots,a_{n,N}$ with $a_{n,i}\in R_{n}$ and $\left|a_{n,i}\right|\leq 1$ for all $1\leq i\leq N$ . Hence if we set $a_{i}=\left(a_{n,i}\right)$ , we have $a_{i}\in A^{\varepsilon}$ . We thus obtain an $A^{\varepsilon}$ -point $\left(a_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{N}$ of $Y$ that commutes with the projection map $\pi_{n}:A^{\varepsilon}\to K_{n}$ . Projecting it down to $X$ , we obtain our $\left(\varepsilon_{n}\right)$ -degeneration as desired. ∎

#### Remark 3.12.

Observe that in Proposition 3.11, the resulting $\left(\varepsilon_{n}\right)$ -degeneration is actually a $B^{\varepsilon}$ -point of $X$ for

$$ B^{\varepsilon}=\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}R_{n}, $$

where $R_{n}$ is the valuation ring of $K_{n}$ .

Now if $X$ is only quasi-projective, we may embed it into some projective compactification $\overline{X}$ . Then the $\left(\varepsilon_{n}\right)$ -degeneration exists on $\overline{X}$ and we can try to check whether our $A^{\varepsilon}$ -point lies on $X$ . Recall that for each valued field $K^{\prime}$ containing our number field $K$ , we have a local distance function $\lambda_{\partial X}$ depending on the compactification $\overline{X}$ . On an affine open $U_{i}\subseteq\overline{X}$ such that the reduced closed subscheme $\left(\overline{X}\setminus X\right)\cap U_{i}$ is given by $\left\{f_{1}=f_{2}=\cdots=f_{m}=0\right\}$ for $f_{j}\in\mathcal{O}\left(U_{i}\right)$ , Proposition 3.5 implies that for $x\in U_{i}\left(K\right)$ whose affine coordinates in $U_{i}$ have norm $\leq 1$ , we can find $p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}\in K^{\times}$ and $A>0$ so that

$$ \left|\lambda_{\partial X}\left(x\right)-\min_{1\leq i\leq n}-\log\left|f_{i}\left(x\right)\right|\right|\leq A\log^{+}\max\left\{\left|p_{1}\right|,\ldots,\left|p_{m}\right|\right\}. $$

The function $\lambda_{\partial X}$ depends on the choice of compactification, but $\frac{\lambda_{\partial X}}{\lambda^{\prime}_{\partial X}}$ (up to an additive constant of $\log^{+}\max\{|p_{1}|,\ldots,|p_{m}\}$ is bounded from above and below for any two compactifications.

#### Proposition 3.13.

Let $X$ be a quasi-projective variety over $K$ . Let $x_{n}\in X\left(K_{n}\right)$ and let $\left(\varepsilon_{n}\right)$ be a sequence of positive reals. Assume that for any $p\in K^{\times}$ , the sequence $\{\varepsilon_{n}\log^{+}|p|_{n}\}$ is uniformly bounded from above. Then an $\left(\varepsilon_{n}\right)$ -degeneration of $\left(x_{n}\right)$ exists on $X$ if and only if $\varepsilon_{n}\lambda_{\partial X}\left(x_{n}\right)$ is uniformly bounded from above.

#### Proof.

Pick any projective compactification $\overline{X}$ of $X$ and let $U_{i}$ be a finite affine open cover of $\overline{X}$ . Let $Y=\bigsqcup U_{i}$ and let $\pi:Y\to\overline{X}$ be the natural morphism. Then $\pi^{-1}\left(X\right)$ is Zariski open in $Y$ . Let $f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}\in\mathcal{O}\left(Y\right)$ cut out $Y\setminus\pi^{-1}\left(X\right)$ . Note that $\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}D\left(f_{i}\right)=X$ where $D\left(f_{i}\right)$ is the distinguished open for $f_{i}$ .

Now given $x_{n}\in\overline{X}\left(K_{n}\right)$ , we lift (as in the proof of Proposition 3.11) $x_{n}$ to an $R_{n}$ -point of some $U_{i}$ and hence to an $R_{n}$ -point $\tilde{x}_{n}$ of $Y$ . We then have

$$ \left|\varepsilon_{n}\lambda_{\partial X}\left(x_{n}\right)-\min_{1\leq i\leq n}-\left(\varepsilon_{n}\right)\log\left|f_{i}\left(\tilde{x}_{n}\right)\right|_{n}\right|\leq\varepsilon_{n}A\log^{+}\max\left\{\left|p_{1}\right|_{n},\ldots,\left|p_{m}\right|_{n}\right\} $$

as given in (3.1). If we let $a_{n,1},\ldots,a_{n,N}$ be the affine coordinates of $x_{n}$ , then the affine coordinates of our $A^{\varepsilon}$ -point $\left(x_{n}\right)$ are given by $\left(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}\right)$ where each $a_{i}=\left(a_{n,i}\right)$ . We wish to check whether our $A^{\varepsilon}$ -point lies on $\pi^{-1}\left(X\right)$ . This is equivalent to checking that

$$ \left(f_{1}\left(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}\right),\ldots,f_{m}\left(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}\right)\right) $$

generate the unit ideal in $\left(A^{\varepsilon}\right)$ as the condition is equivalent to the pullback of the opens $D\left(f_{i}\right)$ covering $\operatorname{Spec}A^{\varepsilon}$ . But an element $b=\left(b_{n}\right)$ in $A^{\varepsilon}$ is in $\left(A^{\varepsilon}\right)^{\times}$ if and only if $\left(\left|b_{n}\right|^{-1}\right)^{\varepsilon_{n}}$ is uniformly bounded from above [34, Remark 3.7]. Hence if there exists $c_{i}$ with $c_{i}=\left(c_{n,i}\right)^{\infty}_{n=1}$ with

$$ \sum c_{i}f_{i}\left(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}\right)\in\left(A^{\varepsilon}\right)^{\times} $$

then as $\left|c_{i,n}\right|^{\varepsilon_{n}}$ is bounded from above as $n$ varies, (3.2) implies that

$$ \max_{1\leq i\leq m}\left|f_{i}\left(a_{n,1},\ldots,a_{n,N}\right)\right|_{n}^{\varepsilon_{n}} $$

is uniformly bounded away from $0$ and so $\varepsilon_{n}\lambda_{\partial X}\left(x_{n}\right)$ is uniformly bounded from above since $\varepsilon_{n}A\log^{+}\max\left\{\left|p_{i}\right|\right\}$ is uniformly bounded from above. Conversely suppose that $\varepsilon_{n}\lambda_{\partial X}\left(x_{n}\right)\leq C$ for some $C>0$ . For each $n$ , let $i_{n}$ be an index such that

$$ \left|-\log\left|f_{i_{n}}\left(a_{n,1},\ldots,a_{n,N}\right)\right|_{n}-\lambda_{\partial X}\left(x_{n}\right)\right|\leq A\log^{+}\max\left\{\left|p_{1}\right|_{n},\ldots,\left|p_{m}\right|_{n}\right\}. $$

We define $c_{i}\in A^{\varepsilon}$ as $c_{i}=\left(c_{1,i},\ldots,c_{n,i},\ldots\right)$ where $c_{n,i}=1$ if $i_{n}=i$ and $0$ otherwise. Then

$$ \left|\sum c_{n,i}f_{i}\left(a_{n,1},\ldots,a_{n,N}\right)\right|^{\varepsilon_{n}}=e^{-\lambda_{\partial X}\left(x_{n}\right)\varepsilon_{n}+O\left(1\right)} $$

and hence the left-hand side is uniformly bounded away from $0$ as $\lambda_{\partial X}\left(x_{n}\right)\varepsilon_{n}$ is uniformly bounded from above. Thus $\sum c_{i}f_{i}\left(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}\right)\in\left(A^{\varepsilon}\right)^{\times}$ and so our $A^{\varepsilon}$ -point lies in $X$ as desired. ∎

Note that there are two natural situations where $\varepsilon_{n}\log^{+}\left|p\right|_{n}$ is uniformly bounded from above. The first is if the valued field $\left(K_{n},\left|\cdot\right|_{n}\right)$ is the same for all $n$ and $\varepsilon_{n}$ is bounded from above. The second is if the residue characteristic of $K_{n}$ is either $0$ for all sufficiently large $n$ or goes to $\infty$ . This will be the two specific cases for which we will apply Proposition 3.13 to.

## 4. Non-Archimedean Rigidity

The main result of this section is Theorem 4.1, which is a strengthening of the non-archimedean rigidity statement of Theorem 1.1. Let $\left(K,\left|\cdot\right|\right)$ be a complete non-archimedean algebraically closed field with residue characteristic $0$ . Assume that $\left|\cdot\right|$ is non-trivial. We will prove the following statement.

#### Theorem 4.1.

Let $f,g:\mathbb{P}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be two rational maps of degrees $d_{1},d_{2}\geq 2$ respectively, that are defined over $K$ . Let $C\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ be an irreducible curve over $K$ that projects dominantly to both coordinates. Assume that $\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f\right)>0$ and that there exist an open subset $U\subseteq C^{\operatorname{an}}$ and a constant $\rho>0$ such that

$$ \left(\pi_{1}^{*}\mu_{f}\right)|_{U}=\rho\left(\pi_{2}^{*}\mu_{g}\right)|_{U}\neq 0. $$

Then there exist positive integers $a,b$ with $d_{1}^{a}=d_{2}^{b}$ such that $C$ is preperiodic under $\left(f^{a},g^{b}\right)$ .

When $K=\mathbb{C}$ is archimedean and $U=C^{\operatorname{an}}$ , a weaker version of Theorem 4.1 is the key complex dynamical input to the solution of the dynamical Manin–Mumford for $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ by Ghioca–Nguyen–Ye [47, 46]. In their setting, they are able to assume that $C$ contains infinitely many preperiodic points for $\left(f,g\right)$ which is a necessary ingredient in their proof. Mavraki–Schmidt [68] subsequently removed this assumption and used it in their proof of the uniform dynamical Bogomolov for one-parameter families of split maps.

Both the arguments of [47] and [68] for $K=\mathbb{C}$ proceed by constructing a family of symmetries of the equilibrium measure $\mu_{f}$ using the condition on equilibrium measures, before applying Levin–Przytycki [61] to obtain that outside of the exceptional maps, the family of symmetries has to be finite in size. It then easily follows that $C$ has to be preperiodic for $\left(f,g\right)$ .

There are two main obstacles in adapting this argument to the non-archimedean case. The first is that Levin–Przytycki relies on Montel’s theorem, i.e. that any family of holomorphic maps $\psi_{n}:U\to V$ for $U,V$ bounded open subsets of $\mathbb{C}$ , has a convergent subsequence. This is false in the non-archimedean case due to the failure of local compactness. The second is even if we knew that $\left\{\psi_{n}\right\}$ had a convergent subsequence, Levin–Przytycki’s argument relies on the Euclidean topology and does not work for non-archimedean fields.

Both obstacles are handled by the following simple observation. Let $\psi_{n}:D\to\psi_{n}\left(D\right)$ be injective analytic maps such that

$$ \mu_{f}\left(\psi_{n}\left(E\right)\right)\geq c\mu_{f}\left(E\right) $$

for every Borel subset $E\subseteq D$ , with $c>0$ independent of $n$ . If $\mu_{f}\left(D\right)>0$ , the images $\psi_{n}\left(D\right)$ cannot be pairwise disjoint, since $\mu_{f}$ has finite mass. Applied on smaller discs, this observation produces a convergent subsequence.

We will follow the proof strategy by Ji–Xie [56] which uses ergodicitiy properties of $\mu_{f}$ , see also [30]. We first collect some basic facts of $f$ and $\mu_{f}$ which are classical in the archimedean case, but have only been recently proved in the non-archimedean setting. We then state some independent lemmas that will help us prove that if our constructed family $\left\{\psi_{n}\right\}$ has a convergent subsequence, then the family has to be finite. Finally, we will prove Theorem 4.1.

### 4.1. Basic Facts

For the next two subsections, let $f:\mathbb{P}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}$ have degree $d\geq 2$ and satisfy $\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f\right)>0$ . In particular, the valuation of $K$ is non-trivial.

The measure $\mu_{f}$ (and similarly for $\mu_{g}$ ) is the equilibrium measure of $f$ . It is a probability measures that is supported on the Berkovich space $\mathbb{P}^{1,\operatorname{an}}_{k}$ . By [37][Proposition 3.5], the measure $\mu_{f}$ is ergodic. When working on $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ , we will let $B\left(x,r\right)$ denote the ball of radius $r$ and centered at $x$ using the spherical metric.

The quantity $\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f\right)$ is the Lyapunov exponent of $f$ . Working with the spherical metric. we may let $|f^{\prime}|$ denote the spherical derivative which satisfies the formula

$$ |f^{\prime}|(x)=|f^{\prime}(x)|\frac{\max\{1,|x|\}^{2}}{\max\{1,|f(x)|\}^{2}} $$

for $x\not\in f^{-1}(\infty)$ . This extends continuously to the entire $\mathbb{P}^{1,\operatorname{an}}$ . We may now define

$$ \mathrm{Lyap}(f)=\int\log|f^{\prime}|(x)d\mu_{f}(x). $$

By [38, Theorems B and C, Corollary D], in residue characteristic $0$ , positive Lyapunov exponent is equivalent to $\mu_{f}\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\left(K\right)\right)=1$ , and to the existence of a type I repelling periodic point. Moreover, [38, Theorem B (3)] gives the equidistribution of type I repelling periodic points towards $\mu_{f}$ . The measure $\mu_{f}$ has no atoms, since an atom would imply potential good reduction by [37, Theorem E].

#### Proposition 4.2.

For $\mu_{f}$ -almost every $x$ , we must have

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log|(f^{n})|^{\prime}(x)\to\mathrm{Lyap}(f). $$

#### Proof.

Since $\mu_{f}$ is ergodic and $\log|f^{\prime}|(x)\in L^{1}(\mu_{f})$ , by Birkhoff’s ergodic theorem we must have

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\log|f^{\prime}|(f^{i}(x))\to\mathrm{Lyap}(f) $$

for $\mu_{f}$ -almost every $x$ . Since

$$ |f_{1}\circ f_{2}|^{\prime}(x)=|f_{1}|^{\prime}(f_{2}(x))\cdot|f_{2}|^{\prime}(x), $$

this is equivalent to

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log|(f^{n})|^{\prime}(x)\to\mathrm{Lyap}(f) $$

as desired. ∎

We now state [38][Lemma 3.18]. We set

$$ \hat{J}=\{(x_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}\in(J_{f}\cap\mathbb{P}^{1}(K))^{\mathbb{Z}},f(x_{i})=x_{i+1}\} $$

and we let $\sigma$ be the left-shift operator. We have a projection map $\pi:\hat{J}\to J_{f}\cap\mathbb{P}^{1}(K)$ that satisfies $f\circ\pi=\pi\circ\sigma$ . We let $\hat{\mu_{f}}$ be the unique probability measure that is invariant under $\sigma$ and projects to $\mu_{f}$ .

#### Proposition 4.3.

There exists a subset $\hat{J}_{0}$ of $\hat{J}$ , with full measure, and a measurable function $\tau,L:\hat{J}_{0}\to\left(0,\infty\right)$ such that for any $\hat{x}\in\hat{J}_{0}$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , the function $f^{n}$ admits an inverse branch sending $x_{0}$ to $x_{-n}$ defined on $B\left(x_{0},\tau\left(\hat{x}\right)\right)$ .

#### Proof.

This is [38][Lemma 3.18] ∎

With this, we can deduce the non-archimedean analogue of [56][Lemma 4.10]. Given a subset $A$ of $\mathbb{N}$ , we let $d\left(A\right)$ denote its density if it exists.

#### Proposition 4.4.

For every $\varepsilon>0$ , there is $r>0$ such that for $\mu_{f}$ -almost every $x\in\mathbb{P}^{1}\left(K\right)$ , there exists a subset $A=A_{x}$ of positive integers with $d\left(A\right)>1-\varepsilon$ such that for every $n\in A$ , if we denote by $W$ the connected component of $f^{-n}\left(B\left(f^{n}\left(x\right),r\right)\right)$ containing $x$ , then the map $f^{n}:W\to B\left(f^{n}\left(x\right),r\right)$ is a bijection.

#### Proof.

We apply Proposition 4.3. For any fixed $\varepsilon>0$ , we have a $r>0$ so that

$$ \hat{F}=\left\{\hat{x}\in\hat{J}_{0}\mid\tau\left(\hat{x}\right)\geq r\right\} $$

has measure $\hat{\mu}\left(\hat{F}\right)>1-\varepsilon$ . By Birkhoff’s ergodic theorem, there is some $\hat{G}$ with $\hat{\mu}_{f}\left(\hat{G}\right)=1$ , so that if $A\left(\hat{x}\right)=\left\{n\geq 1\mid\sigma^{n}\left(\hat{x}\right)\in\hat{F}\right\}$ , then $d\left(A\left(\hat{x}\right)\right)=\hat{\mu}\left(\hat{F}\right)$ for all $\hat{x}\in\hat{G}$ . We now set $G_{0}=\pi_{0}\left(\hat{G}\right)$ so that $\mu_{f}\left(G_{0}\right)=1$ . For $x\in G_{0}$ , we may choose $\hat{x}\in\pi_{0}^{-1}\left(x\right)\cap\hat{G}$ and set $A_{x}=A_{\hat{x}}$ , which gives us what we want. ∎

### 4.2. Convergent Sequences of Symmetries

In this section, we will study the situation of a family of analytic maps $\sigma_{n}:D\to D$ , that preserves $\mu_{f}$ , and also has a convergent subsequence. With some assumptions, we will be able to prove that $\{\sigma_{n}\}$ must have only finitely many distinct maps. This is the non-archimedean analogue of [56, Theorem 3.2].

Continue to assume $\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f\right)>0$ , and write $\mu=\mu_{f}$ . Let $D$ be a closed analytic disc of positive radius with $\mu\left(D\right)>0$ . Since $\mu$ gives full mass to classical points and has no atoms, the interior of $D$ has positive measure.

For an injective analytic map $u:D\to u\left(D\right)$ , we interpret $u^{*}\mu=c\mu$ on $D$ as

$$ \mu\left(u\left(E\right)\right)=c\mu\left(E\right)\qquad\text{for every Borel }E\subseteq D. $$

#### Lemma 4.1.

Let $p$ be a repelling $N$ -periodic point of $f$ in $D$ , $N\geq 1$ . Let $\mu$ denote the equilibrium measure of $f$ . Then there does not exist a family of injective analytic maps $\sigma_{n}:D\to D$ such that

- • $\sigma_{n}^{*}\mu=c_{n}\mu$ on $D$ , $c_{n}>0$ .

- • $\sigma_{n}\left(p\right)\neq p$ .

- • $\sigma_{n}\to\operatorname{id}$ uniformly on $D$ .

#### Proof.

Assume by contradiction such family $\sigma_{n}$ exists. By passing to an iterate of $f$ we may assume that $p$ is fixed, and we write $d$ for the degree of this iterate of $f$ . We now use Poincare’s linearization at $p$ [5, Section 4.2], which gives us a neighborhood $U$ of $p$ so that $f$ is conjugated to $[\lambda]:z\mapsto\lambda z$ , where $\lambda$ is the multiplier at $p$ . Since $\sigma_{n}\to\operatorname{id}$ uniformly, for sufficiently large enough $n$ we have $\sigma_{n}(U)=U$ . We may then replace $D$ with $U$ .

After conjugating, we may further assume that $D=D(0,1)$ is the closed unit disc, $p=0$ , and and $f$ is given by $[\lambda]$ . If we view $[\lambda]$ as a map from $D(0,|\lambda|^{-1})\to D(0,1)$ , we then have $[\lambda]^{*}\mu=d\cdot\mu$ . Note that as $p$ is a repelling fixed point, it is in the closure of the Julia set $J_{f}$ and so $\mu(D(0,\varepsilon))>0$ for any $\varepsilon>0$ .

We first claim that there is a uniform $\delta>0$ such that $c_{n}\geq\delta$ for every $n\geq 1$ . Since $\sigma_{n}\to\operatorname{id}$ , we can choose $M$ large enough such that $|\sigma_{n}(0)|<1/2$ and $|\sigma^{\prime}_{n}(0)|>1/2$ for $n\geq M$ . Thus $D^{\prime}:=D(0,1/2)\subset\sigma_{n}(D)$ for every $n\geq M$ . Then for $n\geq M$ ,

$$ c_{n}\mu(D)=\sigma^{*}_{n}\mu(D)=\mu(\sigma_{n}(D))\geq\mu(D^{\prime})>0. $$

Thus $c_{n}\geq\mu(D^{\prime})/\mu(D)>0$ for $n\geq M$ , which implies the claim since $\mu(D^{\prime})/\mu(D)$ is a fixed positive constant. Also $c_{n}\leq 1$ , since $\sigma_{n}(D)\subseteq D$ and $\mu(\sigma_{n}(D))=c_{n}\mu(D)$ .

For each $n\geq 1$ , let $l_{n}$ be the maximal positive integer such that

$$ |\lambda^{-1}|<|\lambda^{l_{n}}\sigma_{n}(0)|\leq 1. $$

Then $l_{n}\to+\infty$ , since $\sigma_{n}(0)\to 0$ . Consider the injective analytic map

$$ \tau_{n}:=[\lambda^{l_{n}}]\circ\sigma_{n}\circ[\lambda^{-l_{n}}]:D\to D. $$

Since $\sigma_{n}$ is an isometry and $|\sigma_{n}(0)|\leq|\lambda|^{-l_{n}}$ , it maps $D(0,|\lambda|^{-l_{n}})$ onto itself. Thus $\tau_{n}$ is an analytic automorphism of $D$ .

Then $\tau_{n}^{*}\mu=c_{n}\mu$ on $D$ . Expanding $\sigma_{n}$ as a power series centered at $0$ , if $a_{k}$ is the coefficient for $z^{k}$ , then the coefficient of $z^{k}$ for $\tau_{n}$ is $\lambda^{-l_{n}(k-1)}a_{k}$ . Since $|a_{k}|\leq 1$ , it follows that if we define

$$ \varepsilon_{n}(z):=\tau_{n}(z)-\tau_{n}(0)-\tau^{\prime}_{n}(0)z, $$

then $\varepsilon_{n}(z)\to 0$ uniformly on $D$ as $l_{n}\to\infty$ . In particular, $\tau_{n}(z)$ becomes close to linear as $n\to\infty$ . Uniform convergence $\sigma_{n}\to\operatorname{id}$ also gives $\tau^{\prime}_{n}(0)=\sigma^{\prime}_{n}(0)\to 1$ .

We now have two cases, depending on whether $\tau_{n}(0)$ has a subsequential limit or not.

Case 1: We assume here that $\tau_{n}(0)$ has a subseuqential limit. Hence by passing to a subsequence, we may assume that $\tau_{n}(0)\to b$ for some $b\in D$ . We may also assume that $c_{n}$ has a subsequential limit $c>0$ . By our choice of $l_{n}$ , we have $|b|\geq|\lambda^{-1}|$ and thus $b\not=0$ . Then $\tau_{n}\to T_{b}$ uniformly on $D$ , and $T_{b}^{*}\mu=c\mu$ on $D$ , where $T_{b}(z):=z+b$ is a translation. Since $T_{b}:D\to D$ is a bijection, we have

$$ c\mu(D)=T_{b}^{*}\mu(D)=\mu(T_{b}(D))=\mu(D), $$

thus $c=1$ , i.e. $T_{b}$ preserves the measure $\mu$ on $D$ .

Since the residue field of $K_{v}$ has characteristic $0$ , we have $|mb|=|b|$ for every every integer $m\neq 0$ . Let $D_{0}=D(0,r)$ be a closed disk with $0<r<|b|$ , define $D_{n}:=D(nb,r)=T_{b}^{n}(D_{0})\subset D$ . Assume $i\neq j$ , since $|(i-j)b|=|b|$ , we have $D_{i}\cap D_{j}=\emptyset$ . Since $T_{b}^{n}$ preserves the measure $\mu$ on $D$ , we have $\mu(D_{n})=\mu(D_{0})>0$ for every $n\geq 0$ . Thus

$$ \mu(D)\geq\mu(\bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty}D_{n})=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\mu(D_{n})=+\infty, $$

which contradicts to $\mu(D)\leq 1$ .

Case 2: We now assume that $\tau_{n}(0)$ has no subsequential limit. Hence there exists $r_{0}>0$ such that after passing to a subsequence, we have $|\tau_{i}(0)-\tau_{j}(0)|>r_{0}$ for every $i\neq j$ . Let $D_{0}=D(0,r)$ be a closed disk with $0<r<r_{0}$ , let $D_{n}:=\tau_{n}(D_{0})$ . Then for every $n\geq 0$ , $D_{n}$ has radius at most $r$ . Let $i\neq j$ , since $|\tau_{i}(0)-\tau_{j}(0)|>r_{0}$ , we have $D_{i}\cap D_{j}=\emptyset$ .

Since $c_{n}\geq\delta>0$ , we have $(\tau_{n})^{*}(\mu)\geq\delta\mu$ on $D$ . Thus $\mu(D_{n})\geq\delta\mu(D_{0})>0$ . Hence

$$ \mu(D)\geq\mu(\bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty}D_{n})=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\mu(D_{n})=+\infty, $$

which contradicts to $\mu(D)\leq 1$ .

In both cases, we obtain a contradiction. This finishes our proof. ∎

We now remove the hypothesis of $\sigma_{n}\left(p\right)\neq p$ from Lemma 4.1. In this setting, such a family of $\{\sigma_{n}\}$ may exist but they must be equal to the identity map eventually.

#### Lemma 4.2.

Let $\sigma_{n}:D\to D$ be a family of injective analytic maps such that

- • $\sigma_{n}^{*}\mu=c_{n}\mu$ on $D$ , $c_{n}>0$ .

- • $\sigma_{n}\to\operatorname{id}$ uniformly on $D$ .

Then $\sigma_{n}=\operatorname{id}$ for $n$ large enough.

#### Proof.

We assume by contradiction that our lemma is false. By passing to a subsequence we may assume $\sigma_{n}\neq\operatorname{id}$ for every $n\geq 1$ . Again as in Lemma 4.1, after passing to an iterate of $f$ and using Poincaré’s linearization for a repelling fixed point in $D$ , we may assume that $D=D(0,1)$ is the closed unit disk, $f$ is the map given by $[\lambda]:z\mapsto\lambda z$ , $|\lambda|>1$ and $[\lambda]^{*}\mu=d\mu$ on $D$ . By Lemma 4.1 we may assume $\sigma_{n}(0)=0$ for all $n\geq 1$ .

We now split into two cases, depending on whether there exists $i$ such that the multiplier $\sigma_{i}^{\prime}(0)$ is $1$ .

Case 1: There is $i\geq 1$ such that $\sigma_{i}^{\prime}(0)=1$ . Let $\tau_{n}$ be the map

$$ \tau_{n}:=[\lambda^{n}]\circ\sigma_{i}\circ[\lambda^{-n}]:D\to D. $$

Then since $\sigma_{i}^{\prime}(0)=1$ , we may check that $\tau_{n}\to\operatorname{id}$ uniformly on $D$ . Furthermore $\tau_{n}\neq\operatorname{id}$ for every $n\geq 1$ as $\sigma_{n}\neq\operatorname{id}$ , and $\tau_{n}^{*}\mu=c_{i}\mu$ on $D$ . In particular, the family $\{\tau_{n}\}$ satisfies the conditions of Lemma 4.1.

For each repelling periodic point $p\in D$ , let $N_{p}\subset\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ be the set of $n$ such that $\tau_{n}(p)=p$ . By Lemma 4.1, $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\setminus N_{p}$ must be a finite set. Fix a repelling periodic point $p\not=0$ in $D$ . Then we may find infinitely many $n$ so that $\tau_{n}(p)=p$ and thus $\lambda^{-n}p$ is a fixed point $\sigma_{i}$ . This implies that $\{\sigma_{i}(z)=z\}$ has $\{0\}$ as an accumulation point and hence $\sigma_{i}=\operatorname{id}$ , which is a contradiction.

Case 2: We now assume that $\sigma_{i}^{\prime}(0)\neq 1$ for every $i\geq 1$ . For each $i,n\geq 1$ , let

$$ \tau_{i,n}=[\lambda^{n}]\circ\sigma_{i}\circ[\lambda^{-n}]. $$

As $n\to\infty$ , this converges uniformly to $\tau_{i}:z\mapsto\sigma^{\prime}_{i}(0)z$ and $\tau_{i}^{*}\mu=c_{i}\mu$ on $D$ . Furthermore as $\sigma^{\prime}_{i}(0)\to 1$ , we have $\tau_{i}\to\operatorname{id}$ . Hence we may replace $\{\sigma_{i}\}$ with the family of linear maps $\{\tau_{i}\}$ instead.

Now let $p\in D$ be a repelling periodic point which is not $0$ . As $\sigma_{n}$ are linear maps which is not $\operatorname{id}$ , we must have $\sigma_{n}\left(p\right)\neq p$ for every $n\geq 1$ . Lemma 4.1 then gives us a contradiction.

We get a contradiction in both cases and thus we may conclude our lemma.

∎

### 4.3. Proof of Theorem 4.1

We now begin the proof of Theorem 4.1. Let $U$ and $\rho>0$ be as in its statement. If the valuation on $K$ were trivial, then $f$ would have good reduction and its equilibrium measure would be the Dirac mass at the Gauss point, where its spherical derivative has norm $1$ . This would give $\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f\right)=0$ , contrary to our assumption. Thus the valuation is non-trivial.

By [38, Theorem B], $\mu_{f}$ gives full mass to $\mathbb{P}^{1}\left(K\right)$ , and it has no atoms. Hence $\pi_{1}^{*}\mu_{f}$ gives full mass to $C\left(K\right)$ and no mass to the finite singular and ramification loci of the two projections. We may therefore choose a classical smooth point $\left(x,y\right)\in U$ in its support, where both projections are unramified. Shrinking about this point, we obtain a disc $V$ around $x$ and an analytic bijection $h:V\to h\left(V\right)$ whose graph lies in $U$ , with $\mu_{f}\left(V\right)>0$ and

$$ h_{*}\left(\mu_{f}|_{V}\right)=\rho\mu_{g}|_{h\left(V\right)}. $$

In particular, $\mu_{g}$ gives positive mass to classical points. Since the residue characteristic is $0$ , [38, Theorem C and Corollary D] imply that $\mathrm{Lyap}\left(g\right)>0$ . Fix an $L>1$ larger than the spherical Lipschitz constants of both $f$ and $g$ , and let $K\geq 1$ be a Lipschitz constant for both $h$ and $h^{-1}$ .

We now state a lemma that gives a uniform lower bound for $\mu_{g}\left(B\left(g^{n}\left(y\right),r\right)\right)$ from for a fixed $r>0$ .

#### Proposition 4.5.

Fix $r>0$ and $\varepsilon>0$ . Then there exists a finite collection of balls $\left\{B\left(x_{i},r\right)\right\}_{i=1}^{n}$ such that that for $\mu_{g}$ -almost all $y$ , the set

$$ A_{y}=\left\{n\in\mathbb{N}\mid B\left(g^{n}\left(y\right),r\right)=B\left(x_{i},r\right)\text{ for some }i\right\} $$

satisfies $\uline{d}\left(A_{y}\right)\geq 1-\varepsilon.$ In particular there exists $\delta>0$ such that for $n\in A_{y}$ , we have $\mu_{g}(B(g^{n}(y),r))\geq\delta$ .

#### Proof.

First as $\mathrm{Lyap}\left(g\right)>0$ , we have $\mu_{g}\left(\mathbb{H}\right)=0$ where $\mathbb{H}$ denotes $\mathbb{P}^{1,\operatorname{an}}\setminus\mathbb{P}^{1}\left(K\right)$ . Since $\mathbb{H}$ is Borel measurable [3, Proposition 5.5] and $\mu_{g}$ is a Radon measure [5, Theorem 13.37], there exists an open set $U$ containing $\mathbb{H}$ such that $\mu_{g}\left(U\right)<\varepsilon$ . Now for every type I point $x\in J_{g}$ , we consider the union of all balls $B\left(x,r\right)$ along with $U$ . This is a collection of open sets that contain $J_{g}$ which is compact. Hence there exists a finite set of balls $B\left(x_{1},r\right),\ldots,B\left(x_{n},r\right)$ that along with $U$ cover $J_{g}$ .

By Birkhoff’s ergodic theorem, the density of $n$ so that $g^{n}\left(x\right)$ does not lie in $U$ is $\geq 1-\varepsilon$ . For such $n$ ’s we must have $B\left(g^{n}\left(x\right),r\right)=B\left(x_{i},r\right)$ for some $i$ . Since each $B\left(x_{i},r\right)$ has positive mass, there must exist a uniform $\delta>0$ so that $\mu_{g}\left(B\left(g^{n}\left(x\right),r\right)\right)\geq\delta$ as desired. ∎

Now for any $\varepsilon>0$ , by Proposition 4.3 there exists $r>0$ so that if we set

$$ B_{y}=\left\{n\in\mathbb{N}\mid g^{n}:W\to B\left(g^{n}\left(y\right),r\right)\text{ is a bijection}\right\}, $$

where $W$ is the connected component containing $y$ in $g^{-n}(B(g^{n}(y),r)$ , then $\uline{d}\left(B_{y}\right)\geq 1-\varepsilon$ for $\mu_{g}$ -almost all $y$ . Now applying Proposition 4.5, there exists a finite collection of discs $\left\{B\left(x_{i},r\right)\right\}_{i=1}^{n}$ so that if we let $B^{\prime}_{y}$ be the subset of $B_{y}$ for which $\left(B\left(g^{n}\left(y\right),r\right)\right)=B\left(x_{i},r\right)$ , then $\uline{d}\left(B^{\prime}_{y}\right)\geq 1-2\varepsilon$ .

We may similarly apply Proposition 4.4 to $f$ . Since $h_{*}\left(\mu_{f}|_{V}\right)=\rho\mu_{g}|_{h\left(V\right)}$ with $\rho>0$ , if a property holds for $\mu_{g}$ -almost all $y$ in $h\left(V\right)$ , then it holds for $h\left(x\right)$ for $\mu_{f}$ -almost all $x$ in $V$ . We thus obtain the following.

#### Proposition 4.6.

Fix an $\varepsilon>0$ . For $\mu_{f}$ -almost all $x$ in $V$ where $y=h\left(x\right)$ , we have:

- (1) $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log\left|g^{n}\right|^{\prime}\left(y\right)=\mathrm{Lyap}\left(g\right)$ and $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log\left|f^{n}\right|^{\prime}\left(x\right)=\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f\right)$ .

- (2) There exists $r>0$ and $B^{\prime}_{y}\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ with $\uline{d}\left(B^{\prime}_{y}\right)\geq 1-2\varepsilon$ so that for $n\in B^{\prime}_{y}$ , the ball $B\left(g^{n}\left(y\right),r\right)$ is one of finitely many possible balls $\left\{B\left(x_{i},r\right)\right\}_{i=1}^{n}$ . Furthermore,

$$ g^{n}:W\to B\left(g^{n}\left(y\right),r\right) $$

is a bijection where $W$ is the component of $g^{-n}\left(B\left(g^{n}\left(y\right),r\right)\right)$ containing $y$ . We will denote the inverse branch by $g_{-n}$ .

- (3) There exists $A_{x}\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ with $d\left(A_{x}\right)\geq 1-\varepsilon$ so that for $n\in A_{x}$ , if $W^{\prime}$ is the component of $f^{-n}\left(B\left(f^{n}\left(x\right),r\right)\right)$ containing $x$ , then $f^{n}:W^{\prime}\to B\left(f^{n}\left(x\right),r\right)$ is a bijection, where $r$ is the same $r$ as in (2).

Fix an $\varepsilon>0$ , so that we have a corresponding $x\in V$ and $r>0$ that satisfies (1),(2) and (3) in Proposition 4.6. For each positive integer $n$ , we may consider $h^{-1}\circ g_{-n}$ which is a map from $B\left(g^{n}\left(y\right),r\right)$ to $B\left(x,r^{\prime}\right)$ , where $r^{\prime}$ is very small. We want to precompose it with an iterate of $f$ , say $f^{\theta\left(n\right)}$ , so that

$$ f^{\theta\left(n\right)}\circ h^{-1}\circ g_{-n}:B\left(g^{n}\left(y\right),r\right)\to B\left(f^{\theta\left(n\right)}\left(x\right),R_{n}\right) $$

is still injective, and $\theta\left(n\right)$ is almost as large as possible, so that $R_{n}$ is uniformly bounded away from $0$ .

We will quantify this as follows. Recall that we have fixed a constant $L>1$ that is larger than the spherical Lipschitz constant for both $f$ and $g$ and also a $K\geq 1$ which serves as a Lipschitz constant for both $h$ and $h^{-1}$ . We define $\alpha_{f,x}\left(n\right)$ to be the minimal $m$ so that $\log\left|f^{m}\right|^{\prime}\left(x\right)\geq\left(n-1\right)\log L-\log K$ . Then $\alpha_{f,x}$ is strictly increasing for sufficiently large $n$ and there exists constants $\lambda,Q>1$ so that

$$ m-Q\leq\alpha_{f,x}\left(m\right)\leq\frac{m\log L+Q}{\log\lambda}. $$
