We similarly define $\alpha_{g,y}\left(n\right)$ to be the minimal $m$ so that $\log\left|g^{m}\right|^{\prime}\left(y\right)\geq n\log L$ . Then again $\alpha_{g,y}$ is strictly increasing and we have a constant $Q$ so that

$$ m\leq\alpha_{g,y}\left(m\right)\leq\frac{m\log L+Q}{\log\lambda}. $$

We now set

$$ G=B^{\prime}_{y}\cap\left(\alpha_{g,y}\circ\alpha_{f,x}^{-1}\left(A_{x}\right)\right). $$

For $n\in G$ , we define $\theta\left(n\right)=\alpha_{f,x}\circ\alpha_{g,y}^{-1}\left(n\right).$ Given $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ , we will let $\uline{d}\left(A\right)$ denote the lower density of $A$ , i.e.

$$ \uline{d}\left(A\right):=\liminf_{n}\frac{\left|A\cap\left\{1,2,\ldots,n\right\}\right|}{n}. $$

#### Proposition 4.7.

For $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small, we have $\uline{d}\left(G\right)$ and $\uline{d}\left(\theta\left(G\right)\right)>0$ . For sufficiently large $n\in G$ , we have that

$$ f^{\theta\left(n\right)}\circ h^{-1}\circ g_{-n}:B\left(g^{n}\left(y\right),r\right)\to B\left(f^{\theta\left(n\right)}\left(x\right),R_{n}\right) $$

where $\frac{r}{K^{2}L^{2}}\leq R_{n}\leq r$ for all sufficiently large $n$

#### Proof.

The proof of this is very similar to [56, Lemma 4.14]. As $\alpha_{f,x},\alpha_{g,y}$ are both strictly increasing functions and there exists $c>0$ , depending only on $L$ , $K$ and $\lambda$ , such that

$$ \frac{\left|\alpha_{f,x}(\mathbb{N})\cap\{1,2,\ldots,m\}\right|}{m}\geq c $$

for all sufficiently large $m$ and also for $\alpha_{g,y}$ , we have

$$ \uline{d}\left(\alpha_{f,x}^{-1}\left(A_{x}\right)\right)\geq 1-\frac{\varepsilon}{c},\quad\uline{d}\left(\alpha_{g,y}\circ\alpha_{f,x}^{-1}\left(A_{x}\right)\right)\geq c\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon}{c}\right). $$

As $\uline{d}\left(B^{\prime}_{y}\right)\geq 1-2\varepsilon$ , if $\varepsilon$ is sufficiently small we have $\uline{d}\left(G\right)>0$ . Similarly we have $\uline{d}\left(\theta\left(G\right)\right)>0$ .

Now let $n\in G$ . Let $\alpha_{g,y}\left(m\right)=n$ . Then $n$ is the smallest positive integer so that $\log\left|g^{n}\right|^{\prime}\left(y\right)\geq m\log L$ and in particular

$$ \left(m+1\right)\log L\geq\log\left|g^{n}\right|^{\prime}\left(y\right)\geq m\log L. $$

Similarly since $\theta\left(n\right)=\alpha_{f,x}\left(m\right)$ , for all sufficiently large $n$ we must have

$$ m\log L-\log K\geq\log\left|f^{\theta\left(n\right)}\right|^{\prime}\left(x\right)\geq\left(m-1\right)\log L-\log K. $$

Now let $W$ be the connected component of $g^{-n}\left(B\left(g^{n}\left(y\right),r\right)\right)$ that contains $y$ , so that

$$ g^{n}:W\to B\left(g^{n}\left(y\right),r\right) $$

is injective. It follows that

$$ \log r-\left(m+1\right)\log L\leq\log\operatorname{diam}\left(W\right)\leq\log r-m\log L. $$

Now applying $h^{-1}$ , we obtain a disc $h^{-1}\left(W\right)$ containing $x$ satisfying

$$ \log r-\left(m+1\right)\log L-\log K\leq\log\operatorname{diam}\left(h^{-1}\left(W\right)\right)\leq\log r-m\log L+\log K. $$

Since $\theta(n)\in A_{x}$ , Proposition 4.6 (3) gives a component $W^{\prime}$ containing $x$ such that

$$ f^{\theta(n)}:W^{\prime}\longrightarrow B(f^{\theta(n)}(x),r) $$

is bijective. By (4.1),

$$ \log\operatorname{diam}(W^{\prime})\geq\log r-m\log L+\log K. $$

Thus $h^{-1}(W)\subseteq W^{\prime}$ , so $f^{\theta(n)}$ is injective on $h^{-1}(W)$ and its image has radius at most $r$ . The lower bounds for $\operatorname{diam}(h^{-1}(W))$ and in (4.1) give $R_{n}\geq r/(K^{2}L^{2})$ , as desired. ∎

Let $h_{n}=f^{\theta\left(n\right)}\circ h^{-1}\circ g_{-n}$ for $n\in G$ . We now claim that we may choose a subsequence $n_{1},n_{2},\ldots$ with $n_{i}\in G$ so that $f^{\theta\left(n_{i}\right)}\left(x\right)$ converges to a Type I point in $J_{f}$ .

#### Proposition 4.8.

There exists a subsequence $n_{1},n_{2},\ldots$ with $n_{i}\in G$ so that $f^{\theta\left(n_{i}\right)}\left(x\right)$ converges to a Type I point in $J_{f}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $Z$ be the closure of $\left\{f^{\theta\left(n\right)}\left(x\right)\mid n\in G\right\}$ . Recall that $x$ has was chosen to be $\mu_{f}$ -generic. Since $\uline{d}\left(\theta\left(G\right)\right)>0$ , it follows that $\mu_{f}\left(Z\right)>0$ . As $\mu\left(\mathbb{H}\right)=0$ , it must be that $Z$ contains a type I point as desired. ∎

Passing to this subsequence $\left\{n_{k}\right\}$ and then to a possibly further subsequence, we may assume that $B\left(g^{n_{k}}\left(y\right),r\right)$ are all the same disc $D$ by (2) of Proposition 4.6. Hence we have a family of injective maps

$$ h_{n_{k}}:D\to B\left(f^{\theta\left(n_{k}\right)}\left(x\right),R_{n_{k}}\right) $$

with $f^{\theta\left(n_{k}\right)}\left(x\right)$ converging to a Type I point, say $z\in J_{f}$ . Since $z\in J_{f}$ , it follows that $\mu_{f}(B\left(z,\frac{r}{2K^{2}L^{2}}\right))=\delta^{\prime}>0$ . As $R_{n_{k}}\geq\frac{r}{K^{2}L^{2}}$ , passing to a subsequence, we may assume that

$$ B\left(z,\frac{r}{2K^{2}L^{2}}\right)\subseteq B(f^{\theta(n_{k})}(x),R_{n_{k}}). $$

In particular $\mu_{f}\left(B\left(f^{\theta\left(n_{k}\right)}\left(x\right),R_{n_{k}}\right)\right)\geq\delta^{\prime}$ .

#### Proposition 4.9.

For any Borel set $E\subseteq D$ , we have

$$ \mu_{f}\left(h_{n_{k}}\left(E\right)\right)=\rho d_{1}^{\theta\left(n_{k}\right)}d_{2}^{-n_{k}}\mu_{g}\left(E\right). $$

Furthermore, there exists $\delta>0$ such that

$$ d_{1}^{\theta\left(n_{k}\right)}d_{2}^{-n_{k}}\geq\delta>0 $$

for all $k\geq 1$ .

#### Proof.

As $f^{*}\mu_{f}=d_{1}\mu_{f}$ , it follows that if $f:E\to f\left(E\right)$ is injective, then $\mu_{f}\left(f\left(E\right)\right)=d_{1}\mu_{f}\left(E\right)$ . By our assumption about proportionality of two measures, $\mu_{f}\left(h^{-1}\left(E\right)\right)=\rho\mu_{g}\left(E\right)$ for Borel sets $E\subseteq h\left(V\right)$ . Since $g_{-n_{k}}\left(D\right)\subseteq h\left(V\right)$ , $g^{n_{k}}$ is injective on $g_{-n_{k}}\left(D\right)$ , and $f^{\theta\left(n_{k}\right)}$ is injective on $h^{-1}\circ g_{-n_{k}}\left(D\right)$ , we have

$$ \mu_{g}\left(g_{-n_{k}}\left(D\right)\right)=d_{2}^{-n_{k}}\mu_{g}\left(D\right) $$

and

$$ \mu_{f}\left(f^{\theta\left(n_{k}\right)}\circ h^{-1}\circ g_{-n_{k}}\left(D\right)\right)=\rho d_{1}^{\theta\left(n_{k}\right)}d_{2}^{-n_{k}}\mu_{g}\left(D\right). $$

The same argument applies to any Borel set $E\subseteq D$ . Now since $\mu_{f}\left(h_{n_{k}}\left(D\right)\right)\geq\delta^{\prime}>0$ , we have

$$ 1\geq\rho d_{1}^{\theta\left(n_{k}\right)}d_{2}^{-n_{k}}\mu_{g}\left(D\right)\geq\delta^{\prime}, $$

giving us $\delta>0$ such that $d_{1}^{\theta\left(n_{k}\right)}d_{2}^{-n_{k}}\geq\delta$ as desired. ∎

We will now show that we can further choose a subsequence of $h_{n_{k}}$ so that it converges as a power series on $D$ , after possibly shrinking $D$ .

#### Proposition 4.10.

We may replace $n_{k}$ with a subsequence and $D$ with a smaller disc $D^{\prime}$ so that $\mu_{g}\left(D^{\prime}\right)>0$ and $h_{n_{k}}:D^{\prime}\to h_{n_{k}}\left(D^{\prime}\right)$ converges to a power series $h^{\prime}:D^{\prime}\to h(D^{\prime})$ .

#### Proof.

Let $y^{\prime}\in J_{g}$ be a point that lies on $D$ . After translating and possibly inverting, we may assume that $D$ is centered at $y^{\prime}=0$ . Similarly after passing to a subsequence and possibly inverting, we may assume there exists $R>0$ such that $h_{n_{k}}\left(D\right)\subseteq D\left(0,R\right)$ , where $D\left(0,R\right)$ represents the disc centered at $0$ with Euclidean radius $\leq R$ instead of the spherical metric.

We may then expand $h_{n_{k}}$ as a convergent power series $h_{n_{k}}=a_{k,0}+a_{k,1}z+a_{k,2}z^{2}+\cdots$ . Since $D$ has radius $r$ , we must have $\left|a_{k,n}\right|\leq Rr^{-n}$ as $h_{n_{k}}\left(D\right)\subseteq D\left(0,R\right)$ . We now let $D^{\prime}=D\left(0,\frac{r}{2}\right)$ . Since $0$ is a point of $J_{g}$ , it follows that $\mu_{g}\left(D^{\prime}\right)>0$ . Then to show that there is a subsequence of $h_{n_{k}}$ that converges on $D^{\prime}$ , it suffices to show that there is a subsequence of $h_{n_{k}}$ such that $a_{k,i}$ converges pointwise for each $i$ . To show this, we will induct on the assumption that we can find a subsequence so that $a_{k,i}$ converges for all $i<N$ . We then show we can further extract a subsequence so that $a_{k,N}$ converges too. A diagonalization argument then gives us the subsequence we want.

Now let’s assume that $a_{k,i}$ converges to $a_{k}$ for all $i<N$ . If $a_{k,N}$ has a subsequence that converges to a Type I point, then we can simply pass to that subsequence and we are done. Else, passing to a subsequence, we may assume that there is $r^{\prime}>0$ such that $\left|a_{k,N}-a_{k^{\prime},N}\right|\geq r^{\prime}$ for all $k\not=k^{\prime}$ . We will show that this leads to a contradiction.

Consider a $z\in D$ with $0<\left|z\right|<1$ small enough so that

$$ \left|a_{k,n}z^{n-N}\right|<r^{\prime} $$

for all $k$ and $n\geq N+1$ . For such a $z$ , as it is non-zero, we can choose $M>0$ so that for all $k,k^{\prime}\geq M$ , we have

$$ \left|a_{k,i}-a_{k^{\prime},i}\right|<r^{\prime}\left|z\right|^{N} $$

for all $i<N$ . It follows that

$$ \left|h_{n_{k}}\left(z\right)-h_{n_{k^{\prime}}}\left(z\right)\right|=\left|a_{k,N}-a_{k^{\prime},N}\right|z^{N}\geq r^{\prime}\left|z\right|^{N}. $$

Let $C$ be a uniform Lipschitz constant for $h_{n_{k}}$ for all $k\geq 1$ . Then if we take $\varepsilon>0$ such that $C\varepsilon<r^{\prime}\left|z\right|^{N}$ , it follows that $h_{n_{k}}\left(D\left(z,\varepsilon\right)\right)$ are all disjoint for all $k\geq M$ .

Now since $0$ is a Type I point in $J_{g}$ , we may find a non-zero $z$ satisfying (4.2) that is also a Type I point in $J_{g}$ . Then we for any $\varepsilon>0$ , it follows that $\mu_{g}\left(D\left(z,\varepsilon\right)\right)>0$ . If we choose $\varepsilon<\frac{r}{2}\left|z\right|^{N}$ , it follows that

$$ \mu_{f}\left(h_{n_{k}}\left(D\left(z,\varepsilon\right)\right)\right)\geq\rho d_{1}^{\theta\left(n_{k}\right)}d_{2}^{-n_{k}}\mu_{g}\left(D\left(z,\varepsilon\right)\right)\geq\rho\delta\mu_{g}\left(D\left(z,\varepsilon\right)\right). $$

Since each $h_{n_{k}}\left(D\left(z,\varepsilon\right)\right)$ is disjoint, this implies that $\mu_{f}$ has infinite mass which is a contradiction. Hence $a_{k,N}$ must have a Type I point as a subsequential limit. This finishes our induction as desired. ∎

We may now assume that $h_{n_{k}}$ converges to a power series $h^{\prime}$ on $D^{\prime}$ with $\mu_{g}\left(D^{\prime}\right)>0$ . Since $h_{n_{k}}$ is injective, it follows that

$$ \operatorname{diam}\left(h_{n_{k}}\left(D\right)\right)=\left|h^{\prime}_{n_{k}}\left(x\right)\right|\operatorname{diam}\left(D\right) $$

for any $x\in D$ . As $\operatorname{diam}\left(h_{n_{k}}\left(D\right)\right)$ is bounded from below, it follows that $\liminf_{x\in D}\left|h^{\prime}_{n_{k}}\left(x\right)\right|>0$ and in particular, we must have $\left|h^{\prime}_{n_{k}}\left(x\right)\right|$ being all equal for sufficiently large $k$ . It then follows that $h_{n_{k}}\left(D^{\prime}\right)$ are all equal for $k$ sufficiently large, say to $D^{\prime\prime}$ . We may then assume that $h_{n_{k}}\left(D^{\prime}\right)=D^{\prime\prime}$ for all $k$ . Our aim now is to show that $\left\{h_{n_{k}}\right\}$ is a finite set. This will then imply that $h_{n_{k}}=h_{n_{k^{\prime}}}$ for $k^{\prime}>k$ which will provide for us a local semiconjugacy between $f$ and $g$ .

#### Proof of Theorem 4.1.

The limit $h^{\prime}:D^{\prime}\to D^{\prime\prime}$ is an analytic bijection. By Proposition 4.9, the common image $D^{\prime\prime}$ implies

$$ \rho d_{1}^{\theta\left(n_{k}\right)}d_{2}^{-n_{k}}=\frac{\mu_{f}\left(D^{\prime\prime}\right)}{\mu_{g}\left(D^{\prime}\right)}=:A>0. $$

Hence $\left(h_{n_{k}}\right)_{*}\left(\mu_{g}|_{D^{\prime}}\right)=A^{-1}\mu_{f}|_{D^{\prime\prime}}$ and $h^{\prime}_{*}\left(\mu_{g}|_{D^{\prime}}\right)=A^{-1}\mu_{f}|_{D^{\prime\prime}}$ . For each positive integer $k$ , consider the analytic map

$$ \sigma_{k}=\left(h^{\prime}\right)^{-1}\circ h_{n_{k}}:D^{\prime}\to D^{\prime}. $$

Then $\sigma_{k}$ is injective and $\sigma_{k}^{*}\left(\mu_{g}|_{D^{\prime}}\right)=\mu_{g}|_{D^{\prime}}$ . Furthermore as $k\to\infty$ , we have $\sigma_{k}\to\operatorname{id}$ and $\mu_{g}\left(D^{\prime}\right)>0$ . We may now apply Lemma 4.2 to the family and obtain that $\left\{\sigma_{k}\right\}$ is a finite family. Hence $\left\{h_{n_{k}}\right\}$ must be a finite family, and passing to a subsequence, we may assume that all of them are equal to each other. We thus get

$$ f^{\theta\left(n_{i}\right)}\circ h^{-1}\circ g_{-n_{i}}=f^{\theta\left(n_{j}\right)}\circ h^{-1}\circ g_{-n_{j}} $$

as maps from $D^{\prime}$ to $D^{\prime\prime}$ . For each $j$ , the infinite set

$$ X_{j}=\left\{\left(h^{-1}\circ g_{-n_{j}}\left(t\right),g_{-n_{j}}\left(t\right)\right)\mid t\in D^{\prime}\right\} $$

lies in $C$ , and its image under $\left(f^{\theta\left(n_{j}\right)},g^{n_{j}}\right)$ is the same graph $\left\{\left(h_{n_{i}}\left(t\right),t\right)\mid t\in D^{\prime}\right\}$ , independently of $j$ . Hence for two $j^{\prime}>j$ , we have that

$$ \left(f^{\theta\left(n_{j}\right)},g^{n_{j}}\right)\left(C\right)\cap\left(f^{\theta\left(n_{j^{\prime}}\right)},g^{n_{j^{\prime}}}\right)\left(C\right) $$

has infinite intersection and thus they must actually be equal as curves. Let $a=\theta\left(n_{j^{\prime}}\right)-\theta\left(n_{j}\right)$ and $b=n_{j^{\prime}}-n_{j}$ . Then $C^{\prime}=\left(f^{\theta\left(n_{j}\right)},g^{n_{j}}\right)\left(C\right)$ is fixed by $\left(f^{a},g^{b}\right)$ . By the discussion after the statement of Lemma 6.1 in [46], it follows that $\deg\left(f^{a}\right)=\deg\left(g^{b}\right)$ , i.e. $d_{1}^{a}=d_{2}^{b}$ .

Now consider the forward iterates of $C$ under $\left(f^{a},g^{b}\right)$ , which we will label as $C_{1},C_{2},\ldots$ . Since $\left(f^{\theta\left(n_{j}\right)},g^{n_{j}}\right)$ commutes with $\left(f^{a},g^{b}\right)$ , it follows that $(f^{\theta(n_{j})},g^{n_{j}})(C_{i})=C^{\prime}$ . Hence $C_{i}\subseteq(f^{\theta(n_{j})},g^{n_{j}})^{-1}(C^{\prime})$ . This implies that the sequence $C_{1},C_{2},\ldots$ take on only finitely many possible curves and in particular $C$ must be preperiodic under $\left(f^{a},g^{b}\right)$ as desired.

∎

We need another rigidity statement when $f$ is a Lattès map that does not have potentially good reduction and $g$ is a map with good reduction.

#### Proposition 4.11.

Let $f,g$ be two rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$ and assume that $f$ is a Lattès map that does not have potentially good reduction and $g$ has good reduction. Then for any curve $C\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{2}$ such that $\pi_{1},\pi_{2}$ projects dominantly, we have

$$ \left(\deg\pi_{2}\right)\pi_{1}^{*}\mu_{f}\neq\left(\deg\pi_{1}\right)\pi_{2}^{*}\mu_{g}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $g$ has good reduction, we know that $\mu_{g}$ is a delta mass at the Gauss point. As $\pi_{2}:C^{\operatorname{an}}\to\mathbb{P}^{1,\operatorname{an}}$ is a finite morphism, this implies that $\pi_{2}^{*}\mu_{g}$ is supported on a finite set of points. On the other hand, we know that $\operatorname{Supp}\mu_{f}$ is an interval and thus infinite in size. As $\pi_{1}:C^{\operatorname{an}}\to\mathbb{P}^{1,\operatorname{an}}$ is also finite, it cannot be that $\operatorname{Supp}(\pi_{1}^{*}\mu_{f})$ is a finite set of points and hence

$$ \left(\deg\pi_{2}\right)\pi_{1}^{*}\mu_{f}\neq\left(\deg\pi_{1}\right)\pi_{2}^{*}\mu_{g}. $$

∎

## 5. Flat Metrics of Curves in Families

In this section, given two rational maps $f,g$ and a curve $C$ over a non-trivially valued field $K$ , we will define a local energy pairing $\langle f,g\rangle_{v,C}$ . We will then prove that it is continuous under some mild hypothesis in Proposition 5.4.

Let $S$ be a quasi-projective variety over a number field $K$ and let $\cal{C}$ be a family of smooth projective curves over $S$ , i.e. a flat family whose fibers are smooth, projective and geometrically irreducible curves. Then for each non-trivial $s\in S^{\operatorname{an}}$ , we obtain a non-trivially valued field $\cal{H}\left(s\right)$ and a geometrically irreducible curve $\cal{C}_{s}$ over $\cal{H}\left(s\right)$ . Let $L$ be a line bundle on $\cal{C}$ such that $L_{s}$ is numerically trivial on $\cal{C}_{s}$ for each $s\in S$ and hence $s\in S^{\operatorname{an}}$ .

Recall from [87] that for a smooth projective curve $C$ and numerically trivial line bundle $L$ over a non-trivially valued field $K$ , there exists a metrized line bundle $\overline{L}$ with underlying bundle $L$ such that $c_{1}\left(\overline{L}\right)=0$ on $C^{\operatorname{an}}$ , where $c_{1}\left(\overline{L}\right)$ is the Chambert–Loir measure associated to $\overline{L}$ . Furthermore this metric is unique up to constants. We will say that $\overline{L}=\left(L,\left|\cdot\right|\right)$ is flat, or that $\left|\cdot\right|$ is a flat metric.

Hence for each $s\in S^{\operatorname{an}}$ , we obtain a flat metric on $L_{s}$ . We would like to say that these flat metrics vary in a family, i.e. there exists an integrable adelic line bundle $\overline{L}\in\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}\left(\cal{C}/\mathbb{Z}\right)$ such that the restriction to each $s\in S^{\operatorname{an}}$ gives us a flat line bundle $\overline{L}_{s}$ . Here, $\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}\left(\cal{C}/\mathbb{Z}\right)$ is the space of adelic line bundles on $\cal{C}/K$ , where we view $K$ as a finitely generated field over $\mathbb{Q}$ , see [88, Section 2] for the definitions and basic facts.

When $L_{s}$ is numerically trivial for each $s$ , such an adelic line bundle $\overline{L}$ is also called an admissible adelic extension of $L$ [90, Definition 2.5].

#### Proposition 5.1.

Let $\cal{C}/S$ be a flat family of smooth projective curves over $S$ where $S$ is a quasi-projective variety over a number field $K$ . Assume further that $S$ is normal and integral. Let $L$ be a line bundle on $\cal{C}$ for which $L_{s}$ is numerically trivial for each $s\in S$ . Then there exists an admissible adelic extension $\overline{L}$ of $L$ .

#### Proof.

[90, Proposition 2.6] proves this in the case that $S$ is a quasi-projective variety over $\mathbb{Z}$ instead of $K$ . In our case, we may take some model $\cal{C}^{\prime}/\cal{S}$ of $\cal{C}/S$ , along with $\cal{L}$ extending $L$ , so that $\cal{S}$ is now a quasi-projective variety over $\mathbb{Z}$ . We may then apply [90, Proposition 2.6] and conclude. ∎

The flat metric is important as it allows us to generalize the energy pairing of Favre–Rivera-Letelier [36] (see also Fili [40]), of two rational maps $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle$ to the more general setting of $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C}$ for a pair of rational maps $\left(f,g\right)$ and a non-vertical/horizontal curve $C\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{2}$ . When $C=\Delta$ is the diagonal, we recover the original Favre–Rivera-Letelier pairing. The energy pairing has been used by DeMarco–Krieger–Ye [21, 22] and Poineau [77] to prove instances of the uniform dynamical Bogomolov when $C=\Delta$ . This more general pairing has been used by Mavraki–Schmidt [68] in the proof of the uniform dynamical Bogomolov for $1$ -parameter families.

We first define the local energy pairing for a pair of rational maps $\left(f,g\right)$ of degree $d\geq 2$ that are defined over a non-trivially valued field $\left(K,\left|\cdot\right|\right)$ . Let $C\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{2}$ be our geometrically irreducible curve over $K$ , not necessarily smooth, and let it be of bidegree $\left(d_{1},d_{2}\right)$ , with $d_{i}>0$ . Here $d_{i}=\deg(\pi_{i}|_{C})$ . Let $\overline{L}_{f}$ be the metrized line bundles, unique up to constants, on $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ with underlying line bundle $O\left(1\right)$ and with $c_{1}\left(\overline{L}_{f}\right)=\mu_{f}$ , the equilibrium measure of $f$ . We similarly define $\overline{L}_{g}$ . We then set

$$ \overline{L}=d_{2}\pi_{1}^{*}\overline{L}_{f}-d_{1}\pi_{2}^{*}\overline{L}_{g}. $$

If $L$ is the underlying line bundle of $\overline{L}$ , then $L$ is numerically trivial. Let $\pi:C^{\prime}\to C$ be its normalization. Then we may pullback and obtain $\pi^{*}\overline{L}$ with underlying line bundle $\pi^{*}L$ and furthermore, $\pi^{*}L$ is still numerically trivial. Hence has a flat metric, which we denote by $\overline{M}$ . We now set $\overline{N}=\pi^{*}\overline{L}-\overline{M}$ , where the underlying line bundle of $\overline{N}$ is $N\simeq O_{C^{\prime}}$ the trivial bundle. We then define the local energy pairing

$$ \left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C}=-\overline{N}^{2}\geq 0, $$

where we use the sections $\left(\bf{1},\bf{1}\right)$ to compute $\overline{N}^{2}$ . The quantity $-\overline{N}^{2}$ is independent of the choice of isomorphism between $N$ and $O_{C^{\prime}}$ and thus $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C}$ is well-defined. Now if $\left(f,g,C\right)$ are defined over a number field $K$ , we define the global energy pairing

$$ \left(f,g\right)_{C}=\sum_{v\in M_{K}}n_{v}\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,v} $$

where $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,v}$ is the local pairing over the valued field $\mathbb{C}_{v}$ and $n_{v}=\left[K_{v}:\mathbb{Q}_{p}\right]/\left[K:\mathbb{Q}\right]$ is the normalization factor.

The global energy pairing is related to the normalized canonical height $\widehat{h}_{\left(f,g\right)}\left(C\right)$ by the following inequality. Note that by definition, we have

$$ \widehat{h}_{(f,g)}(C)=\frac{(\pi_{1}^{*}\overline{L}_{f}+\pi_{2}^{*}\overline{L}_{g})^{2}}{[K:\mathbb{Q}](d_{1}+d_{2})}=\frac{2(\pi_{1}^{*}\overline{L}_{f})\cdot(\pi_{2}^{*}\overline{L}_{g})}{[K:\mathbb{Q}](d_{1}+d_{2})} $$

as $\overline{L}_{f}^{2}=\overline{L}_{g}^{2}=0$ .

#### Proposition 5.2.

We have the inequality

$$ \widehat{h}_{(f,g)}(C)\geq\frac{1}{d_{1}d_{2}(d_{1}+d_{2})}(f,g)_{C}. $$

#### Proof.

Working over the number field $K$ on the normalization of $C$ , let $\overline{L}_{f},\overline{L}_{g}$ be the invariant adelic line bundles for $f,g$ and $\overline{L}=d_{2}\pi_{1}^{*}\overline{L}_{f}-d_{1}\pi_{2}^{*}\overline{L}_{g}$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\overline{L}^{2} \displaystyle=(d_{2}\pi_{1}^{*}\overline{L}_{f}-d_{1}\pi_{2}^{*}\overline{L}_{g})^{2}=-2d_{1}d_{2}(\pi_{1}^{*}\overline{L}_{f})\cdot(\pi_{2}^{*}\overline{L}_{g}) \displaystyle=-[K:\mathbb{Q}]d_{1}d_{2}(d_{1}+d_{2})\widehat{h}_{(f,g)}(C). $$

On the other hand, we may find a flat adelic line bundle $\overline{M}$ with same underlying line bundle as $\overline{L}$ , so that $\overline{N}=\overline{L}-\overline{M}$ has the trivial underlying line bundle and

$$ -\overline{N}^{2}=[K:\mathbb{Q}](f,g)_{C}. $$

Due to flatness of $\overline{M}$ and $N$ being trivial, we have

$$ \overline{L}^{2}=\overline{N}^{2}+\overline{M}^{2} $$

and furthermore, $\overline{M}^{2}\leq 0$ [87, Section 2.2]. thus

$$ d_{1}d_{2}(d_{1}+d_{2})\widehat{h}_{(f,g)}(C)=\frac{-\overline{L}^{2}}{[K:\mathbb{Q}]}\geq\frac{-\overline{N}^{2}}{[K:\mathbb{Q}]}=(f,g)_{C} $$

as desired. ∎

Now let $S$ be a quasi-projective variety over s number field $K^{\prime}$ and let $S$ parametrize a family of triples $\left(f,g,C\right)$ where $\left(f,g\right)$ are rational maps on $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ of degree $d\geq 2$ and $C$ a degree $\left(d_{1},d_{2}\right)$ curve. For each non-trivially valued $s\in S^{\operatorname{an}}$ , we obtain a complete valued residue field $\cal{H}\left(s\right)$ and a triple $\left(f,g,C\right)$ defined over $\cal{H}\left(s\right)$ and hence a the pairing $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,s}$ . This gives us a function

$$ \left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,s}:S^{\operatorname{an}}\setminus S^{\operatorname{triv}}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} $$

where $S^{\operatorname{triv}}$ is the set of $s\in S^{\operatorname{an}}$ for which the residue field $\cal{H}\left(s\right)$ is trivially valued. We wish to prove that this function is continuous. We will instead prove a weaker claim that we may cover $S$ with finitely many locally closed subvarieties $Z_{i}$ so that the function restricted to each $Z_{i}^{\operatorname{an}}$ is continuous.

#### Proposition 5.3.

Let $\cal{C}/S$ be a flat family of geometrically irreducible, projective curves where $S$ is a quasi-projective variety over a number field $K$ . We may cover $S$ with finitely many locally closed irreducible normal subvarieties $Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{m}$ such that for each $i$ :

- (1) There exists a flat family of smooth projective curves $\cal{Y}_{i}/Z_{i}$ where $Z_{i}$ ’s is a quasi-projective variety over $K$ with a morphism $\pi:\cal{Y}_{i}/Z_{i}\to\cal{C}_{Z_{i}}/Z_{i}$ where $\cal{C}_{Z_{i}}$ is the restriction of $X$ to $Z_{i}$ .

- (2) For each $s\in Z_{i}$ , the morphism $\pi:\cal{Y}_{i,s}\to\cal{C}_{i,s}$ is birational.

#### Proof.

We may assume that $S$ is irreducible. We note that it suffices to construct a Zariski open $Z_{1}$ satisfying the properties we want by induction on the complement $S\setminus Z_{1}$ , where finiteness follows from noetherianess.

To obtain $Z_{1}$ , let $\eta\in S$ be the generic point and let $\cal{C}_{\eta}/k\left(S\right)$ be the generic fiber where $k=K^{\prime}$ . We may resolve its singularities by taking a normalization and so obtaining $\pi:Y_{\eta}\to X_{\eta}$ over $k\left(S\right)$ with $Y_{\eta}$ being a smooth projective curve.

This spreads out to a family $\cal{Y}/U^{\prime}$ of smooth projective curves with a morphism $\pi:\cal{Y}/U^{\prime}\to\cal{C}/U$ for some Zariski open $U$ of $S$ . By shrinking $U$ , we may assume that $U$ is normal since $S$ is integral. Furthermore, each fiber $\pi:\cal{Y}_{s}\to\cal{C}_{s}$ is birational. Finally we may shrink $U^{\prime}$ so that $\pi:U^{\prime}\to U$ is isomorphic as $k\left(U^{\prime}\right)$ is isomorphic to $k\left(U\right)$ . We thus obtain our $Z_{1}$ by setting $Z_{1}=U$ as desired. ∎

We now show that when restricted to such $Z_{i}$ ’s, our function $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,s}$ is continuous. Let $S$ be our quasi-projective variety parametrizing our triples $\left(f,g,C\right)$ . By Proposition 5.3, we may cover $S$ with $Z_{i}$ ’s so that on each $Z_{i}$ , our family of curves $\cal{C}_{Z_{i}}/Z_{i}$ has a simultaneous resolution $\pi:\cal{C}^{\prime}/Z_{i}\to\cal{C}_{Z_{i}}/Z_{i}$ . Before we begin the proof, as we will have to use the theory of adelic line bundles over quasi-projective varieties by Yuan–Zhang [88], we will quickly recall some definitions and facts here.

Let $X$ be a flat integral projective scheme over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Z}$ . Then an arithmetic $\mathbb{Q}$ -divisor $\cal{D}$ is a pair $\left(D,g_{\cal{D}}\right)$ where $D$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$ -Cartier divisor and $g_{\cal{D}}$ a continuous Green’s function for the divisor $D$ on $X\left(\mathbb{C}\right)$ . Now if $U$ is a quasi-projective scheme flat over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Z}$ , we define the space of arithemtic model divisors $\widehat{\operatorname{Div}}_{\mathbb{Q}}\left(U\right)_{\mathrm{mod}}$ as

$$ \widehat{\operatorname{Div}}_{\mathbb{Q}}\left(U\right)_{\mathrm{mod}}=\lim_{\rightarrow}\widehat{\operatorname{Div}}_{\mathbb{Q}}\left(X\right) $$

where $X$ ranges over all compactifications of $U$ . Now fixing some compactification $\overline{U}$ , we may define a boundary divisor $\cal{E}$ which is a model divisor whose support is $\overline{U}\setminus U$ and $g_{\cal{E}}>0$ everywhere. We may then endow $\widehat{\operatorname{Div}}_{\mathbb{Q}}\left(U\right)_{\mathrm{mod}}$ with a suitable boundary topology and form its completion, giving us the space of adelic divisors $\widehat{\operatorname{Div}}_{\mathbb{Q}}\left(U\right)$ . Quotienting out by a suitable equivalence gives us the space of adelic line bundles $\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}\left(U/\mathbb{Z}\right)$ .

Finally if $X$ is simply a quasi-projective variety over a number field $K$ , we will let

$$ \widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}\left(X/\mathbb{Z}\right):=\lim_{\rightarrow}\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}\left(\cal{U}/\mathbb{Z}\right) $$

where the limit is taken over all quasi-projective models $\cal{U}$ of $X$ over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Z}$ .

The space $\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}\left(X/\mathbb{Z}\right)$ is usually too big and we will work with a subset of it known as the integrable adelic line bundles. All adelic line bundles/divisors we will use are integrable and so we will simply impose integrability as an additional condition to being an adelic divisor. We can now begin our proof that the function $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,s}$ is continuous. We will further assume that our base $S$ is normal, so that we can apply the theory of Deligne pairings for adelic line bundles [88, Section 4].

#### Proposition 5.4.

Assume that $S$ is both integral and normal. Also assume that our family of curves $\cal{C}/S$ has a simultaneous resolution $\pi:\cal{C}^{\prime}/S\to\cal{C}/S$ . Then the function

$$ \left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,s}:S^{\operatorname{an}}\setminus S^{\operatorname{triv}}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} $$

is continuous.

#### Proof.

As $S$ parametrizes a family of triples $\left(f,g,C\right)$ , we obtain a morphism $f:\mathbb{P}^{1}_{S}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}_{S}$ which is polarizable for the line bundle $O\left(1\right)$ . By [88, Theorem 6.1.1], we have a $f$ -invariant adelic line bundles $\overline{L}_{f}\in\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}_{S}/\mathbb{Z}\right)$ with underlying line bundle $\tilde{L}_{f}\in\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}_{S}/\mathbb{Q}\right)$ . Similarly we obtain $\overline{L}_{g}$ . Then viewing $\cal{C}/S$ as embedded in $\left(\mathbb{P}_{S}^{1}\right)^{2}$ , we may form the adelic line bundle

$$ \overline{L}=d_{2}\pi_{1}^{*}\overline{L}_{f}-d_{1}\pi_{2}^{*}\overline{L}_{g}\in\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}\left(\cal{C}/\mathbb{Z}\right). $$

Then if $\tilde{L}$ is its underlying line bundle, restricting to each fiber gives us a numerically trivial line bundle $L_{s}$ . Now we may pull this back under $\pi$ to obtain $\pi^{*}\overline{L}\in\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}\left(\cal{C}^{\prime}/\mathbb{Z}\right)$ with underlying line bundle $\pi^{*}L$ . As $\pi^{*}L$ is numerically trivial for each $s\in S$ , there exists a flat adelic metric on it given by an adelic line bundle $\overline{M}\in\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}\left(\cal{C}^{\prime}/\mathbb{Z}\right)$ . Then

$$ \overline{N}=\pi^{*}\overline{L}-\overline{M}\in\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}\left(\cal{C}^{\prime}/\mathbb{Z}\right) $$

is an adelic line bundle with underlying line bundle isomorphic to $O_{\cal{C}^{\prime}}$ . Furthermore for each $s\in S^{\operatorname{an}}$ , we have

$$ -\overline{N}^{2}_{s}=\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,s} $$

where $\overline{N}^{2}_{s}$ is the induced metrized line bundle over the residue valued field $\cal{H}\left(s\right)$ . Now consider the Deligne pairing

$$ \left\langle\overline{N},\overline{N}\right\rangle\in\widehat{\operatorname{Pic}}\left(S/\mathbb{Z}\right). $$

Then there is a global section of $\left\langle N,N\right\rangle$ given by $\left\langle\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1}\right\rangle$ where $\bf{1}$ is a constant section in $O_{\cal{C}^{\prime}}$ . Taking its norm, it follows that

$$ -\log\left|\left\langle\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1}\right\rangle\right|_{s}:S^{\operatorname{an}}\to\mathbb{R} $$

is a continuous function. When $\cal{H}\left(s\right)$ is not trivially valued, the fiberwise formula [88, Sections 4.2.2 and 4.6.2] imply that

$$ -\log\left|\left\langle\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1}\right\rangle\right|_{s}=\overline{N}_{s}^{2} $$

and so the function $-\overline{N}_{s}^{2}=\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,s}$ is continuous on $S^{\operatorname{an}}\setminus S^{\operatorname{triv}}$ as desired. ∎

## 6. Uniform Energy Pairing Bounds

The main results of this section are the uniform local energy bounds in Proposition 1.8 and their variants in Propositions 6.4–6.6. Recall from Section 5 that if $\left(K,\left|\cdot\right|\right)$ is a complete valued field, $f,g:\mathbb{P}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}$ two rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$ over $K$ and $C\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{2}$ a geometrically irreducible degree $\left(d_{1},d_{2}\right)$ -curve over $K$ , then we have a local energy pairing $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C}$ . We have the following basic positivity property of the pairing.

#### Proposition 6.1.

The inequality

$$ \left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C}\geq 0 $$

holds, with equality if and only if

$$ d_{2}\pi_{1}^{*}\mu_{f}=d_{1}\pi_{2}^{*}\mu_{g}. $$

#### Proof.

The inequality follows from the local Hodge index theorem applied on $\overline{N}$ and the curve $C^{\prime}$ [87, Theorem 1.1]. Then equality holds if and only if $c_{1}\left(\overline{N}\right)=0$ , which is equivalent to

$$ d_{2}\phi^{*}\pi_{1}^{*}\mu_{f}=d_{1}\phi^{*}\pi_{2}^{*}\mu_{g}. $$

Since $\phi:C^{\prime}\to C$ is birational, the map $\phi:\left(C^{\prime}\right)^{\operatorname{an}}\to C^{\operatorname{an}}$ is an isomorphism outside of a finite set of Type I points and as $\mu_{f},\mu_{g}$ do not charge any Type I points, it follows that

$$ d_{2}\pi_{1}^{*}\mu_{f}=d_{1}\pi_{2}^{*}\mu_{g} $$

as desired. ∎

We note if $K^{\prime}$ is another complete valued field containing $K$ , then the quantity $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C}$ remains invariant if we work over $K^{\prime}$ instead of $K$ . When $K$ is archimedean this is clear. For non-archimedean $K$ , because $\overline{N}$ is constructed from line bundles coming from dynamics, there exists a sequence of model line bundles $\left\{\overline{N}_{i}\right\}_{i\geq 1}$ such that if $K^{\prime}$ is any complete value field extending $K$ , then the base change $\left\{\overline{N}_{K^{\prime},i}\right\}$ converges to $\overline{N}_{K^{\prime}}$ . By [51, Remark 3.10], the local intersection number for model metrics is invariant, i.e. $\overline{N}^{2}_{i}=\overline{N}_{K^{\prime},i}^{2}$ . Thus taking limits, we obtain $\overline{N}^{2}=\overline{N}_{K^{\prime}}^{2}$ as desired.

Now if $K$ is a number field and $f,g,K$ are defined over $K$ , we may consider the global energy pairing

$$ \left(f,g\right)_{C}:=\sum_{v\in M_{K}}n_{v}\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,v} $$

where $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,v}$ is the energy pairing over the field $\mathbb{C}_{v}$ .

Let $X=\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times C_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ be the moduli space of all triples $\left(f,g,C\right)$ where $f,g$ are rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$ and $C_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ is a degree $\left(d_{1},d_{2}\right)$ -curve. This is a fine moduli space defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ , and even over $\mathbb{Z}$ although the latter is not important for us. By Propositions 5.3 and 5.4 and taking normalizations, we may find finitely many normal quasi-projective subvarieties $\left\{Z_{k}\right\}$ that cover $X$ . Then each $Z_{k}$ can be considered as paremetrizing a family of triples $\left(f,g,C\right)$ . As $Z_{k}$ is normal, we know that the function

$$ \left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,s}:Z_{k}^{\operatorname{an}}\setminus Z_{k}^{\operatorname{triv}}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} $$

is continuous. We will now restrict ourselves to each $Z_{k}$ . We first study its preperiodic locus.

#### Proposition 6.2.

There exists a countable collection of subvarieties $V_{1},V_{2},\ldots,$ of $Z_{k}$ such that if $s\in Z_{k}$ corresponds to a triplet $\left(f_{s},g_{s},C_{s}\right)$ over the residue field $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\left(s\right)$ , then $C_{s}$ is preperiodic if and only if $s\in V_{i}$ for some $i$ .

#### Proof.

It suffices to handle the case of $X=\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times C_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ . For each pair $\left(m,n\right)$ of positive integers, we let $V_{m,n}$ be the locus for which $\left(f_{s},g_{s}\right)^{m}\left(C_{s}\right)=\left(f_{s},g_{s}\right)^{n}\left(C_{s}\right)$ . We claim that this cuts out a Zariski closed set in $X$ . Indeed, let $C^{\prime}_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ denote the space of all degree $\left(d_{2},d_{1}\right)$ -bihomogeneous forms up to scalars. We may view $C_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ as an open variety of $C^{\prime}_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ . Then we have an algebraic map

$$ \Phi^{m}:\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times C^{\prime}_{d_{1},d_{2}}\to\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times C^{\prime}_{d^{m}d_{1},d^{m}d_{2}} $$

given by

$$ \left(f,g,C\right)\mapsto\left(f,g,\left(f^{m},g^{m}\right)_{*}C\right) $$

where $\left(f^{m},g^{m}\right)_{*}$ denotes the pushforward operator on cycles (for example, see the proof of [54, Theorem 3.8]. For $m>n$ , we have a multiplication by $d^{m-n}$ map sending $C^{\prime}_{d^{n}d_{1},d^{n}d_{2}}$ to $C^{\prime}_{d^{m}d_{1},d^{m}d_{2}}$ , given by $C\mapsto C^{d^{m-n}}$ .

Since $C$ is irreducible, so is $\left(f^{m},g^{m}\right)\left(C\right)$ and thus the locus we are interested in is thus given by $V_{m,n}=\left\{\Phi^{m}=d^{m-n}\cdot\Phi^{n}\right\}$ which is Zariski closed. Restricting to $C_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ gives us a closed subvariety. Now letting $\left(m,n\right)$ vary over all pairs of non-negative integers gives us our countable collection $V_{1},V_{2},\ldots$ as desired. ∎

We can now our state our first main uniform lower bound on the energy pairing. Let $V_{1},V_{2},\ldots$ be our countable collection of closed subvarieties whose union is the preperiodic locus. Following Section 3.2, we fix local height functions $\lambda_{\partial V_{i}}$ for each subvariety $V_{i}$ and a local height function $\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}$ for the boundary of $Z_{k}$ . We will prove a uniform energy bound on $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C}$ , assuming that our triplet $\left(f,g,C\right)$ is not too close to any $V_{i}$ and also that the Lyapunov exponent $\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f\right)$ of $f$ is not too small.

#### Proposition 6.3.

Let $\left(K,\left|\cdot\right|\right)$ be a complete non-trivially valued field of characteristic $0$ . Let $\delta,c_{1},c_{2},\ldots$ be positive constants. Then there exists constants $N>0$ and $c>0$ depending on $K,\delta,c_{1},c_{2},\ldots$ such that if $s=\left(f,g,C\right)\in Z_{k}\left(K\right)$ satisfies:

- (1) $\lambda_{V_{i}}\left(s\right)\leq c_{i}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right)$ for all $i\geq 1$ ;

- (2) $\mathrm{Lyap}(f)\geq\delta\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}(s)$ ;

- (3) $\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right)\geq N$ .

Then we have the uniform lower bound

$$ \left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C}\geq c\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right). $$

#### Proof.

We assume otherwise. Then we have a sequence of points $s_{n}=\left(f_{n},g_{n},C_{n}\right)$ such that

$$ \lambda_{\partial V_{i}}(s_{n})\leq c_{i}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}(s_{n}),\mathrm{Lyap}(f_{n})\geq\delta\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}(s_{n}),\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}(s_{n})\geq n\text{ and }\langle f_{n},g_{n}\rangle_{C_{n}}\leq\frac{1}{n}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}(s_{n}). $$

We now degenerate using ultrafilters with the scaling $\varepsilon_{n}=\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s_{n}\right)^{-1}$ as in Section 3.3. By Proposition 3.13, as $\varepsilon_{n}\to\infty$ , we obtain a morphism $s:\operatorname{Spec}A^{\varepsilon}\to Z_{k}$ that restricts to $s_{n}:\operatorname{Spec}K\to Z_{k}$ for each $n$ . Observe that we have an induced morphsim $s:\cal{M}\left(A^{\varepsilon}\right)\to Z_{k}^{\operatorname{an}}$ which is continuous. To see why, observe that we have a continuous morphism $(\operatorname{Spec}A^{\varepsilon})^{\operatorname{an}}\to Z_{k}^{\operatorname{an}}$ coming from the analytification of $\operatorname{Spec}A^{\varepsilon}\to Z_{k}$ . Then we have a natural inclusion $\cal{M}\left(A^{\varepsilon}\right)\xhookrightarrow{}\left(\operatorname{Spec}A^{\varepsilon}\right)^{\operatorname{an}}$ which is continuous as the topology on both sides is the Gelfand topology. Then $s$ is the composition of the two.

Letting $\omega$ be a non-principal ultrafilter, we obtain a triple $\left(f_{\omega},g_{\omega},C_{\omega}\right)$ over the residue field $\cal{H}\left(\omega\right)$ , given by our morphism $s$ . Observe that $\cal{H}\left(\omega\right)$ is of residue characteristic $0$ since $\varepsilon_{n}\to 0$ . Furthermore,

$$ \mathrm{Lyap}\left(f_{\omega}\right)=\lim_{\omega}\varepsilon_{n}\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f_{n}\right)\geq\delta>0 $$

as the Lyapunov exponent is a continuous function on $Z_{k}^{\operatorname{an}}$ an thus on $\cal{M}\left(A^{\varepsilon}\right)$ by [88, Theorem 6.3.7]. Hence $f$ has bad reduction and in particular $\cal{H}\left(\omega\right)$ is not trivially valued.

As $\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C}$ is continuous on $Z_{k}^{\operatorname{an}}\setminus Z_{k}^{\operatorname{triv}}$ , it is also continuous on $\cal{M}\left(A^{\varepsilon}\right)$ and so we obtain

$$ \left\langle f_{\omega},g_{\omega}\right\rangle_{C_{\omega}}=\lim_{\omega}\varepsilon_{n}\left\langle f_{n},g_{n}\right\rangle_{C_{n}}=0. $$

By Proposition 6.1, we must have $d_{2}\pi_{1}^{*}\mu_{f_{\omega}}=d_{1}\pi_{2}^{*}\mu_{g_{\omega}}$ . Since $\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f_{\omega}\right)>0$ , by Proposition 4.1, our curve $C_{\omega}$ must be preperiodic for $\left(f_{\omega},g_{\omega}\right)$ . Thus $s_{\omega}$ must lie in $V_{m}$ for some $m\geq 1$ . However, we also have

$$ \lambda_{V_{m}}\left(s_{\omega}\right)=\lim_{\omega}\varepsilon_{n}\lambda_{V_{m}}\left(s_{n}\right)\leq c_{m}<+\infty, $$

which implies that $s_{\omega}\not\in V_{m}$ . This is a contradiction and we are done. ∎

We can now obtain independence from $K$ and remove the requirement that $\lambda_{\partial K}$ assuming the residue characteristic is large enough.

#### Proposition 6.4.

Let $\delta,c_{1},c_{2},\ldots$ be positive constants. Then there exists constants $N>0$ and $c>0$ depending on $\delta,c_{1},c_{2},\ldots$ such that for any algebraically closed complete non-trivially valued field $\left(K,\left|\cdot\right|\right)$ with residue characteristic $\geq N$ , if $s=\left(f,g,C\right)\in Z_{k}\left(K\right)$ satisfies:

- (1) ${\lambda_{V_{i}}}(s)\leq c_{i}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}(s)$ for all $i\geq 1$ ;

- (2) $\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f\right)\geq\delta\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right),$

then we have the uniform lower bound

$$ \left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C}\geq c\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right). $$

#### Proof.

Similar to the proof of Proposition 6.3, we assume otherwise. Then we obtain a sequence of valued fields $\left(K_{n},\left|\cdot\right|\right)$ with residue characteristic of $K_{n}$ being $\geq n$ , along with a sequence $s_{n}=\left(f_{n},g_{n},C_{n}\right)\in Z_{k}\left(K_{n}\right)$ so that:

$$ {\lambda_{V_{i}}}(s_{n})\leq c_{i}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}(s_{n}),\mathrm{Lyap}(f_{n})\geq\delta\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}(s),\text{ and }\langle f_{n},g_{n}\rangle_{C_{n}}<\frac{1}{n}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}(s_{n}). $$

We may also assume that $\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s_{n}\right)>0$ as the energy pairing is non-negative. We degenerate with the scaling $\varepsilon_{n}=\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s_{n}\right)^{-1}$ . Since the residue characteristic of $K_{n}$ is either $0$ or goes to $\infty$ , by Proposition 3.13 we obtain a morphism $s:\operatorname{Spec}A^{\varepsilon}\to Z_{k}$ restricting to $s_{n}:\operatorname{Spec}K_{n}\to Z_{k}$ for each $n$ and thus a morphism $s:\cal{M}\left(A^{\varepsilon}\right)\to Z_{k}^{\operatorname{an}}$ .

Picking $\omega$ to be a non-principal ultrafilter, the residue field $\cal{H}\left(\omega\right)$ is of residue characteristic $0$ and we obtain a triple $\left(f_{\omega},g_{\omega},C_{\omega}\right)$ over $\cal{H}\left(\omega\right)$ using $s$ . We then have

$$ \left\langle f_{\omega},g_{\omega}\right\rangle_{C_{\omega}}=\lim_{\omega}\varepsilon_{n}\left\langle f_{n},g_{n}\right\rangle_{C_{n}}=0. $$

Since $\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f_{\omega}\right)\geq\delta>0$ , it must be that $d_{2}\pi_{1}^{*}\mu_{f_{\omega}}=d_{1}\pi_{2}^{*}\mu_{g_{\omega}}$ . Hence $C_{\omega}$ must be preperiodic and so $s_{\omega}=\left(f_{\omega},g_{\omega},C_{\omega}\right)$ must lie on $V_{m}$ for some $m\geq 1$ , But this can’t happen as $\lambda_{V_{m}}\left(s_{\omega}\right)\leq c_{m}<+\infty$ which gives us a contradiction. ∎

We next handle the setting where $f$ is a Lattès map and $g$ is a map with good reduction. We note that the locus of triplets $(f,g,C)\in Z_{k}$ with $f$ being Lattès is Zariski closed since the flexible Lattès locus is closed in $\operatorname{rat}_{d}$ and the rigid Lattès maps correspond to a finite set of points. Hence their union in $\operatorname{rat}_{d}$ is closed and so is their preimage in $\operatorname{Rat}_{d}$ . We fix a local height function $\lambda_{\partial\operatorname{rat}_{d}}$ for the boundary of $\operatorname{rat}_{d}$ . For $f\in\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\left(K\right)$ , we let $\left\langle f\right\rangle$ be the induced point on $\operatorname{rat}_{d}\left(K\right)$ .

#### Proposition 6.5.

Let $\left(K,\left|\cdot\right|\right)$ be a complete non-trivially valued field of characteristic $0$ . Let $\delta>0$ be a positive constant. Then there exists constants $N>0$ and $c>0$ depending on $K,\delta$ such that if $s=\left(f,g,C\right)\in Z_{k}\left(K\right)$ satisfies:

- (1) $f$ is a Lattès map with $\lambda_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(\langle f\rangle)\geq\delta\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}(s)$ and $\lambda_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(\langle f\rangle)\geq N\lambda_{\partial\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}(g)$ ;

- (2) $\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right)\geq N$ .

Then we have the uniform lower bound

$$ \left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C}\geq c\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right). $$

#### Proof.

The proof is similar to Proposition 6.3. We assume otherwise and obtain a sequence of triplets $(f_{n},g_{n},C_{n})\in Z_{k}(K)$ where $f_{n}$ is a Lattès map satisfying

$$ \lambda_{\partial\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(\langle f_{n}\rangle)\geq\delta\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}(s_{n}),\lambda_{\partial\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(\langle f_{n}\rangle)\geq n\lambda_{\partial\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}(g_{n})\text{ and }\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}(s_{n})\geq n. $$

Degenerating with $\varepsilon_{n}=\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s_{n}\right)^{-1}$ gives us $\left(f_{\omega},g_{\omega},C_{\omega}\right)$ such that $f_{\omega}$ is a Lattès map with $\lambda_{\partial\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(\langle f_{\omega}\rangle)>0$ and $\lambda_{\partial\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}(g_{\omega})=0$ . Here, $f_{\omega}$ is a Lattès map because the locus of Lattès maps is closed. This means that $f_{\omega}$ does not have potentially good reduction and $g_{\omega}$ has good reduction. By Proposition 4.11, we cannot have $d_{2}\pi_{1}^{*}\mu_{f_{\omega}}=d_{1}\pi_{2}^{*}{\mu_{g_{\omega}}}$ which implies that $\langle f_{\omega},g_{\omega}\rangle_{C_{\omega}}>0$ . However this contradicts

$$ \langle f_{\omega},g_{\omega}\rangle_{C_{\omega}}=\lim_{\omega}\varepsilon_{n}\langle f_{n},g_{n},\rangle_{C_{n}}=0 $$

and we are done. ∎

Similarly we have the analogue of Proposition 6.4.

#### Proposition 6.6.

Let $\delta>0$ be a positive constant. Then there exists constants $N>0$ and $c>0$ depending on $\delta$ such that for any algebraically closed complete non-trivially valued field $\left(K,\left|\cdot\right|\right)$ with residue characteristic $\geq N$ , if $s=\left(f,g,C\right)\in Z_{k}\left(K\right)$ satisfies

$$ \lambda_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(\langle f\rangle)\geq\delta\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}(s)\text{ and }\lambda_{\partial\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(\langle f\rangle)\geq N\lambda_{\partial\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}(g), $$

then we have the uniform lower bound

$$ \left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C}\geq c\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right). $$

#### Proof.

This is similar to Propositions 6.4 and 6.5. We omit the proof. ∎

## 7. Uniform Dynamical Bogomolov for Curves

The main result of this section is Theorem 7.2, a uniform dynamical height gap for non-weakly special curves on $\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}$ . As $\operatorname{Rat}_{d},\operatorname{rat}_{d},C_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ are affine, we fix height functions $h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}},h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}$ and $h_{C_{d_{1},d_{2}}}$ coming from a height function of a choice of compactification so that their boundary is ample and hence they correspond to ample height functions. We similarly let $\lambda_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}},\lambda_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}},\lambda_{C_{d_{1},d_{2}}}$ be their local height functions.

#### Definition 7.1.

Let $f,g$ be rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$ and let $C\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{2}$ be an irreducible curve over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$ . We say that $C$ is weakly $\left(f,g\right)$ -special if either:

- (1) $C$ does not project dominantly to one of the coordinates;

- (2) $C$ is $\left(f,g\right)$ -preperiodic;

- (3) Both $f$ and $g$ are exceptional, with associated algebraic groups $G_{f},G_{g}$ , isogenies $\psi_{f},\psi_{g}$ and dominant maps $\varphi_{f},\varphi_{g}$ to $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ satisfying

$$ f\circ\varphi_{f}=\varphi_{f}\circ\psi_{f},\qquad g\circ\varphi_{g}=\varphi_{g}\circ\psi_{g}, $$

and there exists a coset $H\subseteq G_{f}\times G_{g}$ such that

$$ C\cap\operatorname{Im}\left(\varphi_{f},\varphi_{g}\right)=\left(\varphi_{f},\varphi_{g}\right)\left(H\right). $$

Here each of $G_{f},G_{g}$ is either $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ or an elliptic curve, and a coset is a translate of a connected algebraic subgroup.

#### Theorem 7.2.

Let $f,g$ be two rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$ defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Let $C\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{2}$ be a degree $\left(d_{1},d_{2}\right)$ curve which is not weakly $\left(f,g\right)$ -special. Then there exists $c=c\left(d_{1},d_{2},d\right)$ such that

$$ \widehat{h}_{\left(f,g\right)}\left(C\right)\geq c\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right),h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(g\right),1\right\}. $$

Before we begin proving Theorem 7.2, we need to first compare the sum of Lyapunov exponents of $f$ at every place $v$ to its height $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}$ . For $f$ a rational map of degree $d\geq 2$ over a number field $K$ , we define the Lyapunov height

$$ h_{\mathrm{Lyap}}\left(f\right)=\sum_{v\in M_{K}}n_{v}\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f_{v}\right) $$

We will show that if $f$ is not a Lattès map, then this is comparable to $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)$ .

#### Theorem 7.3.

Let $f$ be a rational map of degree $d\geq 2$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ that is not a Lattès map. Then there exists constants $c_{1},c_{2}>0$ , depending only on $d$ , such that

$$ h_{\mathrm{Lyap}}\left(f\right)\geq c_{1}h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right)-c_{2}. $$

#### Proof.

Let

$$ h_{\operatorname{crit}}\left(f\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{2d-2}\widehat{h}_{f}\left(c_{i}\right) $$

be the critical height of $f$ , where $c_{1},\ldots,c_{2d-2}$ are the critical points of $f$ counted with multiplicity. By Ingram[55], using McMullen’s theorem on multipliers of rational maps[70], we know that there are constants $A,B>0$ depending only on $d$ such that

$$ h_{\operatorname{crit}}\left(f\right)\geq Ah_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right)-B $$

for $f$ outside of the Lattès locus. We now apply [43, Proposition 2.7] which states that after choosing a homogeneous lift $F$ of $f$ , for any place $v$ , we have

$$ \mathrm{Lyap}\left(f_{v}\right)\geq-\log\left|d\right|_{v}+\sum_{c\in\mathrm{Crit}\left(f\right)}g_{F,v}\left(c\right)-\frac{2}{d}\log\left|\operatorname{Res}F\right|_{v}+\log\left|C_{F}\right|_{v} $$

where $C_{F}$ is some constant associated to $F$ and $g_{F}$ is the local homogeneous escape rate function. Summing up over all places and using the product formula, we obtain

$$ h_{\mathrm{Lyap}}\left(f\right)\geq h_{\operatorname{crit}}\left(f\right)\geq Ah_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right)-B $$

for $f$ outside the Lattès locus as desired. ∎

We begin the proof of Theorem 7.2 by making some reductions. First, we may assume there is a constant $A=A\left(d\right)>0$ depending only on $d$ so that

$$ h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)\leq A\max\left\{1,h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)\right\},h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(g\right)\leq c_{1}\max\left\{1,h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(g\right)\right\}. $$

Indeed for any $\varphi_{1},\varphi_{2}\in\operatorname{GL}_{2}\left(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\right)$ , we may replace $\left(f,g,C\right)$ with $\left(\varphi_{1}f\varphi_{1}^{-1},\varphi_{2}g\varphi_{2}^{-1},\left(\varphi_{1},\varphi_{2}\right)\left(C\right)\right)$ since $\widehat{h}_{\varphi_{1}f\varphi_{1}^{-1}}\left(\varphi\left(x\right)\right)=\widehat{h}_{f}\left(x\right)$ and similarly for $g$ . By [80, Lemma 6.3.2], we know there exists $A,B>0$ , depending only on $d$ , so that

$$ \min_{f^{\prime}\in\left\langle f\right\rangle}h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f^{\prime}\right)\leq Ah_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)+B, $$

which we may clearly assume that $A\geq B$ . By symmetry, we may assume that $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)\geq h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(g\right)$ . Next, we may assume that

$$ h_{C_{d_{1},d_{2}}}\left(C\right)\leq M_{1}\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right),1\right\} $$

for some $M_{1}=M_{1}\left(d_{1},d_{2},d\right)>0$ depending only on $\left(d_{1},d_{2},d\right)$ . This is because by Section 2, we can find $M_{1}^{\prime},M_{2}^{\prime}>0$ depending only on $\left(d_{1},d_{2},d\right)$

$$ M^{\prime}_{1}\widehat{h}_{\left(f,g\right)}\left(C\right)+M^{\prime}_{2}\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right),h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(g\right),1\right\}\geq h_{C_{d_{1},d_{2}}}\left(C\right). $$

Hence if $h_{C_{d_{1},d_{2}}}\left(C\right)$ is too large, then Theorem 7.2 is automatically true. Thus we may assume (7.2) holds.

We now prove Theorem 7.2 when $h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)$ is sufficiently large. For flexibility, we will assume the weaker inequality $M_{2}h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)\geq h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(g\right)$ for some fixed constant $M_{2}>0$ .

#### Proposition 7.4.

Let $f,g$ be two rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$ defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Let $C\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{2}$ be a degree $\left(d_{1},d_{2}\right)$ curve which is not weakly $\left(f,g\right)$ -special. Assume that $f$ is not a Lattès map and there exists constants $M_{1},M_{2}>1$ such that

$$ h_{C_{d_{1},d_{2}}}\left(C\right)\leq M_{1}\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right),1\right\}\text{ and }M_{2}h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right)\geq\max\left\{1,h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right),h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(g\right)\right\}. $$

Then there exists $c=c\left(d_{1},d_{2},d,M_{1},M_{2}\right)>0$ and $N=N\left(d_{1},d_{2},d,M_{1},M_{2}\right)>0$ so that if $h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)\geq N$ , then

$$ \widehat{h}_{\left(f,g\right)}\left(C\right)\geq c\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right),h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(g\right),1\right\}. $$

#### Proof.

Let $s=\left(f,g,C\right)$ be a triple satisfying the hypothesis of Proposition 7.4 and let $K$ be a number field that they are defined over. We may assume that $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)\geq 1$ . Recall from Section 6 that we have a covering of $X=\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times C_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ by locally closed subvarieties $Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{m}$ . Let $\left(f,g,C\right)\in Z_{k}\left(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\right)$ . Recall that we have a countable collection of subvarieties $V_{1},V_{2},\ldots$ of $Z_{k}$ so that $\left(f,g,C\right)\in V_{m}$ for some $m$ if and only if $C$ is preperiodic for $\left(f,g\right)$ . We fix local height functions $\lambda_{V_{i}}$ for each $V_{i}$ along with a local height function $\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}$ for the boundary of $Z_{k}$ . Observe that the boundary $\partial X$ is ample

Now since $X=\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times C_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ is affine, there exists a compactification $\overline{X}$ for which $\partial X$ is ample. We may thus choose $\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}$ so that $\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right)\geq\lambda_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)$ and thus $h_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right)\geq h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)$ . Also note that

$$ h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)+h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(g\right)+h_{C_{d_{1},d_{2}}}\left(C\right) $$

is an ample height for $X$ . By our hypothesis, this quantity is dominated by some multiple of $\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right),1\right\}=h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)$ and thus both $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)$ and $h_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right)$ dominates some ample height. Since $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)\geq 1$ , we hence obtain positive constants $a_{1},a_{2}\ldots$ , depending on $\left(d_{1},d_{2},d,M_{1},M_{2}\right)$ so that

$$ h_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right)\geq h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)\geq a_{i}h_{V_{i}}\left(s\right) $$

holds for all $i$ if $s\in\left(Z_{k}\setminus V_{i}\right)\left(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\right)$ . By Theorem 7.3. we also get a constant $a_{0}>0$ depending on $\left(d_{1},d_{2},d,M_{1},M_{2}\right)$ so that

$$ h_{\mathrm{Lyap}}\left(f\right)\geq a_{0}h_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right). $$

Note that we also have constants $b_{1},b_{2}>0$ so that

$$ \lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}\left(s\right)\geq\lambda_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d},v}\left(f\right)\geq b_{1}\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f_{v}\right)-b_{2} $$

where we may take $b_{2}=0$ for all sufficiently large residue characteristics depending only on $d$ . We now wish to apply Propositions 6.3 and 6.4. We choose constants

$$ \delta=\frac{a_{0}}{100},c_{i}=10^{i}({a_{0}b_{1}}a_{i})^{-1}. $$

Let $N^{\prime}$ and $c^{\prime}$ be common constants for $N$ and $c$ in both Propositions 6.3 and 6.4. We may take $N^{\prime}$ large enough so that $b_{2}=0$ for all residue characteristic $\geq N^{\prime}$ . We split into two cases. Let $M^{\prime}_{K}$ denote the places of $K$ which have residue characteristic $\geq N^{\prime}$ .

Case 1: We have

$$ \sum_{v\in M^{\prime}_{K}}n_{v}\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f_{v}\right)\geq\frac{1}{2}h_{\mathrm{Lyap}}\left(f\right). $$

Let $S$ be the subset of places of $v\in M^{\prime}_{K}$ such that

$$ c_{i}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}\left(s\right)\geq\lambda_{V_{i},v}\left(s\right)\text{ for all }i\geq 1\text{ and }\mathrm{Lyap}\left(f_{v}\right)\geq\delta\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}\left(s\right). $$

#### Lemma 7.5.

We have

$$ \sum_{v\in S}n_{v}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}(s)\geq\frac{b_{1}}{4}{h_{\mathrm{Lyap}}(f)}. $$

#### Proof.

Let $T_{0}$ be the set of places of $M^{\prime}_{K}$ so that $\mathrm{Lyap}(f_{v})<\delta\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}(s)$ and let $T_{i}$ be the set of places in $M^{\prime}_{K}$ so that $c_{i}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}(s)<\lambda_{V_{i},v}(s)$ but $v\notin T_{0}\cup\cdots\cup T_{i-1}$ . Then $S$ is the complement of $\cup_{i\geq 0}T_{i}$ in $M^{\prime}_{K}$ . For $i\geq 1$ , we have

$$ {h_{\partial Z_{k}}}(s)\geq a_{i}\sum_{v\in T_{i}}n_{v}\lambda_{V_{i},v}(s)\geq a_{i}c_{i}\sum_{v\in T_{i}}n_{v}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}(s) $$

and hence

$$ \sum_{v\in T_{i}}n_{v}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}(s)\leq\frac{1}{a_{i}c_{i}}{h_{\partial Z_{k}}}(s)\leq\frac{{a_{0}b_{1}}}{10^{i}}{h_{\partial Z_{k}}}(s). $$

For $T_{0}$ , we have

$$ \sum_{v\in T_{0}}n_{v}\mathrm{Lyap}(f_{v})\mathrel{\leq}\delta\sum_{v\in T_{0}}n_{v}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}(s)\leq\frac{a_{0}}{100}{h_{\partial Z_{k}}}(s). $$

By (7.4), we have

$$ \sum_{v\in M_{K}}n_{v}\mathrm{Lyap}(f_{v})\geq a_{0}{h_{\partial Z_{k}}}(s) $$

and so

$$ \sum_{v\in T_{0}}n_{v}\mathrm{Lyap}(f_{v})\leq\frac{1}{100}\sum_{v\in M_{K}}n_{v}\mathrm{Lyap}(f_{v})=\frac{1}{100}h_{\mathrm{Lyap}}(f). $$

Summing up (7.6) and (7.7) and using (7.5) on the disjoint $T_{i}$ for $i\geq 1$ , we get

$$ \sum_{v\in M^{\prime}_{K}\setminus S}n_{v}\mathrm{Lyap}(f_{v})\leq\left(\frac{1}{100}+\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{10^{i}}\right)h_{\mathrm{Lyap}}(f)\leq\frac{1}{5}h_{\mathrm{Lyap}}(f). $$

By assumption, we must have

$$ \sum_{v\in S}n_{v}\mathrm{Lyap}(f_{v})\geq\frac{1}{4}h_{\mathrm{Lyap}}(f). $$

We now apply (7.5) to get

$$ \sum_{v\in S}n_{v}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}{,v}}(s)\geq b_{1}\sum_{v\in S}n_{v}\mathrm{Lyap}(f_{v})\geq\frac{b_{1}}{4}h_{\mathrm{Lyap}}(f) $$

as desired. ∎

We now apply Proposition 6.4. We hence obtain

$$ \sum_{v\in S}n_{v}\langle f,g\rangle_{C,v}\geq{c^{\prime}}\sum_{v\in S}n_{v}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}(s)\geq\frac{b_{1}c^{\prime}}{4}h_{\mathrm{Lyap}}(f). $$

By Proposition 5.2 and Theorem 7.3, this proves Proposition 7.4 in this case.

Case 2: Let $T=M_{K}\setminus M_{K}^{\prime}$ . Then we have

$$ \sum_{v\in T}n_{v}\mathrm{Lyap}(f_{v})\geq\frac{1}{2}h_{\mathrm{Lyap}}(f). $$

Note that $\sum_{v\in T}n_{v}$ is a finite number bounded only in terms of $\left(d_{1},d_{2},d,M_{1},M_{2}\right)$ as $T$ consists of archimedean places and places with residue characteristic $\mathrel{<}N^{\prime}$ , where $N^{\prime}$ itself depends only on $\left(d_{1},d_{2},d,M_{1},M_{2}\right)$ . Similar to Lemma 7.5, if we let $S$ be the subset of places of $T$ so that

$$ c_{i}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}(s)\geq\lambda_{V_{i},v}(s)\text{ for all }i\geq 1\text{ and }\mathrm{Lyap}(f_{v})\geq\delta\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}(s), $$

we again obtain

$$ \sum_{v\in S}n_{v}\mathrm{Lyap}(f_{v})\geq\frac{1}{4}h_{\mathrm{Lyap}}(f). $$

We now apply (7.5) to obtain that

$$ \sum_{v\in{S}}n_{v}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}(s)\geq\sum_{v\in{S}}n_{v}(b_{1}\mathrm{Lyap}(f_{v})-b_{2})\geq\frac{b_{1}}{4}h_{\mathrm{Lyap}}(f)-B_{2} $$

where $B_{2}=b_{2}\sum_{v\in T}n_{v}$ is some constant depending only on ${\left(d_{1},d_{2},d,M_{1},M_{2}\right)}$ . We now apply Proposition 6.3 (or Proposition 6.4 when $p\geq P$ ), where we remove the condition $\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}\left(s\right)\geq N^{\prime}$ using nonnegativity of the pairing and instead have the conclusion $\langle f,g\rangle_{C{,v}}\geq{c^{\prime}}(\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}(s)-N^{\prime})$ . We thus get

$$ \sum_{v\in{S}}n_{v}\langle f,g\rangle_{C,v}\geq{c^{\prime}}\sum_{v\in{S}}n_{v}(\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}{(s)}-N^{\prime})\geq{c^{\prime}}\left(\frac{b_{1}}{4}h_{\mathrm{Lyap}}(f)-B_{2}\right)-{c^{\prime}}N^{\prime}\sum_{v\in T}n_{v}. $$

Again ${c^{\prime}}N^{\prime}\sum_{v\in T}n_{v}$ is some constant which depends only on $\left(d_{1},d_{2},d,M_{1},M_{2}\right)$ . Hence, by Proposition 5.2 and Theorem 7.3, if $h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)$ is large enough, we conclude Proposition 7.4. ∎

We now handle the case where $f$ is a Lattès map and $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)$ is much larger than $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(g\right)$ .

#### Proposition 7.6.

Let $f,g$ be two rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$ defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Let $C\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{2}$ be a degree $\left(d_{1},d_{2}\right)$ curve. Assume there is a constant $A>0$ , so that $f$ is a Lattès map with

$$ h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right)\geq A\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right),1\right\} $$

and that there exists a constant $M>1$ such that

$$ h_{C_{d_{1},d_{2}}}\left(C\right)\leq M\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right),1\right\}. $$

Then there exists constants $c,N>0$ , depending only on $\left(d_{1},d_{2},d,M,A\right)$ , so that if

$$ h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right)\geq N\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(g\right),1\right\}, $$

then

$$ \widehat{h}_{f,g}\left(C\right)\geq c\max\left\{1,h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right),h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(g\right)\right\}. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is similar to Proposition 7.4 but is much simpler in this case. We will use Propositions 6.5 and 6.6. Let $s=\left(f,g,C\right)$ be such a triplet and assume that $s\in Z_{k}\left(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\right)$ . Let $K$ be a number field such that $\left(f,g,C\right)$ is defined over. As in Proposition 7.4, after assuming $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)\geq 1$ , we may obtain constants $a,b>0$ depending on $\left(d_{1},d_{2},d,M,A\right)$ so that

$$ bh_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)\geq h_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right)\geq ah_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right). $$

Let $c^{\prime},N^{\prime}$ be constants for Propositions 6.5 and 6.6 for $\delta=\frac{1}{100b}$ . We let $M_{K}^{\prime}$ be the set of places with residue characteristic $\geq N^{\prime}$ . We again split into two cases. Note that we have constants $b_{1},b_{2}>0$ so that

$$ \lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}\left(s\right)\geq b_{1}\lambda_{\operatorname{rat}_{d},v}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right)-b_{2}. $$

where again $b_{2}=0$ for all sufficiently large residue characteristics, which after increasing $N^{\prime}$ we may assume it holds for all residue characteristics $\geq N^{\prime}$ .

Case 1: We have

$$ \sum_{v\in M_{K}^{\prime}}n_{v}\lambda_{\operatorname{rat}_{d},v}\left(f\right)\geq\frac{1}{2}h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right). $$

Now assume that $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right)\geq 6N^{\prime}h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(g\right)$ . Then if $S$ is the subset of places of $M_{K}^{\prime}$ so that

$$ \lambda_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(\langle f\rangle)\geq N^{\prime}\lambda_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d},v}(g)\text{ and }\lambda_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(\langle f\rangle)\geq\delta\lambda_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(f). $$

Then

$$ \sum_{v\in M_{K}^{\prime}\setminus S}n_{v}\lambda_{\operatorname{rat}_{d},v}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right)\leq N^{\prime}\sum_{v\in M_{K}}n_{v}\lambda_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d},v}\left(g\right)+\frac{1}{100b}\sum_{v\in M_{K}}n_{v}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right) $$

$$ \leq N^{\prime}h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(g\right)+\frac{1}{100b}h_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right)\leq\frac{1}{3}h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right). $$

Hence we must have

$$ \sum_{v\in S}n_{v}\lambda_{\operatorname{rat}_{d},v}\left(f\right)\geq\frac{1}{6}h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right). $$

We now apply Proposition 6.6 to obtain

$$ \sum_{v\in S}n_{v}\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,v}\geq c^{\prime}\sum_{v\in S}n_{v}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}\left(s\right)\geq\frac{c^{\prime}b_{1}}{6}h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right) $$

which proves what we want.

Case 2: Let $T=M_{K^{\prime}}\setminus M_{K}$ . We have

$$ \sum_{v\in T}n_{v}\lambda_{\operatorname{rat}_{d},v}\left(f\right)\geq\frac{1}{2}h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right). $$

Again let $S$ be the subset of places of $M_{K}^{\prime}$ so that

$$ \lambda_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(\langle f\rangle)\geq N\lambda_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d},v}(g)\text{ and }\lambda_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(\langle f\rangle)\geq\delta\lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}(s). $$

Then similarly if $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right)\geq 6N^{\prime}h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(g\right)$ , we have

$$ \sum_{v\in S}n_{v}\lambda_{\operatorname{rat}_{d},v}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right)\geq\frac{1}{6}h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right). $$

Hence we have

$$ \sum_{v\in S}n_{v}\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}\left(s\right)\geq\frac{b_{1}}{6}h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right)-b_{2}\sum_{v\in T}n_{v}=\frac{b_{1}}{6}h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right)-B_{2} $$

where $B_{2}=b_{2}\sum_{v\in T}n_{v}$ depends only on $\left(d,d_{1},d_{2},M,A\right)$ . We then apply Proposition 6.5, removing the condition $\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}\left(s\right)\geq N^{\prime}$ and replacing the lower bound $c\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}\left(s\right)$ with $c\left(\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}\left(s\right)-N^{\prime}\right)$ , we obtain

$$ \sum_{v\in S}n_{v}\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,v}\geq c\left(\frac{b_{1}}{6}h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right)-B_{2}-N^{\prime}\sum_{v\in T}n_{v}\right). $$

Again $N^{\prime}\sum_{v\in T}n_{v}$ is some constant depending only on $\left(d,d_{1},d_{2},M,A\right)$ and so if $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right)$ is large enough, Proposition 7.6 follows as desired. ∎

Combining Propositions 7.4 and 7.6, we obtain Theorem 7.2 for $\left(f,g,C\right)$ with the quantity $\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right),h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(g\right),h_{C_{d_{1},d_{2}}}\left(C\right)\right\}$ being sufficiently large.

#### Proposition 7.7.

Let $\left(f,g\right)$ be two rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$ defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Let $C\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{2}$ be a degree $\left(d_{1},d_{2}\right)$ -curve defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ which is not weakly $\left(f,g\right)$ -special. Assume that there is a $A>0$ so that

$$ Ah_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right)\geq\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right),1\right\} $$

and similarly for $g$ . Then there exists $c,N>0$ depending only on $\left(d,d_{1},d_{2},A\right)$ so that if

$$ \max\left\{h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right),h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(g\right),h_{C_{d_{1},d_{2}}}\left(C\right)\right\}\geq N. $$

then

$$ \widehat{h}_{\left(f,g\right)}\left(C\right)\geq c\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right),h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(g\right)\right\}. $$

#### Proof.

If both $f$ and $g$ are Lattès, it follows directly from the case of uniform Bogomolov for curves in $E_{1}\times E_{2}$ by using either Kuhne’s relative Bogomolov for fibered powers of elliptic curves [59] or Gao–Ge–Kuhne’s height gap principle [41]. Hence we may assume that not both $f$ and $g$ are Lattès.

By symmetry, we may assume that $h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)\geq h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(g\right)$ . By (7.2), we may assume there exists $M^{\prime}=M^{\prime}\left(d,d_{1},d_{2},d,A\right)>0$ so that

$$ h_{C_{d_{1},d_{2}}}\left(C\right)\leq M^{\prime}\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right),1\right\} $$

Let $N_{1}$ be a constant for $N$ in Proposition 7.6. Then if $f$ is Lattès and $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(\langle f\rangle)\geq N_{1}\max\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(g),1\}$ , we are done. Hence we may assume either $f$ is non-Lattès, or $f$ is Lattès but

$$ N_{1}A\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(g\right),1\right\}\geq Ah_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right)\geq h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right). $$

If $f$ is non-Lattès, then the triplet $\left(f,g,C\right)$ satisfies the conditions of Proposition 7.4 with $M_{1}=M^{\prime}$ and $M_{2}=A$ . Then if $h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)$ is sufficiently large, we are done. In the other case, we have $N_{1}\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle g\right\rangle\right),1\right\}\geq h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right).$ and $g$ is non-Lattès. Then the triplet $\left(g,f,C\right)$ satisfies Proposition 7.4 with $M_{1}=M^{\prime}N_{1}A,M_{2}=N_{1}A$ .Hence if $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(g\right)$ is sufficiently large, we are done. By (7.8), this is implied by $h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)$ being sufficiently large, concluding the proof of our Proposition.

∎

We now handle the case where $\left(f,g,C\right)$ are of bounded height. In this case, we will use the archimiedean analogue of our rigidity result, which was proven by Mavraki–Schmidt [68, Theorem 1.10].

#### Theorem 7.8.

Let $f,g\in\mathbb{C}\left(z\right)$ be two rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$ . Let $C\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{2}$ be an irreducible complex algebraic curve which projects dominantly to both coordinates. If $\left(\deg\pi_{2}\right)\pi_{1}^{*}\mu_{f}=\left(\deg\pi_{1}\right)\pi_{2}^{*}\mu_{g}$ , then $C$ is weakly $\left(f,g\right)$ -special.

For our subvariety $Z_{k}\subseteq\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times C_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ , we let $W_{k}$ be the closed subvariety cutting out triplets $\left(f,g,C\right)$ such that either $f$ and $g$ are both Lattès maps, or where each $f$ and $g$ are conjugate to either a power or Chebyshev map. If $s=\left(f,g,C\right)\in Z_{k}\setminus W_{k}$ , then $C$ is weakly $\left(f,g\right)$ -special if and only if $C$ is preperiodic for $\left(f,g\right)$ .

#### Proposition 7.9.

Let $\left(f,g\right)$ be two rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$ defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ and $C\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{2}$ an irreducible degree $\left(d_{1},d_{2}\right)$ -curve. Let $N>0$ be a constant such that

$$ \max\left\{h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right),h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(g\right),h_{C_{d_{1},d_{2}}}\left(C\right)\right\}\leq N. $$

Assume that the pair $\left(f,g\right)$ are not both Lattès maps, and that at least one of them is not conjugate to either a monomial or a Chebyshev map. Then there exists $\delta=\delta\left(d,d_{1},d_{2},N\right)>0$ such that if $C$ is not weakly $\left(f,g\right)$ -special, then

$$ \widehat{h}_{\left(f,g\right)}\left(C\right)\geq\delta. $$

#### Proof.

Let $s=\left(f,g,C\right)$ lie on $Z_{k}\left(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\right)$ satisfying the hypothesis of our Proposition. Then by assumption, $s\in\left(Z_{k}\setminus W_{k}\right)\left(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\right)$ and $s\in\left(Z_{k}\setminus V_{i}\right)\left(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\right)$ for all $i\geq 1$ . Let

$$ h_{X}\left(s\right)=h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)+h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(g\right)+h_{C_{d_{1},d_{2}}}\left(C\right)+1 $$

so that $h_{X}$ is an ample height on $X=\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times\operatorname{Rat}_{d}\times C_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ and $h_{X}\left(s\right)\leq 3N+1\leq 4N$ as we may assume $N\geq 1$ . Then there are positive constants $a_{1},a_{2},\ldots$ so that

$$ h_{V_{i}}\left(s\right)\leq a_{i}h_{X}\left(s\right) $$

for all $s\in\left(Z_{k}\setminus V_{i}\right)\left(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\right)$ . We let $b_{1},b_{2}$ be positive constants $h_{\partial Z_{k}}\left(s\right)\leq b_{1}h_{X}\left(s\right)\text{ and }h_{W_{k}}\left(s\right)\leq b_{2}h_{X}\left(s\right).$ Now on $Z_{k}\left(\mathbb{C}\right)$ , consider the subset $D_{k}\subseteq Z_{k}\left(\mathbb{C}\right)$ consisting of points $s$ satisfying

$$ \lambda_{\partial Z_{k}}(s)\leq 300N{b_{1}},\lambda_{W_{k}}(s)\leq 300N{b_{2}},\lambda_{V_{i}}(s)\leq 10^{i}(4N){a_{i}} $$

where we use the local height functions over $\mathbb{C}$ . Then $D_{k}$ is a closed subset of $\overline{Z_{k}}\left(\mathbb{C}\right)$ for some compactification of $\overline{Z_{k}}$ and hence a compact subset of $Z_{k}\left(\mathbb{C}\right)$ since it has empty intersection with the boundary. Furthermore, our function $\left\langle\,,\,\right\rangle$ is strictly positive on $D_{k}$ and hence there exists a $c>0$ such that

$$ \left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C}\geq c>0 $$

for all $s=\left(f,g,C\right)\in D_{k}$ . Now let $K$ be a number field for which $\left(f,g,C\right)$ is defined over and let $T$ be the archimedean places of $K$ . Let $S\subseteq T$ be the subset of places for which $s\in D_{k}$ when embedded via $v\in S$ into $Z_{k}\left(\mathbb{C}\right)$ . We claim that

$$ \sum_{v\in S}n_{v}\geq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{v\in T}n_{v}=\frac{1}{2}. $$

To estimate this, for $i\geq 1$ let $T_{i}$ be the subset of $T$ so that

$$ {\lambda_{V_{i},v}}(s)\geq 10^{i}(4N){a_{i}} $$

and let $T_{0}$ be the subset so that $\lambda_{\partial Z_{k},v}(s)\geq 300N{b_{1}}$ and $T_{0}^{\prime}$ the subset so that ${\lambda_{W_{k},v}}(s)\geq 300N{b_{2}}.$ For $i\geq 1$ , we have

$$ 10^{i}(4N){a_{i}}\sum_{v\in T_{i}}n_{v}\leq\sum_{v\in T_{i}}n_{v}{\lambda_{V_{i},v}}(s)\leq{h_{V_{i}}}(s)\leq a_{i}h_{X}(s)\leq 4Na_{i} $$

and so

$$ \sum_{v\in T_{i}}n_{v}\leq\frac{1}{10^{i}}. $$

Similarly, we obtain that

$$ \sum_{v\in T_{0}}n_{v},\sum_{v\in T_{0}^{\prime}}n_{v}\leq\frac{{4}}{300}. $$

As $S$ contains the complement of $T_{0},T_{0}^{\prime}$ and $\cup_{i\geq 1}T_{i}$ in $T$ , we thus have

$$ \sum_{v\in S}n_{v}\geq\sum_{v\in T}n_{v}-\frac{{8}}{300}-\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{10^{i}}\geq\frac{1}{2} $$

since $\sum_{v\in T}n_{v}=1$ . Now for each $v\in S$ , we have

$$ \left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,v}\geq c $$

and so

$$ \sum_{v\in S}n_{v}\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{C,v}\geq\frac{1}{2}c $$

which gives us our uniform $\delta{{}=c/[2d_{1}d_{2}(d_{1}+d_{2})]}$ as desired. ∎

We now conclude the proof of Theorem 7.2.

#### Proof of Theorem 7.2.

As explained in our reductions at the start of the section, we may assume that $A\max\left\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}\left(\left\langle f\right\rangle\right),1\right\}\geq h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right)$ and similarly for $g$ for some $A>0$ depending only on $d$ . Then Proposition 7.7 implies that we are done unless $h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(f\right),h_{\operatorname{Rat}_{d}}\left(g\right),h_{C_{d_{1},d_{2}}}\left(C\right)$ have height bounded above by some $N=N\left(d,d_{1},d_{2}\right)>0$ . If $\left(f,g\right)$ are not both Lattès map, and at least one of them is not conjugate to a monomial or Chebyshev map, then Proposition 7.9 implies that we are done in the bounded height case. Finally if both $\left(f,g\right)$ are Lattès map, then we can conclude by uniform Bogomolov for products of elliptic curves by using Gao–Ge–Kuhne’s [41] height gap principle, or by Kuhne’s relative Bogomolov for fibered powers of elliptic curves [59]. Here, one should note that $\max\{h_{\operatorname{rat}_{d}}(f),1\}$ is comparable to $\{h_{\mathrm{Fal}}(E),1\}$ if $E$ is the elliptic curve that the Lattès map $f$ comes from. If both $\left(f,g\right)$ are conjugate to either the monomial or Chebyshev map, then we can instead conclude by the uniform Bogomolov conjecture for $\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}$ due to Bombieri–Zannier[8]. ∎

We can now deduce Theorem 1.2. Applying Theorem 2.1 to Theorem 7.2, it suffices to handle the weakly $\left(f,g\right)$ -special curves, in which case it is easy to see that Theorem 1.2 holds. We hence conclude Theorem 1.2.

## 8. Higher Dimensional Subvarieties

The main results of this section are the hypersurface height gap in Theorem 1.5 and uniform dynamical Manin–Mumford over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ in Corollary 8.8.

We now consider the general case of subvarieties $V\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ where $\Phi=\left(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\right)$ is a split endomorphism of $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ with $\deg f_{i}=d\geq 2$ . For the height gap for hypersurfaces, we assume only that at least one $f_{i}$ is non-exceptional. For uniform dynamical Manin–Mumford for arbitrary subvarieties, we assume that at most one $f_{i}$ is exceptional.

We say that a subvariety $V\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ is weakly $\Phi$ -special if either of the following occurs:

- (1) $V$ does not projects dominantly to all coordinates;

- (2) $V$ is preperiodic;

- (3) $V$ is of the form $\pi^{-1}\left(W\right)$ where $\pi:\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}\to\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n-1}$ is a projection away from one of the coordinates.

We will prove the following height gap principle for hypersurfaces $H\subseteq\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ that are not weakly $\Phi$ -special.

#### Theorem 8.1.

Let $\Phi=\left(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\right)$ be a split endomorphism of $\left(\mathbb{P}^{1}\right)^{n}$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ such that $\deg f_{i}=d\geq 2$ and each $f_{i}$ is non-exceptional.
